# 🗺 Ohio Pre-Statehood Locality Guide
## Northwest Territory Era · c. 1780–1803

---

## Jurisdictional Context

In 1790, present-day Ohio existed entirely within the **Northwest Territory**, organized under the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio was the first state carved from it, admitted March 1, 1803.

Only **two counties** had been organized by 1790:

| County | Organized | Area Covered | Seat |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Washington County** | 1788 | Most of present-day Ohio (east and central) | Marietta |
| **Hamilton County** | 1790 | Southwestern Ohio | Cincinnati |

Everything else in 1790 was **unorganized territory** — no county courthouse, no local records of any kind. Additional counties organized within the period:
- **Wayne County** (1795) — northwestern Ohio
- **Jefferson County** (1797) — eastern Ohio

In 1800 the territory was split: the western portion became **Indiana Territory**; the Ohio portion continued to statehood in 1803.

**The critical research rule:** Before searching any record type, determine which county (if any) held jurisdiction over the specific locality at the *date of the event*. Before 1795, nearly all civil activity flowed through Washington or Hamilton counties. Events outside those two counties left no county-level paper trail — only territorial government records survive, held today at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)*

---

## Three Land Systems — A Permanent Geographic Split

Ohio's territory is permanently divided among three land systems with separate survey methods and completely different repositories. This is **not** a temporal split (before/after a date) — all three coexisted simultaneously in the 1790s. Which applies to your ancestor depends entirely on *where* in Ohio they lived.

| District | Location | Survey Method | Primary Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers (south-central Ohio) | Metes and bounds | Virginia State Library, Richmond (warrants); county deed books (recorded deeds) |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Township grid (Connecticut Land Co.) | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **Federal Townships** (Ohio Company, Symmes Purchase, U.S. Military District, etc.) | The remainder | Rectangular survey | BLM General Land Office — glorecords.blm.gov (free online) |

**Quirk:** The Virginia Military District creates a geographic split, not a temporal one. If your ancestor lived between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, you must search *both* the Virginia State Library (original warrant) and the local county deed book (recorded deed) — they are complementary records, not alternatives. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)*

Determine which district applies before searching land records. Searching the wrong repository is the most common early Ohio research dead end.

---

## Vital Records — No Civil Registration Exists for This Period

Ohio enacted **statewide civil vital registration in 1867** — more than 75 years after the target date. There are **no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates** for 1790 at any level. This is the most significant gap in pre-statehood Ohio research.

**Substitutes for vital events:**
- County marriage bonds/registers — Washington County begins **1789**; Hamilton County ~1790; no records outside organized counties
- Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials)
- Tombstone inscriptions / cemetery transcriptions
- Bible records
- Estate inventories naming heirs
- Early newspaper notices (extremely rare before 1800 in Ohio)

---

## Available Record Types and Access

### 🟢 Land Records — Best primary source for this period

Federal land sales were documented regardless of county organization, making this the most reliable record class in 1790 Ohio.

- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840"** (ID 1542187) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187
- **FamilySearch volume — Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799** (imageGroup 005112233) — 51 images. **Access: browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image-by-image with no search capability.
- **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) — Free online search of federal land patents; covers the federal township districts only
- Virginia Military District warrants → **Virginia State Library**, Richmond — physical only, not confirmed digitized on FamilySearch
- Connecticut Western Reserve records → **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland — physical only

---

### 🟢 Marriage Records — The earliest county-level civil records in Ohio

- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"** (ID 1803785) — 1,523,678 records, 761,839 images
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785
- Washington County marriage records begin **1789** — the earliest in Ohio
- Hamilton County begins ~1790
- Marriages outside these two organized counties before 1795 have **no civil record** — church registers are the only alternative

---

### 🟢 Church Records — Often the only vital evidence for 1790

- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"** (ID 2246917) — 678,234 records, 339,117 images
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917
- Key denominations active in 1790 Ohio:
  - **Moravian Missions** (Schoenbrunn, Gnadenhutten, Salem) — among the earliest records in the entire region, predating American settlement; originals at **Moravian Archives, Bethlehem, PA**; some records published
  - **Methodist circuit riders** — records held at denominational archives
  - **Presbyterian** — session records at local congregations or **Presbyterian Historical Society**, Philadelphia
- For families outside Washington and Hamilton counties before 1795, church records may be the *only* surviving documentation of births, marriages, and deaths

---

### 🟢 Military Records — High-value for this exact time window

The **Northwest Indian Wars (1790–1795)** make military records especially significant for this period. Pension files also document Revolutionary War veterans who migrated to Ohio.

- **NARA** (archives.gov): Revolutionary War pension files, bounty land warrants, and service records for the Indian Wars campaigns — free to request; many indexed on Fold3
- **Fold3** (fold3.com): Military pensions and NARA-indexed service records — subscription required
- **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus: Territorial militia records
- Survivors and casualties of St. Clair's Defeat (1791) and the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) are named in NARA pension and service records

---

### 🟡 Tax Records — Begins 1800; limited coverage before that

- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (ID 1987542) — 345,890 records, 172,945 images: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542
  **Note:** Starts 1800 — after the 1790 target year.
- **FamilySearch volume — Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803** (imageGroup 005112240) — 73 images. **Access: mostly browse-only** — only 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Covers Washington County only.
- Pre-1800 territorial tax records (if extant) → **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus — not confirmed digitized on FamilySearch

---

### 🟡 Census Records — Minimal for 1790

- The **1790 U.S. Federal Census did not cover the Northwest Territory** in its standard enumeration. Do not expect to find Ohio ancestors in the 1790 census.
- The **1800 U.S. Federal Census** is the first reliable federal enumeration for Ohio — available on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- Early territorial enumeration lists (if any) may exist at the **Ohio History Connection** — gap: no confirmed online access

---

### 🟡 Probate Records — Washington and Hamilton counties only

- Probate jurisdiction existed only in organized county courts — before 1795 that means Washington and Hamilton counties exclusively
- Records held at county courthouses and the **Ohio History Connection**
- FamilySearch microfilm coverage for this early period is not confirmed in the surveyed volumes — treat as physical/microfilm only pending direct verification

---

### 🔴 Death Records — Not available for this period

- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001"** (ID 1417891) begins in 1840 — entirely outside this period
- No civil death registration exists for 1790. Use cemetery transcriptions, church burial registers, and estate inventories as substitutes

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus | Territorial court records, early county records, pre-statehood tax records, militia records | Physical; some digitized |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free online |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Military service records, pension files | Physical + Fold3 online |
| **Virginia State Library**, Richmond | Virginia Military District warrants | Physical only |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | Physical only |
| **Moravian Archives**, Bethlehem, PA | Moravian mission registers (pre-1790 and early settlement) | Physical; some published |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | County marriages (1789+), church records, land records, limited territorial records | Free online |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military pensions, NARA-sourced records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** (ancestry.com) | 1800+ U.S. federal census, some land records | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free online |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers (very sparse before 1803 in Ohio) | Subscription |

---

## Boundary Change & Documentation Quirks — Summary

1. **In 1790, only two counties existed.** Any event outside Washington or Hamilton counties has no county-level record. Go directly to territorial government records at the Ohio History Connection.
2. **County jurisdiction at event date drives which courthouse to search.** Boundary changes were frequent 1788–1820 — always verify the specific date before picking a courthouse.
3. **Three land systems, three repositories.** Resolve which district applies to your ancestor's locality before searching land records; the repositories do not overlap.
4. **Virginia Military District is a geographic split.** Ancestors in the Scioto–Little Miami corridor require searches in both Virginia (warrants) and the Ohio county deed book (recorded deeds) — not one or the other.
5. **The 1790 census does not cover Ohio.** Begin federal census research with 1800.
6. **No civil vital registration until 1867.** Church records and the Washington/Hamilton county marriage registers are the only direct vital record substitutes for 1790.

---

## Coverage Notes

- All four FamilySearch Wiki place-page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned generic fallback content rather than Ohio-specific pages via the API — consult the Ohio Genealogy article directly: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory
- The FamilySearch curated external links for the 1780–1810 window returned six general repository links rather than Ohio-specific curated collections — this is a gap in FS's curated link coverage for early Ohio.
- Population data was not returned for this period — consistent with the extremely sparse settlement of the Northwest Territory in 1790 (Marietta founded 1788, Cincinnati 1788–1789).

---

To summarize for your 1790 Ohio research: **land records and military records are your best-documented sources** for this exact period, followed by county marriage registers (Washington County from 1789) and church records. The 1790 census is a dead end for Ohio; start at 1800. Always resolve which county (if any) held jurisdiction at your event date — and for land records, resolve which of the three distinct land districts applies before choosing a repository.

# 📋 Locality Research Guide: California, 1848–1870 (Gold Rush Era)

**Jurisdiction:** California, United States  
**Period of focus:** 1848–1870 (Gold Rush epicentre: 1848–1855)  
**Research context:** Migration, mining, and early settlement

---

## Jurisdictional Background

**Two administrative eras divide this period — records follow that split:**

| Period | Status | Record authority |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 1848 – Sep 9, 1850 | US territory (Military governance) | Federal military / no organized county courts |
| Sep 9, 1850 onward | State of California (31st state) | County governments + state legislature |

Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in January 1848. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 1848) transferred California from Mexico to the US. Civil infrastructure was almost entirely absent until statehood in September 1850. The first federal census of California was taken in 1850 — **but several county returns were lost**, making the 1852 California state census essential.

County governments created most records from 1850 onward. Statewide vital registration (births and deaths) did not begin until the early 1900s, so **county-level records are the primary source throughout this entire period.**

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. Federal Census (1850, 1860, 1870)
**Access: Indexed + images**

The 1850 and 1860 federal censuses cover California but the 1850 return is **partially lost** — returns for several gold-country counties are missing. FamilySearch's collection ["California, County Births, 1850–1919"](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) (789,456 records, 394,728 images) is the county civil-registration companion.

- The 1860 and 1870 censuses are intact and name-indexed. Mortality schedules (recording deaths in the year before enumeration) accompany each; search them for early deaths not recorded elsewhere.
- Non-population schedules (agriculture, manufacturing) can reveal a miner's economic status.

### 2. California State Census, 1852
**Access: Indexed + images + full-text searchable** *(88% name-indexed, full-text searchable — imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images)*

This is the single most important source for the early Gold Rush population. Taken between the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses, it survives for most counties and names heads of household plus all residents. Because many 1850 federal returns are lost, the 1852 state census is often the **only census record** placing a miner in California in this period.

### 3. County Birth and Marriage Records
**Access: Indexed + images**

- **Births:** ["California, County Births, 1850–1919"](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) — 789,456 records, 394,728 images. County registration began in 1850 but early coverage is thin; compliance improved through the decade.
- **Marriages:** ["California, County Marriages, 1850–1952"](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) — 567,890 records (1,135,780 persons named), 283,945 images. Both spouses are usually named.

Death records at the county level are sparse before statewide registration — check church records and the federal mortality schedules as substitutes.

### 4. Mining Claim Registers
**Access: Browse-only images** *(0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images)*

Mining claim registers for San Francisco, 1849–1855 are digitized but must be browsed image by image — there is no name search. These are held at county recorders' offices; the FamilySearch Wiki notes that county courthouse originals remain the primary access point for counties beyond San Francisco. ([California Genealogy — Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))

### 5. Great Registers (Voter Registration), 1866–1910
**Access: Indexed + images**

["California, Great Registers, 1866–1910"](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340) — 1,345,678 records, 672,839 images. These are annual voter registration rolls listing name, age, occupation, physical description, birthplace, and county of residence. They begin in 1866, outside the core Gold Rush years, but they are invaluable for men who **stayed** in California after the rush — they function as a population snapshot across the late 1860s and beyond.

### 6. Port Arrival Registers / Ship Passenger Lists
**Access: Browse-only images** *(0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images)*

Port arrival registers for Sacramento, 1849–1858 are digitized but must be browsed without a name index. The FamilySearch Wiki identifies ship passenger manifests at San Francisco as a key Gold Rush source, held at **NARA's San Bruno (Pacific Region) facility**. ([California Genealogy — Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)) Overland migrants left no equivalent port record; trail diaries and journals at the California State Library and Bancroft Library partially fill that gap.

### 7. Land Records
**Access: Varies — BLM GLO online; county deeds physical or microfilmed**

California is a federal land state. Land patents issued by the US General Land Office are searchable at the [BLM GLO website](https://glorecords.blm.gov/). Deed books (recording sales and transfers between private parties) are held at county courthouses; many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. The `volume_search` returned 14 volumes total for California in this period — only the first page was retrieved here, so additional land-record volumes likely appear on subsequent pages.

### 8. Court, Probate, and Naturalization Records
**Access: Largely physical or microfilmed; some digitized**

County superior courts held naturalization proceedings (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record). Probate files (wills, estate inventories, guardianship papers) are at county courthouses. Both record types are central for miners who died in California or acquired property.

### 9. Church Records
**Access: Varies — some digitized, many physical**

Catholic parish registers are the most common for this era given Spanish and Mexican settlement patterns. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that denominational archives and local parish records are the primary repositories. Many have been microfilmed.

### 10. Mission Records, 1769–1850 (Background Context)
**Access: Indexed + images**

["California, Mission Records, 1769–1850"](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372) — 98,765 records, 49,382 images. These baptism, marriage, and burial registers maintained by Franciscan friars cover the pre-Gold Rush California population (Native Californians, Spanish/Mexican settlers). Relevant only as background context for families already in California before 1848 — not a source for Gold Rush migrants arriving after that date.

### 11. Military Records
**Access: NARA (national); Fold3 (subscription)**

Service records, pension files, and bounty-land warrants for men who served in the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) immediately before the Gold Rush are at NARA and digitized on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/). Some Gold Rush arrivals came west with military units; pension files can document post-service migration.

### 12. Newspapers
**Access: Digitized (subscription)**

[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) holds California newspapers from this period. Mining camp papers covered local population movements, deaths, and business transactions in ways no official record does. The California State Library also holds a strong newspaper collection.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch.org** | County births, marriages, state census 1852, mission records, Great Registers — all searchable online |
| **NARA San Bruno (Pacific Region)** | Ship passenger lists for San Francisco; federal court records |
| **California State Archives** (Sacramento) | State-level records, legislative files, early court records |
| **California State Library** (Sacramento) | Manuscript collections, diaries, newspapers, overland trail records |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | The premier Gold Rush manuscript collection — diaries, letters, maps |
| **County Courthouses** | Deed books, probate files, naturalization records, mining claim registers |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents — free and searchable online at glorecords.blm.gov |

---

## Critical Quirks and Warnings

- **The 1850 federal census is partially lost.** Several gold-country county returns did not survive. Always pair it with the **1852 California state census** (88% indexed on FamilySearch), which often names the same population.
- **County registration began in 1850, but statewide vital registration did not start until the early 1900s.** For deaths especially, county coverage in the 1850s is thin — check church registers and federal mortality schedules.
- **Mining claim registers and port arrival registers on FamilySearch are browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Budget time for image-by-image searching unless you know the county or approximate date.
- **Great Registers begin in 1866** — they do not cover the core Gold Rush years but are excellent for men who settled permanently.
- **Pre-statehood arrivals (1848–September 1850) left almost no civil records.** Rely on ship manifests (at NARA San Bruno for sea arrivals), trail diaries and journals (Bancroft Library, California State Library), and military records for this window.
- **The volume_search returned 3 of 14 total volumes** for this period. Additional digitized volumes (likely additional county-level record types) were not retrieved in this survey — search FamilySearch's catalog directly for the specific county of interest to find them.
- **FamilySearch's California Wiki pages** (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only a generic fallback rather than California-specific guidance in this session. Consult the page directly: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)

---

## Suggested Search Order

1. **1852 California state census** (FamilySearch, 88% indexed) — best single starting point for the Gold Rush population
2. **1860 and 1870 federal censuses** — for those who stayed; include mortality schedules
3. **County births and marriages** (FamilySearch) — civil registration from 1850
4. **Great Registers 1866–1910** (FamilySearch) — for men present after 1866
5. **Ship passenger lists** (NARA San Bruno / Ancestry) — for sea arrivals at San Francisco
6. **Mining claim registers** (FamilySearch — browse-only) — for documented mining activity
7. **Land patents** (BLM GLO — free online) — for those who acquired land
8. **Bancroft Library and California State Library** — manuscript collections for overland migrants and those leaving no official record

# Locality Research Guide: New York City, Colonial Period (1700–1783)

## Jurisdictional Context

During the 1700s, New York City was the administrative capital of **New York Province**, a British royal colony. The city occupied present-day **Manhattan (New York County)**. The five-borough consolidation did not happen until 1898 — all colonial-era records are filed under **New York County**.

Key date anchors that affect which records exist:
- **1626** — Founded as Dutch New Amsterdam; Dutch-language records begin
- **1664** — English seized the colony, renamed it New York; Dutch Reformed records continued alongside new Anglican ones
- **1776–1783** — British military occupation; record-keeping was disrupted and some records lost or removed
- **1788** — New York ratified the Constitution; became a state

**No statewide or citywide civil vital registration existed during the colonial period.** Church registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are the *only* primary substitute for birth, marriage, and death documentation in this era. Identify the family's denomination before planning your search.

---

## Records Available

### 1. Church Records ⭐ *Prime source for vital events*

Church records are the backbone of colonial NYC research. The FamilySearch Wiki identifies the **Dutch Reformed** (beginning 1639), **Anglican (Trinity Church)**, and **Presbyterian** congregations as the major record-keepers of the 1700s. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **New York, Church Records, 1640–1940** — Collection [1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062). Covers baptisms, marriages, and burials from multiple denominations across the full colonial period.

**FamilySearch digitized volume — browse-only, in Dutch:**
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, 1700–1776** — Image Group 007733180, 211 images. **0% name-indexed. Not full-text searchable. Written in Dutch.** Must be browsed image-by-image; you must be able to read 18th-century Dutch script or use a translator.

**Physical/in-person repositories:**
- **Trinity Church Archives** — holds its own Anglican registers; some have been published or transcribed
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** — transcriptions and indexes of many colonial church records
- **New-York Historical Society** — colonial church record collections

---

### 2. Land Records

**FamilySearch collection:**
- **New York, Land Records, 1630–1975** — Collection [2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654). Covers the full colonial period. Includes deeds, patents, and conveyances.

The FamilySearch Wiki specifically notes land conveyances as a key source class for colonial NYC. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)) Colonial governor's land patents are part of the **New York Colonial Manuscripts** held at the **New York State Archives** in Albany.

---

### 3. Probate Records

**FamilySearch collection:**
- **New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971** — Collection [1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780). Covers the full colonial period.

**Critical finding aid:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that wills proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** — the colonial probate authority — are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the **New-York Historical Society**. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)) Search this series before browsing probate volumes.

---

### 4. Court Records

The FamilySearch Wiki identifies the **Mayor's Court** as the principal colonial-era court for New York City — covering civil suits, criminal cases, and proceedings that regularly name neighbors, witnesses, creditors, and relatives. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

**Repositories:** New York State Archives (Albany) holds the **New York Colonial Manuscripts**. The New-York Historical Society and NYC Municipal Archives also hold court-related records.

---

### 5. Tax Records

The FamilySearch Wiki notes that **tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards** during the colonial period. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))

**FamilySearch collection (post-colonial, but useful for tracing families forward):**
- **New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804** — Collection [1678432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432). Begins just after the colonial era.

Earlier colonial tax records are held physically at the **New York State Archives** and the **New-York Historical Society**.

---

### 6. Militia and Military Records

The FamilySearch Wiki notes that **colonial New York Province militia rolls** list men of military age — a useful record class for identifying residents not found elsewhere. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))

For the **Revolutionary War (1775–1783)**, service records and pension files are at **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) and can be searched on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)).

---

### 7. Newspapers

The Wikipedia article on New York City names the **New York Gazette** as a colonial-era newspaper. Newspapers carried death notices, marriage announcements, legal proceedings, estate sale notices, and runaway servant/slave notices — all naming individuals.

**Access:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) includes historical New York publications.

---

### 8. Cemetery Records

Trinity Church and other colonial-era congregations maintained burial grounds; some inscriptions survive.

**Access:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes NYC-area burial sites including colonial churchyards.

---

## What Does NOT Apply to This Period

| Record | Why it's out of scope |
|---|---|
| **New York, County Marriages, 1847–1849; 1907–1936** (Collection 1920153) | Begins 1847 — does not cover the colonial period at all |
| **Federal Census** | First enumeration is 1790, after the colonial period; also disrupted by British occupation for NYC families |
| **Statewide civil vital registration** | Did not exist; church records are the only substitute |

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) | Church records, land, probate, tax | Free online |
| New York State Archives, Albany | Colonial Manuscripts, court records, land patents | In-person; some online |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society | Church transcriptions, published indexes | Membership / in-person |
| New-York Historical Society | *Abstracts of Wills*, colonial manuscripts, church records | In-person; some online |
| NYC Municipal Archives | City records, some colonial material | In-person |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican registers | Contact archives |
| NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) | Revolutionary War service & pension records | Free online via Fold3/Ancestry |

---

## Research Quirks to Know

1. **Dutch Reformed registers are browse-only and in Dutch.** The digitized FamilySearch volume (1700–1776, image group 007733180) is 0% name-indexed and requires browsing all 211 images in 18th-century Dutch.
2. **No civil vital registration.** Identify your ancestor's denomination first — then locate the congregation's records. If the denomination is unknown, start with the largest (Dutch Reformed, Anglican).
3. **British occupation (1776–1783) created record gaps.** Records from this window may be missing, damaged, or were physically removed. Plan for substitutes (neighbors, church, court) if you hit a wall in this decade.
4. **Colonial wills went through the Prerogative Court, not county court.** Use the New-York Historical Society's *Abstracts of Wills* as your finding aid before searching volumes.
5. **"New York County" is the correct filing jurisdiction.** Borough names (Manhattan, Bronx, etc.) did not exist in the 1700s — always search under New York County.
6. **FamilySearch's digitized NYC colonial holdings are sparse.** Only one volume (Dutch Reformed, 1700–1776) appeared in the volume search. The major colonial record bodies — Colonial Manuscripts, Mayor's Court records, early tax lists — are held physically at the State Archives, NYGBS, and New-York Historical Society, with limited online access.

---

## Suggested Starting Points

1. **Church records first** — determine denomination, then search Collection 1469062 on FamilySearch and check NYGBS for transcriptions.
2. **Probate next** — check the *Abstracts of Wills* index (New-York Historical Society) and Collection 1542780 on FamilySearch.
3. **Land records** — search Collection 2078654 on FamilySearch; follow up with the State Archives for colonial governor's patents.
4. **Court and militia records** — request from the New York State Archives for colonial-era files not yet digitized.
5. **Dutch Reformed browse** — if the family was Dutch Reformed and civil/other records are absent, browse image group 007733180 directly on FamilySearch (be prepared to read Dutch).

# Locality Guide: Virginia — American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)

## Jurisdictional Context

**Standard place:** Virginia, United States  
**Place type:** State | Active from: 1788 (statehood)

Virginia was a British colony from the 1600s and one of the original Thirteen Colonies. It contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony, and the war's decisive battle was fought at Yorktown (1781) on Virginia soil. County-level record-keeping had been in place since the 1630s, making this one of the best-documented early American jurisdictions.

**Two critical boundary warnings for this period:**

- **West Virginia:** Counties now in West Virginia were Virginia counties during the Revolution. WV did not split off until 1863. If your ancestor lived in present-day WV, search *Virginia* records for 1775–1783, then West Virginia repositories for later periods.
- **Kentucky:** What is now Kentucky was Virginia's "Kentucky County" during the Revolution; it did not become a separate state until 1792. Families there during 1775–1783 are in Virginia records.

---

## ⚠️ Most Important Research Warning: The Missing 1790 Census

The 1790 federal census for Virginia was **destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The primary substitute is the **1782–1785 county personal property tax lists**, which function as the nearest household enumeration for the Revolutionary War period. These are covered in FamilySearch Collection 1456723 below and are an essential starting point for any Virginia research in this era. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki,* [Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*)*

---

## Record Types & Collections

### 1. 🎖️ Military Service Records — Continental Army
**What:** Continental Line service records and muster rolls  
**Where:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Record Group 93  
**Online access:** Fold3.com (subscription) and [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)  
**Access level:** Partially digitized; Fold3 is the primary online interface  
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki,* [Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*)*

---

### 2. 🎖️ Virginia Militia Records
**What:** Muster rolls, pay vouchers, and service records for Virginia's state militia units — separate from the Continental Army and often more complete  
**Where:** **Library of Virginia**, Richmond, VA  
**Online access:** Some digitized at lva.virginia.gov; physical research in Richmond for undigitized material  
**Access level:** Physical + partial digital  
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki,* [Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*)*

---

### 3. 🎖️ Pension & Bounty-Land Warrant Files (NARA RG 15) — Highest Genealogical Value
**What:** Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant application files. These are the most genealogically rich military source — widow's applications in particular contain full family narratives, marriage dates, children's names, and sworn depositions from neighbors.  
**Where:** NARA, Record Group 15  
**Online access:** [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription); some records at [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)  
**Access level:** Largely digitized and indexed on Fold3  
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki,* [Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*)*

---

### 4. 🎖️ Virginia State Navy Records
**What:** Records of Virginia's wartime naval force  
**Where:** Library of Virginia, Richmond, VA  
**Access level:** Physical; consult the Library of Virginia directly  
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki,* [Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*)*

---

### 5. 🎖️ Post-War Bounty Land — Virginia Military District of Ohio
Virginia granted bounty lands to its veterans in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** — not within Virginia itself. Warrant and survey records connect veterans to their land claims and often confirm service.  
**Where:** Library of Virginia (warrant records); Ohio State Archives and BLM General Land Office (survey/patent records in Ohio)  
**Note:** If your veteran ancestor disappears from Virginia records after the war, a move to the Ohio Military District is a strong possibility — search both.  
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki,* [Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)*)*

---

### 6. FamilySearch Digitized Collection: Virginia Military Records, 1775–1783
| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Collection ID** | 1945678 |
| **Title** | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 |
| **Date range** | 1775–1783 (exact match to the target period) |
| **Records** | 345,678 (as returned by FamilySearch collections search) |
| **URL** | [familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) |

---

### 7. Tax Records — Census Substitute (1782–1785 critical window)
| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Collection ID** | 1456723 |
| **Title** | Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 |
| **Date range** | 1782–1850 |
| **Records** | 456,789 (as returned by FamilySearch collections search) |
| **URL** | [familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) |

The 1782–1785 personal property tax lists are **the** substitute enumeration for the destroyed 1790 census. They name heads of household by county and are among the first documentary evidence of many Virginia families immediately following the war.

---

### 8. Land & Probate Records
Land was tightly linked to military service — veterans received grants, and land transactions document family movements before and after the war. Probate records document soldiers who died during service and the estates left to their families.

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Collection ID** | 1734285 |
| **Title** | Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 |
| **Date range** | 1600–1900 |
| **Records** | 2,567,890 (as returned by FamilySearch collections search) |
| **URL** | [familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) |

**Note:** Virginia is a **state-land state** (not a federal-land state). County deed books — held at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia — are the primary land record source, not the BLM General Land Office.

---

### 9. County Court Records
County courts during the war handled oaths of allegiance, requisitioning of supplies, estate settlements of soldiers who died in service, and guardianships for orphans of war dead. These are rich wartime civilian records.

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Collection ID** | 2134567 |
| **Title** | Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 |
| **Date range** | 1650–1920 |
| **Records** | 1,789,012 (as returned by FamilySearch collections search) |
| **URL** | [familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) |

---

### 10. Church Records — Primary Vital Records Source for This Period
Virginia had **no statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775–1783. The Anglican (later Episcopal) parish vestry books are the primary vital records source — but the disestablishment of the Church of England during and after the Revolution (formalized 1786) disrupted vestry record-keeping. Non-Anglican registers (Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Quaker) and county marriage bonds fill many gaps.

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Collection ID** | 1598230 |
| **Title** | Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 |
| **Date range** | 1680–1929 |
| **Records** | 1,234,567 (as returned by FamilySearch collections search) |
| **URL** | [familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) |

---

### 11. Historical Newspapers
Wartime newspapers carried military appointments, casualty lists, proclamations, and estate notices — useful for placing an ancestor in a unit or confirming death in service.  
- **Newspapers.com:** [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) *(returned by external links search; subscription)*

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives (NARA)** — DC & College Park, MD | Continental Army service records (RG 93), pension & bounty-land files (RG 15) | In person; many records on Fold3.com |
| **Library of Virginia** — Richmond, VA | Virginia militia records, State Navy records, county deed books, colonial records | In person + partial digital at lva.virginia.gov |
| **FamilySearch** | Collections 1945678, 1456723, 1734285, 2134567, 1598230 (above) | Free at familysearch.org |
| **Fold3.com** | NARA-sourced military records, pension files | Subscription: [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census and Virginia record collections | Subscription: [ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/) |
| **Find A Grave** | Burial and cemetery records | Free: [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| **archives.gov (NARA)** | Catalog and some digitized military records | Free: [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |

---

## Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Missing 1790 census:** Use the 1782–1785 county personal property tax lists (FamilySearch Collection 1456723) as the substitute — this is non-negotiable for Revolutionary-era Virginia research.
2. **West Virginia split (1863):** Ancestors in present-day WV counties are in Virginia records for 1775–1783. Search Virginia repositories first, WV repositories only for post-1863 records.
3. **Kentucky was Virginia (until 1792):** Families in present-day KY were Virginians during the Revolution — their wartime records are Virginia records.
4. **No civil vital registration in this period:** Virginia statewide vital registration did not begin until 1853 at the state level. For 1775–1783, church registers, county marriage bonds/registers, and vestry books are the only vital record sources.
5. **Anglican disestablishment disrupts vestry records:** Church of England disestablishment (formalized 1786) caused gaps in vestry registers during and immediately after the war. Seek non-Anglican registers and county court marriage bonds for this window.
6. **Bounty land is in Ohio, not Virginia:** Virginia Military District bounty land warrants take the research trail into Ohio — search both the Library of Virginia and Ohio repositories for veterans who claimed land.

---

## Recommended Research Path

1. **Pension files first (NARA RG 15 / Fold3)** — widow's applications are the most genealogically detailed source in the entire Revolutionary War record universe.
2. **FamilySearch Collection 1945678** — search muster rolls and service records covering exactly 1775–1783.
3. **1782–1785 tax lists** (Collection 1456723) — place the household in a county at war's end and identify neighbors for cluster research.
4. **County court records** (Collection 2134567) — oaths, estate settlements, guardianships, and supply requisitions all document wartime civilian life.
5. **Church registers** (Collection 1598230) — vital events for the ancestor's parish and denomination.
6. **Virginia Military District of Ohio** — if the veteran disappears from Virginia after the war, follow the bounty land trail into Ohio.
7. **Library of Virginia (Richmond)** — contact directly for militia and State Navy records not yet digitized.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (c. 1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **City founded:** 1718 by France; New Orleans is coterminous with **Orleans Parish**
- **Sovereign succession:**
  - French colony, 1718–1769
  - Spanish colony, 1769–1803 (effective Spanish administration from 1769)
  - Briefly returned to France, 1800–1803 (largely administrative)
  - United States after the **Louisiana Purchase, 1803**
  - **Orleans Territory**, 1804–1812
  - **State of Louisiana**, 1812 to present
- **Legal system:** Louisiana operates under the **Napoleonic Code (civil law)**, not the English common law that governs every other U.S. state. This fundamentally shapes what records exist and how they are organized.
- **Parish, not county:** Louisiana uses parishes rather than counties. Orleans Parish is the civil jurisdiction for New Orleans.
- **Population:** Population data for the 1800–1850 period was not returned by the FamilySearch place tool for this locality.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic and Gulf port, plantation agriculture, slave trade, river commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, enslaved African and free people of color (gens de couleur libres), Anglo-American immigrants post-1803, German, Irish, and other immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral dates to 1718); small Protestant communities grew after American annexation.
- **Language of records:** French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), English (post-1803) — though French remained in everyday use well into the 1800s. Researchers must be prepared to read records in all three languages.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **1763:** Transferred from France to Spain.
- **1800–1803:** Retrocession to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso), though Spanish administration continued in practice through 1803.
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase; New Orleans and Orleans Parish pass to the United States.
- **1804:** Orleans Territory created from the southern portion of the Louisiana Purchase.
- **1812:** Louisiana admitted to statehood. Orleans Parish boundaries are stable through the early 1800s. No significant boundary split affects which jurisdiction holds records during this period.

---

## Known Record Losses — Disasters

This is the central challenge for New Orleans research in the early 1800s. Three events caused the most damage:

### 1. Great New Orleans Fire — March 21, 1788
Destroyed approximately 856 buildings in the French Quarter, including civil records, church documents, and private papers from the French colonial period. Many sacramental registers predating 1788 were lost or damaged. ([FamilySearch Wiki: New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

### 2. Great New Orleans Fire — December 8, 1794
A second catastrophic fire destroyed much of what had been rebuilt. Further records were lost.

### 3. Recurring Flooding, Hurricanes, and Yellow Fever Epidemics
Ongoing environmental damage throughout the 18th and 19th centuries continued to degrade archival holdings in storage. Climate and storage conditions remain an issue for original documents.

---

## Records That SURVIVED — and Their Substitutes

Despite these losses, substantial genealogical sources survive. The key is knowing where to look.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Civil registration level and start:** Louisiana did **not** have statewide civil registration of births and deaths during the early 1800s. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892; 2,345,678 index records, no images) begins in 1819, reflecting some local-level death recording, but statewide civil registration of vital events was not comprehensively established until well into the 20th century. No FamilySearch Wiki page returned confirmed the exact statewide-registration start date; do not rely on any single year without verifying at the wiki.
- **What this means for 1800–1850:** Civil vital records are sparse to nonexistent for births and deaths in this period. Civil **marriage** recording exists somewhat earlier — FamilySearch holds "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection 1798054; 567,890 records, 283,945 images), but this only reaches back to 1837 and therefore misses the first 37 years of the target period.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths in the early 1800s are almost entirely undocumented in civil records. Use church sacramental registers as the primary substitute (see below).

### Church Records — THE PRIMARY VITAL RECORDS SUBSTITUTE

Catholic sacramental records are the foundational vital-records source for colonial and antebellum New Orleans. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Church Records — Catholic Sacramental Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic))

- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans** — baptisms, marriages, and burials from **1731 to present** (with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires). This is the single most important surviving record series for early New Orleans families.
- **Where held (originals):** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.
- **Where held (microfilm/digitized):** FamilySearch has microfilmed many of these registers. The collection **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (collection 1612905; 987,654 records, 493,827 images) covers this period and is the primary online access point.
  - **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (the collection is name-searchable).
- **Language:** French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), English (after 1803) — though French continues alongside English in the early American period. Researchers should be prepared to read all three languages.
- **Additional parishes:** Other Catholic churches in New Orleans also kept sacramental registers. Check the Archdiocese of New Orleans and the FamilySearch microfilm holdings beyond St. Louis Cathedral.

### Notarial Records — THE PRIMARY LEGAL RECORDS SUBSTITUTE

This is Louisiana's most distinctive and rich record set. Because Louisiana operates under civil law, **notarial acts replace the common-law deed books, probate files, and many court records** used in other U.S. states. Everything that would be recorded at a county courthouse in another state — property transfers, marriage contracts, wills and successions, tutorships (guardianships), emancipations, slave transactions — was recorded before a notary in Louisiana. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy — Notarial Archives](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives))

- **Volume of records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts dating to 1734.
- **Critical quirk — organization by notary, not party:** Notarial records are indexed by **notary name and date**, not by the names of the parties involved. To find a record, you need an approximate date and the name of the notary your ancestor used. Finding aids and indexes exist but are not comprehensive.
- **Colonial-era records (French 1718–1769; Spanish 1769–1803):** Held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans.
- **Post-1803 records:** Held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**, 1340 Poydras Street, New Orleans.
- **FamilySearch digitization:** FamilySearch has microfilmed surviving notarial acts. Volume search returned **1 digitized volume** (image group 004990115): "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)," covering 1803–1820, 167 images, in French and English.
  - **Digitization level: Browse-only images.** This volume is **0% name-indexed** and **not full-text searchable.** It must be browsed image by image. There is no name search.
- **What types of acts survive in notarial records:**
  - Property sales, purchases, and mortgages
  - Marriage contracts (often name parents, dowry terms)
  - Successions (wills, estate inventories, distributions — Louisiana's equivalent of probate)
  - Tutorships (guardianship of minors — names surviving family members)
  - Emancipation acts (free people of color)
  - Slave sales and manumissions
  - Business contracts, partnerships

### Probate Records (Successions)

In Louisiana, probate is called a **"succession."** It is handled through the notarial system and the civil district courts, not a separate probate court.

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341; 456,789 records, 228,394 images) — covers the target period from 1800.
  - **Digitization level:** Indexed + images.
- **Where held (originals):** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, and the Orleans Parish Civil District Court.
- **Value as a substitute:** Successions name heirs, surviving spouses, and minor children — often providing the family relationships missing from lost vital records.

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** Orleans Parish / Orleans Territory was enumerated in the following federal censuses:
  - **1810** (as Orleans Territory)
  - **1820, 1830, 1840, 1850** (as State of Louisiana)
  - All are accessible on Ancestry.com (subscription) and some on FamilySearch. The 1810 and 1820 censuses are heads-of-household only; the 1850 census lists all individuals by name.
- **1890 Federal Census:** Destroyed by fire (nationwide loss, not New Orleans-specific).
- **State/territorial enumerations:** Louisiana took some territorial-era censuses. Check the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Digitization level:** Federal censuses 1810–1850 are indexed + images on Ancestry. FamilySearch also holds these as part of the national census collections.
- **Substitute for census gaps:** Notarial acts, tax records, and city directories can place individuals in specific years between census enumerations.

### Land Records

- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the **French arpent system** in older areas (long, narrow lots fronting rivers), alongside the U.S. rectangular survey system applied after 1803.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Louisiana is a **federal-land state** — initial land grants and patents are in the records of the federal General Land Office (now BLM). The BLM General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds land patent records.
- **Notarial records substitute deed books:** Subsequent transfers are in notarial acts, not deed books. See Notarial Records above.
- **Spanish land grants:** Many New Orleans families received land under Spanish rule. These grants were adjudicated after the Louisiana Purchase by U.S. land commissioners. Records are at the Louisiana State Archives and NARA.
- **Digitization level:** BLM federal patents are indexed + images online. Notarial-based transfers are largely browse-only or physical-only.

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts (1800–1850):**
  - **War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815)** — significant Louisiana and New Orleans militia involvement
  - **Mexican-American War (1846–1848)** — Louisiana volunteers served
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington, D.C. — service records and pension files for this period. Available on **Fold3** (subscription) for indexed + images access.
- **Louisiana militia records:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge.

### Cemetery Records

- **St. Louis Cemetery No. 1** (est. 1789) — the oldest surviving Catholic cemetery in New Orleans; many early 1800s burials.
- **St. Louis Cemetery No. 2** (est. 1823) and **No. 3** (est. 1854).
- **Above-ground burial:** New Orleans' high water table necessitates above-ground tomb burials; structural damage and flooding have damaged some tombs and records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) — free; coverage is incomplete for early 1800s.
- **Sexton records and burial registers:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and the individual cemeteries. Many early burial registers were lost in the 1788 and 1794 fires.

### Newspapers

- **New Orleans had active newspapers by the early 1800s.** *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (French-language) was publishing from 1794. The *Louisiana Gazette* (English) began 1804.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, estate and succession notices, legal advertisements, and shipping arrivals (useful for immigration research).
- **Where held:** **Newspapers.com** (subscription), Louisiana State University Libraries (Baton Rouge), New Orleans Public Library, and the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Digitization level:** Partial — some titles are digitized and full-text searchable on Newspapers.com; others exist only on microfilm at Louisiana libraries.

### Immigration and Port Records

- **New Orleans was one of the busiest ports of entry in the United States** throughout the early 1800s. It was the primary port of arrival for immigrants settling in the Mississippi Valley.
- **Passenger lists:** NARA holds passenger arrival manifests. These are searchable on Ancestry.com and partially on FamilySearch and Fold3.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. In Louisiana, these appear in district court records and notarial acts. Check Orleans Parish Civil District Court records and the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Digitization level:** Federal passenger lists 1820–1850 are indexed + images on Ancestry. Earlier manifests are spottier.

### Tax Records

- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and establish when an individual arrived, departed, or died.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives and Orleans Parish repositories.
- **Digitization level:** Generally physical-only or microfilm; limited online availability for the early 1800s.

### Free People of Color — Specialized Records

New Orleans had one of the largest free Black communities in antebellum America. Specific records document this population:

- **Emancipation acts** in notarial records
- **Sacramental registers** at St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms of free and enslaved people of color were recorded separately but are in the same registers)
- **Free Negro Registers** — Orleans Parish maintained registers of free people of color. Check Louisiana State Archives.
- **Succession records** — free families of color appear in notarial successions

### Enslaved Persons — Available Record Sources

- **Slave sale acts** in notarial records (organized by notary/date)
- **Sacramental baptism records** at St. Louis Cathedral
- **Estate inventories in successions** — enslaved people listed by name
- **Slave schedules in federal census** (1850 schedule lists enslaved persons by age, sex, and description — not by name — under the enslaver's entry)

---

---

## Records NOT Online

The following exist but are **not** in any searchable online database as of this survey:

- The bulk of notarial acts post-1820 (only the 1803–1820 microfilm volume appears in FamilySearch's digitized holdings, and that volume is browse-only)
- Free Negro Registers held at Louisiana State Archives
- Most original sacramental registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans (some are on FamilySearch microfilm; the originals require in-person or written access)
- Tax records and assessor's records for Orleans Parish
- Spanish colonial administrative records beyond what was microfilmed
- Most New Orleans city directories (the earliest date from the 1820s–1830s; access is largely through libraries)

---

## Known Record Losses and Substitutes — Summary

| Loss | What Was Destroyed | Best Surviving Substitute |
|---|---|---|
| **Fire of 1788** | Much of the French Quarter; civil and church records from the French period | St. Louis Cathedral registers (partial survival); Spanish notarial records from 1769 on; colonial notarial records at Louisiana Historical Center |
| **Fire of 1794** | Additional city records and rebuilt structures | Same substitutes as above; post-1794 notarial and sacramental records are more complete |
| **No statewide civil registration** for births/deaths (early 1800s) | No official birth or death certificates | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms/burials); succession records naming heirs; newspaper death notices |
| **No civil marriage registration** before 1837 (FamilySearch's earliest) | Civil marriage records are sparse before 1837 | Church marriage records (sacramental registers); marriage contracts in notarial records |
| **Common-law deed books** (don't exist in Louisiana) | N/A — Louisiana never had them | Notarial acts (all property transactions recorded before a notary) |
| **Common-law probate court** (doesn't exist in Louisiana) | N/A | Notarial successions; Orleans Parish Civil District Court succession records |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Think notary, not courthouse.** In New Orleans, the notarial archives are what the courthouse deed room is everywhere else in the United States. Every significant legal transaction — property, marriage contract, succession, guardianship — went through a notary. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy — Notarial Archives](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives))

2. **Start with St. Louis Cathedral registers for any vital event before 1837.** Baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps) are the only consistent vital-records series for New Orleans in this period. These are partially indexed on FamilySearch in collection 1612905. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Church Records — Catholic Sacramental Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic))

3. **Colonial-era notarial records are split by language era.** French-era records (1718–1769) and Spanish-era records (1769–1803) are at the Louisiana Historical Center. Post-1803 notarial records are at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. The FamilySearch microfilm volume of surviving notarial acts (image group 004990115, 1803–1820) must be browsed image by image — it has no name index and is not full-text searchable.

4. **Records are in three languages.** French (colonial through early American period), Spanish (1769–1803), and English (post-1803). Many records from the 1800s through at least the 1830s remain in French even under American rule. Researchers unfamiliar with these languages should plan for translation assistance.

5. **Use Louisiana's civil-law vocabulary.** The terms differ from common-law states: *succession* = probate/estate; *tutorship* = guardianship; *interdiction* = legal incapacitation; *act of sale* = deed. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))

6. **For free people of color,** search sacramental registers (which recorded baptisms separately but within the same volumes), emancipation acts in notarial records, and the Free Negro Registers at the Louisiana State Archives. New Orleans' gens de couleur libres community was one of the most documented free Black populations in antebellum America.

7. **For enslaved ancestors,** notarial sale acts (organized by notary/date), estate inventories in succession records, and sacramental baptism registers are the primary sources. The 1850 slave schedule lists enslaved persons by age and sex under the enslaver's name — not by the enslaved person's name — and is the first federal census to enumerate this population for this period.

8. **Check the succession record even if your ancestor was not wealthy.** Louisiana succession law required a formal proceeding even for small estates, and these records often name surviving spouses, children, and other heirs — providing the family relationships that missing vital records cannot.

9. **The 1810 census is the earliest federal enumeration for New Orleans** (then Orleans Territory). It lists heads of household only. Work backward from there using notarial records, sacramental registers, and Spanish colonial records.

10. **Newspapers are underused for this period.** French- and English-language New Orleans newspapers from the early 1800s carried marriage notices, death notices, and succession advertisements. Check Louisiana State University Libraries, the New Orleans Public Library, and Newspapers.com for available digitized titles.

## Locality Research Guide: Boston Port of Entry — 1840s Immigration

**Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**Period of interest:** 1840–1855 (including the Irish Famine wave, 1845–1852)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Boston is the county seat of Suffolk County and the capital of Massachusetts. By 1850, more than a quarter of its residents were Irish-born — the direct result of the Great Famine. Boston was one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry in this era, second in volume only to New York.

**Vital registration levels matter here:** Massachusetts town clerks were ordered by the General Court to record births, marriages, and deaths as early as 1639. *Statewide* registration began in 1841 — meaning the state-level system was brand new during the 1840s and coverage was thin in the early years of the decade. Immigrant events in that window may appear only in town records or church registers, not in state returns.

---

### 1. Customs Passenger Lists (Port of Boston) — PRIMARY SOURCE

**What they are:** Federal customs-era passenger lists (National Archives Record Group 36), capturing all arriving ships at the Port of Boston.

**Coverage:** 1820–1891. The FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) overlaps the full 1840s.

**What the records contain:** 1840s lists are brief by later standards — typically name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only. No hometown, no named relatives, no village of birth. A country of origin of "Ireland" is common and usually tells you no more than that.

**Digitization level:** One digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210) covers 1840–1850 at Boston — 389 images, **3% name-indexed** (effectively not searchable by name), but **full-text searchable**. In practice, you should plan to browse the images page by page for this period, using full-text search as a supplement rather than a primary means of access.

**Originals:** National Archives at Boston, 380 Trapelo Road, Waltham, MA 02452 — [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/). Also indexed and browsable on **Ancestry.com**.

**Tip from the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)):** Unlike Ellis Island–era manifests, these early lists will not give you a hometown or a contact in the country of origin. Use them to confirm arrival and establish a date, then pivot to Irish or European records to go further back.

---

### 2. Naturalization Records — ESSENTIAL FOLLOW-UP

**What they are:** Before 1906, any court of record — federal, state, or local — could naturalize an immigrant. Records from this era are scattered across multiple courts and are not centralized.

**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — spans the 1840s.

**What to search:**
- **Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas / Superior Court** — the most common venue for Boston-area naturalizations
- **U.S. Circuit and District Courts, District of Massachusetts** — held at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham)
- Both "first papers" (declaration of intention) and "second papers" (final petition) may survive; check for both, as they were often filed years apart

**Digitization level:** Collections-level data returned by FamilySearch; detailed digitization status for individual naturalization volumes was not confirmed by the volume search. Verify current image availability on FamilySearch before assuming browse access.

---

### 3. Church Records — CRITICAL FOR IRISH CATHOLIC IMMIGRANTS

**What they are:** Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) documenting immigrants who were unlikely to interact with civil registration in the early 1840s before the state system was established.

**Key parishes for the 1840s Boston immigrant community:**
- **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** (established 1803)
- **St. Patrick's Church** (South End / Fort Hill area, where many Irish settled)
- Additional parishes founded during and immediately after the Famine years

**Where held:** The **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds original registers. Some records have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. See the FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657).

**Archdiocese of Boston Archives:** 66 Brooks Drive, Braintree, MA 02184.

**Critical note:** Church records may be the *only* source of baptism, marriage, or burial data for an immigrant who arrived before 1841 state registration began, or whose events were never recorded in the emerging civil system. Treat these as co-primary sources alongside passenger lists — not afterthoughts.

---

### 4. The Pilot Newspaper — Missing-Persons Advertisements (UNIQUE RESOURCE)

*The Pilot* was Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper and published a standing column of missing-persons notices placed by immigrants seeking separated family members. These notices often name a county or parish of origin in Ireland — making them far more geographically specific than the customs lists.

**Database:** The Boston College "Database of Famine Irish" indexes *Pilot* missing-persons ads, 1831–1921. Search it at no cost at [infowanted.bc.edu](http://infowanted.bc.edu). This is a first stop for Irish Famine-era research and is frequently overlooked.

---

### 5. Federal Census Records

- **1840 Federal Census:** Lists the head of household by name only; other household members are tallied by age/sex category. Limited for immigrant identification.
- **1850 Federal Census:** First census to list every household member by name, age, birthplace, occupation, and real estate value. Birthplace column says only the country ("Ireland," "England," "Germany," etc.) — no more specificity.

Both available fully indexed on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and related platforms.

---

### 6. Massachusetts Town Vital Records

**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — covers the 1840s.

For Boston specifically, these are recorded at the city/town level and predate the state registration system. From 1841 onward, town records were supposed to be forwarded to the state — but compliance was spotty in the early 1840s. Search both the town series and the state series.

**Massachusetts State Archives**, 220 Morrissey Blvd., Boston, MA 02125 — holds original returns and state vital registration volumes.

---

### 7. Probate Records

**FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901). Suffolk County Probate Court files. Wills and estate inventories from 1840s immigrants who settled and died in Boston can name siblings, children, and places of origin mentioned in correspondence or bequests.

---

### 8. Newspapers

**Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) and the **Chronicling America** database (Library of Congress, free) carry Boston-area papers from the 1840s. Search for death notices, ship arrival columns, and neighborhood news in:
- *Boston Daily Atlas*
- *Boston Post*
- *The Pilot* (Irish Catholic — see §4 above)

Ship arrival columns published in commercial papers often list passenger names not captured in official customs manifests, or supplement sparse official lists.

---

### 9. Land and City Records

Newly arrived immigrants who purchased property quickly generated deed records at the **Suffolk County Registry of Deeds**, 24 New Chardon St., Boston — now searchable online at [masslandrecords.com](https://www.masslandrecords.com/). City directories for Boston (published annually from the 1820s onward) are an underused tool for tracking when an immigrant appears as a householder or boarding-house resident. Many are digitized on **Ancestry.com** and at the **Boston Public Library** (via its digital archive).

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston, Waltham | Customs passenger lists (RG 36); federal court naturalizations | In-person; some digitized on FamilySearch/Ancestry |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | State vital records from 1841; state court records | In-person; partial digitization |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives, Braintree | Catholic parish registers | By appointment |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds | Land records | Online at masslandrecords.com |
| Boston Public Library (Digital Collections) | City directories; historical newspapers | Online and in-person |
| FamilySearch ([familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)) | Passenger lists, church records, naturalization, town vitals | Free online |
| Ancestry.com | Passenger lists, census, city directories | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Boston-area historical newspapers | Subscription |

---

### Quirks and Cautions

- **1840s customs lists are thin on detail.** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin is the typical content — no town or county of birth. Do not expect to derive an Irish origin parish from the passenger list alone.
- **State vital registration was new and incomplete in the early 1840s.** Town records and church registers are the better source for vital events before roughly 1845.
- **Naturalizations are scattered.** Before 1906, any court could naturalize — check Suffolk County Superior Court, Probate Court, U.S. District Court, and even police court records.
- **The Pilot missing-persons database is uniquely valuable.** It is the most commonly available source that names a specific Irish county or parish for Famine-era immigrants. Check it before assuming no origin data survives.
- **Browse-only volumes.** The digitized Boston passenger list volume (003345210, 1840–1850) is only 3% name-indexed. Plan to browse images, not rely on name search alone. Full-text search is available but imperfect for handwritten registers.
- **FamilySearch Wiki note:** The four wiki-place-page sections for Massachusetts returned only a generic fallback page during this survey rather than Massachusetts-specific content — meaning no Massachusetts-specific online-records or research-tips pages were served. The immigration-specific guidance above comes from the FamilySearch wiki article [Massachusetts Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston) (returned in the wiki search, relevance 0.92) and the [Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston) article.
