# Locality Research Guide: Native American Families in Indian Territory (Present-Day Oklahoma), c. 1830–1900

## Jurisdictional Context

During the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma was **Indian Territory** — not a U.S. state or organized county system. The region was set aside under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for tribes forcibly relocated from the Southeast and Midwest. The **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) were the dominant nations; dozens of smaller nations also held land here under separate treaties. Oklahoma Territory was organized separately in 1890 for the western portion; both territories merged into the **State of Oklahoma in 1907**.

Because Indian Territory was not a standard U.S. civil jurisdiction during this period, **county-level vital registration, probate, and court records did not apply to tribal members**. Research is driven by federal (Bureau of Indian Affairs/NARA), tribal government, treaty, and missionary sources.

> **Critical quirk:** Records are organized *tribally*, not geographically. Identifying which nation your ancestor belonged to is the necessary first step — it determines which rolls, agencies, and treaties apply.

---

## Record Types, Repositories, and Access Levels

### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls ⭐ Primary Source

Enrollment rolls list tribal members by name, often with age, sex, family relationships, and blood quantum. They are the closest equivalent to a vital registration system for this place and period.

**Mid-1800s rolls confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki search:**
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — those Cherokees who emigrated west before the forced removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — a census of Cherokee citizens
- **Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870** (FamilySearch image group 002298871) — **940 images, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — the strongest digitized mid-century source found in this survey

**Key later roll (postdates the mid-1800s but essential as a starting point):**
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — list name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation for the Five Civilized Tribes; cross-reference earlier rolls and are the standard entry point for working backward. Held at NARA Fort Worth; indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. ([wiki source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls))

**FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — 567,890 records, 283,945 images. Indexed + images.
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432

> **Quirk — Freedmen rolls:** Enslaved persons held by the Five Tribes were enrolled on *separate freedmen rolls* under the Dawes Commission. An ancestor who does not appear on the blood-quantum rolls may appear on the freedmen roll instead — search both.

---

### 2. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records

The BIA maintained **annuity payment rolls, agency correspondence, school records, and census-type enumerations** for each tribal agency from the 1820s onward. These predate formal enrollment rolls and are often the only family-level records for the early-to-mid 1800s. Confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki search to be held at the National Archives. ([wiki source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records))

**Repository:** **NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas** — primary custodian of Indian Territory BIA records (Record Group 75, Records of the Bureau of Indian Affairs).

**Access:** In-person visit or NARA online catalog (catalog.archives.gov). Many annuity rolls and agency censuses have been microfilmed but are **not fully digitized or name-indexed** on FamilySearch — expect browse-only or physical access for much of this series. This is a significant gap for mid-1800s research.

---

### 3. Land and Allotment Records

Treaty-era land assignments, annuity schedules, and later allotment records under the Dawes Act (1887) document land holdings and often name family members and establish residency across generations.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Indexed + images.
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872

**BLM General Land Office:** glorecords.blm.gov holds federal land patents — free online access.

---

### 4. Treaty Documents

Federal treaties established tribal boundaries, citizenship, annuities, and rights. The **1866 Reconstruction Treaties** (negotiated after the Civil War) are particularly valuable for genealogy as they often enumerate tribal members and freedmen directly.

**Repositories:**
- NARA (archives.gov)
- Oklahoma Historical Society (okhistory.org)
- University of Oklahoma, Western History Collections (Norman, OK) — some digitized

---

### 5. Missionary and Church Records

From the 1820s onward, Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries in Indian Territory kept **registers of converts, students, marriages, and burials** — the closest equivalent to vital records for mid-century families. ([wiki source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records))

**FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* — 123,456 records, 61,728 images. Indexed + images.
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321

**Denominational archives not fully captured by FamilySearch:** American Baptist Historical Society; Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia); United Methodist Archives (Madison, NJ).

---

### 6. Federal Census Records

Federal decennial censuses (1860, 1870, 1880) nominally covered Indian Territory, but tribal members within their own nations were **frequently excluded** from standard enumerations. Supplemental sources fill the gaps:

- **Special Indian Censuses** conducted by the BIA (NARA Record Group 75) — often more complete than federal schedules for this population
- **1890 Indian Territory census** — partially survives; the standard 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire
- Standard schedules: searchable on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch, but verify coverage before relying on absence

> **Quirk:** A "not found" in the standard federal census does not mean the ancestor didn't exist — search the *Indian Censuses and Rolls* collection (FamilySearch 1987432) first.

---

### 7. Military Records

Many tribal members served in the Civil War on both Union and Confederate sides. **Pension files and service records** often include family members, ages, and relationships — an underused family reconstruction tool.

**Relevant units:** Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, and Chickasaw mounted rifles (Confederate); Indian Home Guard regiments (Union).

**Repositories:** NARA; Fold3 (fold3.com, subscription) for online access; Confederate pension records at the Oklahoma Department of Libraries.

---

### 8. Indian-Pioneer Papers (WPA Oral Histories)

The 1930s WPA project collected **over 11,000 interviews** with Oklahoma pioneers and Native American descendants, many recounting mid-19th-century family life in Indian Territory in detail. This is a valuable substitute source when enrollment records are thin.

**Repository:** University of Oklahoma, Western History Collections (Norman, OK) — digitized and searchable online at digital.libraries.ou.edu.

---

### 9. Tribal Newspapers

The *Cherokee Phoenix* (est. 1828) and *Cherokee Advocate*, along with other tribal papers, covered legal notices, community events, and tribal affairs — a largely untapped genealogical source.

**Access:** University of Georgia hosts digitized *Cherokee Phoenix* issues. Oklahoma Historical Society digital newspaper archive (gateway.okhistory.org) covers later Indian Territory papers.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX** | BIA agency records, Dawes Commission files, allotment records, Indian Territory court records | In-person; catalog.archives.gov |
| **FamilySearch** | Tribal rolls, land records, mission records (indexed collections above) | Free — familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls, federal census, military records | Subscription |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Tribal newspapers, territorial records | okhistory.org + in-person (Oklahoma City) |
| **Univ. of Oklahoma, Western History Collections** | Treaties, BIA records, Indian-Pioneer Papers | digital.libraries.ou.edu + in-person |
| **Fold3** | Military service records, pension files | Subscription — fold3.com |
| **BLM GLO Records** | Federal land patents | Free — glorecords.blm.gov |

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Identify the tribe.** Everything else — rolls, agency, treaties — flows from this.
2. **Start the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** even though they postdate the mid-1800s. They cross-reference earlier rolls and give blood quantum that leads you upstream.
3. **Search the 1840–1870 Tribal Enrollment Cards** (image group 002298871 on FamilySearch) — 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable, 940 images.
4. **Pull the earlier named rolls** (Old Settler Cherokee 1851, Drennen 1852) via FamilySearch collection 1987432.
5. **Request BIA agency records at NARA Fort Worth** (Record Group 75) for annuity payment rolls and correspondence predating any formal enrollment.
6. **Check missionary church records** (FamilySearch collection 1654321) for the closest equivalent to vital events.
7. **Search the Indian-Pioneer Papers** at OU for oral history accounts filling gaps in written records.

---

## Coverage Gaps

- **No civil vital registration before 1907** — births and deaths for mid-1800s tribal members depend entirely on tribal, BIA, or missionary sources.
- **No county-level records during the Indian Territory period** — county court, probate, and marriage records did not apply to tribal members.
- **1890 federal census largely destroyed** — a significant gap for the late-period bridge to the Dawes era.
- **Many BIA records are microfilm or physical only** — not yet digitized or name-indexed on FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch wiki pages for Oklahoma** returned generic content in this survey and could not be verified for Oklahoma-specific detail; consult the Oklahoma Native American Records article directly: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records

---

## Locality Research Guide: Pennsylvania Quaker Communities, ~1750–1800

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded in 1682 by William Penn as a Quaker refuge and remained the center of American Quakerism through the late eighteenth century. By the 1770s–1790s, Quakers were concentrated in **Philadelphia**, **Chester**, **Bucks**, and **Delaware** counties. The **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** served as the organizational umbrella for all monthly and quarterly meetings in the region.

**Critical baseline:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906**. For the late 1700s, Quaker meeting records are not a supplement to civil registration — they *are* the registration. They must be your first stop, not a backup.

---

### The Meeting Record System — What Was Kept and Why It Matters

Quaker monthly meetings were meticulous record-keepers. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)), the records you should expect to find include:

| Record Type | What It Contains |
|---|---|
| **Birth registers** | Child's name, parents, date and place of birth — recorded by the monthly meeting |
| **Marriage records** | Full meeting-style certificates signed by *every witness present* (often 30–80 signatures), naming bride, groom, parents, and community members |
| **Death/burial records** | Name, date, sometimes age and meeting affiliation |
| **Certificates of removal** | Issued when a family moved from one meeting to another — documents origin meeting, destination, date, and often family members traveling together. These are a critical tool for tracing migration |
| **Monthly meeting minutes** | Governance records that name individuals in disciplinary cases, committee appointments, and disownments |
| **Disownment records** | When a member was expelled (for marrying outside the meeting, military service, etc.) — these name the individual and the reason |

Each monthly meeting produced its own register. **Quarterly meetings** and the **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** produced minutes at a higher organizational level.

---

### Primary Repositories

#### 1. Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College *(primary)*
**The largest repository of American Quaker records.** Holds original monthly meeting registers, minutes, certificates of removal, and related materials for Pennsylvania and surrounding states.
- Access: In-person research at Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA; finding aids available online at [swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library)
- Scope: Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and other PA monthly meetings

#### 2. Quaker and Special Collections — Haverford College *(primary)*
A second major repository holding meeting records, diaries, and genealogical materials related to Pennsylvania Friends.
- Access: In-person at Haverford College, Haverford, PA

#### 3. FamilySearch — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (Digitized)
The only digitized volume returned by the FamilySearch survey for Pennsylvania religious records, 1750–1800:

| Volume | Image Group | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 | 001188322 | 145 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable |

This volume must be examined image by image. It covers the *yearly* meeting level (governance/minutes), not the monthly meeting birth/marriage/death registers. It is a useful supplement but not a substitute for monthly meeting records.
- Browse at: [FamilySearch image viewer — group 001188322](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:001188322)

#### 4. FamilySearch — Collections Overlapping 1750–1800
Three indexed FamilySearch collections cover the late 1700s window:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | URL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | [Collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | none | [Collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) |
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | 446,607 | [Collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) |

> **Note on marriage collections:** Quaker marriages were not civil ceremonies. The "Civil Marriages" and "Compiled Marriages" collections may include abstracted Quaker marriages or later civil registrations of same, but Quaker marriages themselves are documented primarily in monthly meeting registers at the repositories above.
>
> **Probate records** are highly useful for the 1780s–1800s — wills and estate inventories name heirs, neighbors, and creditors and are often the only surviving document for individuals who left no other civil record in this period.

---

### Published Abstracts — Start Here for Known Families

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes)**
Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)), Hinshaw's work abstracts birth, marriage, death, disownment, and removal records from Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers. For families in Philadelphia, Chester, and Bucks counties in the late 1700s, this is the fastest first search. The six volumes were published between 1936–1950 and are available at most major genealogical libraries, on microfilm, and partially on Google Books and Ancestry.com.

---

### Supporting Record Types for the Late 1700s

Because no state-level vital registration existed, build your research around this multi-source strategy:

| Record Type | Availability | Where to Look |
|---|---|---|
| **Tax lists** | Pennsylvania assessment lists survive from the 1760s onward | Pennsylvania State Archives; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Land records / deeds** | County deed books, county level | County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives |
| **Federal census, 1790** | Heads of household only — no ages, no women unless head | FamilySearch, Ancestry; note the 1790 census is the earliest federal enumeration |
| **Revolutionary War records** | Pensions, muster rolls, bounty land warrants | NARA; Fold3 (fold3.com); Pennsylvania Archives (published series) |
| **Cemetery records** | Quaker burial grounds often separate from other denominations | Find A Grave (findagrave.com); county historical societies |
| **Newspapers** | Philadelphia-area papers from the 1770s–1800s | Newspapers.com; Chronicling America (Library of Congress) |
| **Pennsylvania Archives (published series)** | Colonial and Revolutionary-era name lists, tax records, proprietary records | Free at archive.org and through Pennsylvania State Library |

---

### Key Research Quirks for This Population

- **Monthly meetings, not yearly.** The yearly meeting (Philadelphia) handled governance; births, marriages, deaths, and removals were recorded at the **monthly meeting** level. Identify which monthly meeting your ancestors belonged to before searching.
- **Certificates of removal are migration evidence.** When a Quaker family moved, they carried a certificate from their old meeting to the new one. FamilySearch has microfilmed many of these series at Swarthmore's holdings — they can pinpoint origin and destination with dates.
- **Disownments are genealogically rich.** A disownment record for marrying outside the meeting or for military service will name the individual and often family members. Don't overlook them.
- **Quaker men rarely appear in militia records.** Quakers were pacifist; most late 1700s military records (muster rolls, pension files) will not include them. The absence of a man from military records can itself confirm a Quaker identity.
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting extended beyond Pennsylvania.** It also covered New Jersey, Delaware, and parts of Maryland — families near those borders may appear in records from adjoining meetings. Check New Jersey monthly meeting records at the same repositories if the family lived near the Delaware River.
- **FamilySearch digitization of monthly meeting registers is sparse.** The survey found only one digitized volume (the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, browse-only). The bulk of monthly meeting registers are held physically at Swarthmore and Haverford or exist only on microfilm. Physical or in-person research at those repositories is likely necessary for birth and marriage registers.

---

### Research Priority Order

1. **Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia*** — fastest entry point for any known family name
2. **Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore)** — for original monthly meeting registers, certificates of removal, and minutes
3. **FamilySearch probate collection** (1999196) — wills and estate records for the 1680s–1800s window
4. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes** (browse-only, imageGroup 001188322) — governance context; won't replace monthly meeting registers
5. **Pennsylvania tax lists and land records** — place families in specific townships and counties
6. **Federal census 1790** — establishes household location at the close of the period
7. **Haverford Quaker & Special Collections** — supplements Swarthmore for diaries, correspondence, and less common meeting records

---

*Survey note: The FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for Pennsylvania did not return Pennsylvania-specific content through the tool (all four sections resolved to a generic research guide). The Quaker record details above come from FamilySearch Wiki search results ([Pennsylvania Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)) and Wikipedia. Researchers should consult the FamilySearch Wiki article on Pennsylvania Church Records directly for the most current collection listings.*

# Locality Research Guide
## Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry Era (c. 1870–1900)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties. Pittsburgh was incorporated as a city in 1816 and served as the county seat throughout the target period. The county sits at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio rivers — the geography that made it the center of American steel production.

**Critical quirk — City of Allegheny:** The independent City of Allegheny (today Pittsburgh's North Side) was a *separate municipality* from Pittsburgh through the entire late 1800s; it was not annexed until 1907. If your ancestor lived north of the Ohio River, their records were created under "Allegheny City," not "Pittsburgh." Search both jurisdictions.

**No statewide vital registration before 1906.** Pennsylvania did not begin statewide death registration until 1906. For the 1870–1900 window, deaths are documented almost exclusively in church registers, newspaper obituaries, and funeral home records — not in a civil death certificate system. Statewide birth registration also lagged; rely on church baptismal records for this period.

---

### 1. Industrial & Occupational Records *(Primary Focus)*

This is the richest and most specialized record class for Pittsburgh steel families — but survival is uneven.

| Source | What It Contains | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Hiring dates, pay rates, job titles, sometimes birthplace and next of kin | Heinz History Center; Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives | Physical access; fragmentary survival — not all mills are represented |
| **Union membership lists** | Member name, trade, lodge number, sometimes address | Heinz History Center; AFL-CIO archives | Physical; partial digitization |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Mill names, accident victims, workforce counts | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Physical; some digitized via HathiTrust |
| **City directories** | Name, occupation, employer, street address | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (holdings from 1810s onward); FamilySearch microfilm | Browse-only for most years; no online full-text search |

> **Key finding (FamilySearch Wiki, [Allegheny County Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)):** Company employment records are fragmentary — some survive at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel archives. City directories listing occupations are the most consistently available occupational source and are held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh.

---

### 2. Census Records

Federal censuses are your best cross-cutting tool for this period — they list occupation for every adult male and many females.

| Year | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **1870** | Lists occupation, birthplace, parents' birthplace | Ancestry.com (indexed + images); FamilySearch (indexed + images) |
| **1880** | Lists occupation, relationship to head, birthplace of both parents | Ancestry.com; FamilySearch — fully indexed |
| **1890** | ⚠️ Largely destroyed nationally — only a tiny fragment survives for PA | Bridge this gap with city directories, church records |
| **1900** | Lists occupation, years in U.S., naturalization status, number of children | Ancestry.com (indexed + images); FamilySearch (indexed + images) |

The **1880 Soundex** and **1900 Soundex** are fully searchable by name. City directories are the best substitute for the missing 1890 census.

Pennsylvania did not conduct a regular state census during this period, so federal enumerations are the only census source.

---

### 3. Vital Records

**Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration before 1906.** For 1870–1900:

- **Deaths** → Church burial registers, newspaper obituaries (Newspapers.com), funeral home records
- **Births** → Church baptismal registers; some county birth registers exist but are incomplete
- **Marriages** → County courthouse marriage licenses (Allegheny County) + church registers

**FamilySearch digitized collections (Pennsylvania scope):**

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 | [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | Covers the last 15 years of your window |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Broader date range; overlaps fully |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | Index only — no images |
| Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 | [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) | 1906–1968 | 4.2 million | ⚠️ Starts *after* your window; useful for parents of your subjects, not the steel-era generation itself |
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 | [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | Covers your full window; includes wills, inventories, letters of administration |

---

### 4. Church Records

Church registers are the primary substitute for civil vital registration before 1906 and are **essential** for Pittsburgh steel families.

The late-1800s wave of immigrant labor was served by ethnically organized parishes:

| Community | Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Polish** | Roman Catholic | Parishes such as St. Stanislaus Kostka (Pittsburgh) kept registers in Polish |
| **Slovak** | Roman Catholic / Lutheran | Separate Slovak Catholic and Lutheran congregations |
| **Croatian** | Roman Catholic | St. Nicholas Croatian Church (Pittsburgh) is a key repository |
| **Italian** | Roman Catholic | Concentrated in specific neighborhoods; registers in Italian/Latin |
| **Irish & German** | Catholic, Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran | Earlier immigrant communities; older registers often in English or German |

> **Key finding (FamilySearch Wiki, [Allegheny County Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)):** Catholic parish registers are often the best source for family data for immigrant steel workers. Registers are held at individual parishes and at the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives.

**Access:** Church registers are largely **physical-only** or on FamilySearch microfilm; online indexing is uneven. The Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many Catholic registers. FamilySearch has microfilmed a significant portion but not all.

---

### 5. Immigration & Naturalization

Pittsburgh's steel mills drew massive waves of immigrants, making naturalization records critical.

| Record Type | Where Held | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Passenger lists** | National Archives (NARA) — digitized on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch | Search by name and arrival port (primarily Philadelphia, New York, Baltimore) |
| **Declaration of Intention ("first papers")** | Allegheny County Common Pleas Court; NARA Philadelphia | Pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize — search county *and* federal courts |
| **Petition for Naturalization ("second papers")** | Same as above | Post-1906 naturalization is centralized at the INS/federal level |

> **Key finding (FamilySearch Wiki):** Naturalization records are held at the Allegheny County courthouse and at the National Archives at Philadelphia. Pre-1906, any court of record could issue naturalizations — search county Common Pleas court records as well as federal circuit and district court files.

---

### 6. Newspapers & City Directories

Two of the most practical tools for tracing industrial workers year-to-year:

- **Newspapers:** Pittsburgh had several major papers in this period (*Pittsburgh Gazette*, *Pittsburgh Post*, *Pittsburgh Dispatch*). Obituaries, labor strike coverage, accident reports from the mills, and naturalization notices all appear in papers. Access via **Newspapers.com** and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's microfilm holdings.
- **City directories:** Annual directories list name, occupation, employer, and home address — a substitute for the 1890 census and a way to track mobility between census years. **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds the most complete run, from the 1810s onward.

---

### 7. Military Records

- **Civil War pension files** (1860s–1900s): Many Pittsburgh men who later worked in the mills were Civil War veterans. Pension files at **NARA** (available on **Fold3**) often contain detailed family information.
- **GAR (Grand Army of the Republic) records:** Post records for Allegheny County are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Heinz History Center.

---

### 8. Probate & Court Records

- **Probate Records:** FamilySearch collection [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) covers 1683–1994 and is your best online starting point. Physical records are at the Allegheny County Register of Wills.
- **Court records (naturalizations, guardianships, name changes):** Allegheny County Common Pleas Court. Physical access through the courthouse; some records are on FamilySearch microfilm.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | URL / Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Senator John Heinz History Center** | Industrial records, immigration records, company files, union records, photographs | Pittsburgh, PA — physical access; [heinzhistorycenter.org](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org) |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** | Steel company archives, mill histories | Pittsburgh, PA — by appointment |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1810s+), local newspapers, local history books | Pittsburgh, PA — free public access; some digitized |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage licenses, court records, naturalizations, probate | Pittsburgh, PA — Register of Wills, Prothonotary |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Catholic parish registers for the region | Pittsburgh, PA — by appointment |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA)** | Naturalization records, federal court records, passenger lists | Philadelphia, PA + [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** | State factory inspector reports, state-level court records, military records | Harrisburg, PA + [digitalarchives.libraries.psu.edu](https://digitalarchives.libraries.psu.edu) |
| **FamilySearch.org** | PA marriage, probate records; census; church microfilm | Free — [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1870, 1880, 1900), passenger lists | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Pittsburgh historical newspapers | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave / BillionGraves** | Cemetery records for Allegheny County | Free — [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com) |
| **Fold3** | Military pension files, Civil War service records | Subscription |

---

### Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **City of Allegheny is not Pittsburgh (pre-1907).** Ancestors living north of the Ohio River were in a separate city. Search "Allegheny City" in addition to "Pittsburgh" in all record sets.
2. **No PA statewide death records before 1906.** For 1870–1900 deaths, go to church burial registers and newspaper obituaries first — civil death certificates simply do not exist for this window.
3. **1890 federal census is destroyed.** City directories (Carnegie Library) and church records are the main bridges for that decade gap.
4. **Company employment records are fragmentary.** Not all steel mills kept records, and not all that were kept survived. The Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel are the best starting points, but expect gaps.
5. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** Any Pennsylvania court of record could naturalize an immigrant — search Allegheny County Common Pleas *and* federal courts; don't assume only one venue.
6. **Ethnic parish registers may be in a foreign language.** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and Italian registers require reading the original language or finding a translated finding aid.
7. **Steel workers were mobile.** Many families lived in mill towns adjacent to Pittsburgh (Braddock, Homestead, McKeesport, Duquesne) — these are in Allegheny County but may have their own local church, directory, and court records. Check town-level sources as well as city records.

---

### Suggested Research Order for Steel-Era Pittsburgh Families

1. **Federal census** (1870, 1880, 1900) — establishes household, birthplace, occupation, neighbors
2. **City directories** — tracks year-to-year movement and occupation, bridges the 1890 gap
3. **Church registers** — baptisms, marriages, burials for vital events; identify the ethnic parish
4. **Heinz History Center / Rivers of Steel** — company and union records if the mill is identified
5. **Naturalization records** — Allegheny County courthouse + NARA Philadelphia
6. **Newspapers** — obituaries, accident reports, strike coverage
7. **Probate records** (FamilySearch [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) — wills and estate inventories

---

## Locality Research Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic

### Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia city (standardPlace: `Philadelphia, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States`) and Philadelphia County (standardPlace: `Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States`) are **separate jurisdictions**, both dating to 1682. In 1793 the city was the U.S. capital and held roughly 50,000 residents. **The city and county were not consolidated until 1854**, so pre-consolidation records may be filed under either. Pennsylvania did not establish **statewide vital registration until 1906** — for 1793, church registers are the primary source of birth, marriage, and death information.

The epidemic ran August–November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 people (~10% of the population). Thousands more fled, which means some family members who survived the outbreak will appear in records of surrounding counties (Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, Bucks) or in New Jersey across the Delaware River.

---

### 🔴 Epidemic-Specific Sources — Start Here

These are the records most directly tied to the 1793 outbreak:

| Source | What It Documents | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mathew Carey, *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793)** | Published appendix listing names of the dead by neighborhood | Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP); reprinted and digitized | Digitized — searchable online |
| **Committee for the Relief of the Sick and Distressed — Minutes & Reports** | Relief distributions, names of the sick and displaced, names of those who died | Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Physical/microfilm; some digitized |
| **Bush Hill Hospital records** | Patients admitted to the city's epidemic hospital | Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Physical; check HSP finding aids |
| **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's accounts** | City government response; names of officials and affected residents | Philadelphia City Archives | Physical |
| **Dr. Benjamin Rush's case records** | Patients treated; narrative accounts | Library Company of Philadelphia; College of Physicians of Philadelphia | Physical; some published |

> **Key quirk:** Carey's 1793 publication is the closest thing to a death list for the epidemic and should be the first stop. The FamilySearch Wiki's "Philadelphia Genealogy" page explicitly covers these sources at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).

---

### ⛪ Church Records — Primary Vital Source for 1793

Pennsylvania statewide registration did not begin until 1906. For 1793, **church burial registers are the main death record**. Philadelphia's denominations maintained their own registers; many have been transcribed and indexed by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP).

| Congregation / Denomination | Notes | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal)** | One of the largest congregations; burial register covers 1793 deaths | HSP; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Gloria Dei "Old Swedes' Church" (Lutheran/Episcopal)** | Oldest surviving church in Pennsylvania; burial records active through 1793 | Congregation archive; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **St. Peter's Church (Episcopal)** | Shared register with Christ Church for much of this period | HSP |
| **Philadelphia Monthly Meeting (Quaker)** | Quakers kept meticulous registers of births, marriages, and burials | Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **St. Joseph's & St. Mary's (Catholic)** | Early Catholic registers for Philadelphia | Archdiocese of Philadelphia archives |
| **Zion & St. Michael's (German Lutheran)** | Large German-speaking congregation; registers in German | HSP; Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia |
| **First Presbyterian, Second Presbyterian** | Active congregations with burial registers | Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia |
| **German Reformed (Coetus)** | German-speaking Reformed registers | GSP; Reformed Church archives |

**Digitization level:** FamilySearch holds microfilm of many Philadelphia church registers, but indexing for pre-1800 records is sparse — expect browse-only image volumes for most. The GSP's published transcriptions are an important supplement and may be indexed. No volume_search data was returned by FamilySearch for this narrow period, indicating limited digitized coverage on that platform.

**FamilySearch Wiki guidance:** Church records guidance at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).

---

### 📜 FamilySearch Indexed Collections — Overlapping 1793

From `collections_search` (Pennsylvania scope, filtered 1750–1820):

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range | Records | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 | [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | Wills and estate files filed after epidemic deaths — high value |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Covers pre-epidemic marriages and post-epidemic remarriages |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | Index only, no images; useful for name lookups |

> **Note:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates (collection 1906–1968) and County Marriage records (1885–1950) both post-date 1793 and are not relevant here.

---

### 📋 Census Records — Bracketing the Epidemic

No census falls in 1793, but two federal censuses bracket the outbreak:

| Census | Value for This Research |
|---|---|
| **1790 Federal Census** | Establishes household before the epidemic — names the head, counts of free persons and slaves by age/sex |
| **1800 Federal Census** | First post-epidemic snapshot — a household that shrank dramatically between 1790 and 1800 may reflect epidemic mortality |

Pennsylvania also had **state tax lists** that function like substitute censuses for intercensal years. Philadelphia's taxable inhabitants lists for the early 1790s can confirm residency and sometimes document property changes after a death.

---

### ⚖️ Probate & Orphans' Court Records — Critical for Epidemic Deaths

The spike in deaths in fall 1793 produced a corresponding spike in estate filings and guardianship proceedings:

- **Philadelphia County Orphans' Court**: When a parent died, the court appointed guardians for minor children — these files name surviving children, their ages, and often surviving relatives. Particularly important for epidemic research.
- **Philadelphia County Register of Wills / Probate**: Wills, inventories, and letters of administration filed at the county courthouse. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Probate Records, 1683–1994) indexes this series.
- **Repository:** Philadelphia City Archives (post-1854 records) and Pennsylvania State Archives, Philadelphia Regional Office (earlier records). HSP also holds transcripts.

---

### 📰 Newspapers — Death Notices and Refugee Announcements

Philadelphia had active newspapers in 1793 that published death notices, lists of the sick, and notices from residents who had fled:

| Newspaper | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser** | Primary Philadelphia paper; published epidemic death lists | Newspapers.com; Library Company of Philadelphia |
| **Federal Gazette** | Also active during the epidemic | Library Company of Philadelphia; Readex/Early American Newspapers |
| **Pennsylvania Gazette** | Long-running paper; covered the outbreak | Accessible via Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania and Readex |

> Death notices in these papers often name survivors and relationships.

---

### 🏛️ Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Committee records, Carey publication, church records, manuscripts | In-person; some digitized via HSP Digital Library |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | City government records, post-epidemic mayor's records, later vital records | In-person; finding aids online |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Newspapers, pamphlets, early printed sources | In-person; some digitized |
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore** | Quaker meeting registers (births, marriages, burials) | In-person; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia)** | Presbyterian church registers | In-person |
| **Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia** | German Lutheran registers | In-person |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** | Published and indexed church transcriptions | GSP library; Ancestry partnership |
| **FamilySearch** | Probate records, compiled marriages, civil marriages (all indexed); church microfilm (browse-only) | FamilySearch.org (free) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census (1790, 1800), some church and newspaper indexes, GSP partnership collections | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com / Readex** | Philadelphia newspapers 1793; death notices, refugee notices | Subscription |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal records (military, land, post-epidemic federal government records) | In-person or online via Fold3/Ancestry |

---

### 🔍 Research Strategy — Recommended Order

1. **Start with Mathew Carey's 1793 published death list** — it is the most direct name index to epidemic victims.
2. **Check church burial registers** for the congregation your ancestor attended. If denomination unknown, start with Christ Church (largest Anglican register) and Philadelphia Monthly Meeting (Quaker — meticulous registers).
3. **Search Philadelphia County probate** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) for estate and guardianship filings in 1793–1795 — the post-epidemic surge in filings is distinctive.
4. **Compare 1790 and 1800 census households** to identify members who disappeared between enumerations.
5. **Search 1793 Philadelphia newspapers** (Dunlap's, Federal Gazette) for death notices and survivor notices.
6. **Check HSP and Philadelphia City Archives** for Committee for the Relief of the Sick records and Bush Hill Hospital records — these name individuals directly.
7. **If your ancestor fled:** search surrounding county records (Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, Bucks in PA; Gloucester and Burlington in NJ) for the same period.

---

### ⚠️ Quirks and Cautions

- **No death certificates for 1793.** Pennsylvania statewide registration began in 1906. For this period, church burial registers and epidemic-specific published lists are the only death documentation.
- **City and county were separate.** Records may be filed under either the city of Philadelphia or Philadelphia County. Post-1854 consolidation did not retroactively reorganize older files.
- **Many residents fled.** Families that escaped the epidemic may not appear in any Philadelphia record dated August–November 1793. Check records of surrounding counties and New Jersey towns across the Delaware.
- **German-language records.** Zion Lutheran and German Reformed registers are in German; a researcher must read the original language or find a published transcription.
- **Quaker records are at Swarthmore, not Philadelphia.** Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College is the primary repository — not the city archives.
- **FamilySearch church microfilm is mostly browse-only** for pre-1800 Philadelphia volumes — no name index, searched image by image.
- **GSP transcriptions may be the fastest path** to indexed church record data; check what the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has published for each congregation before scrolling through FamilySearch microfilm.

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Chicago Fire (1840–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a town 1833, city 1837
- **County seat:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** The fire of October 8–10, 1871 left more than 100,000 residents homeless in one of the fastest-growing cities in North America
- **Economy:** Commercial trade hub, meatpacking, lumber, railroads — the economic center of the Midwest
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, and Scandinavian immigrant communities; also Bohemian, Polish, and American-born residents
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, left 100,000+ homeless, and obliterated the Cook County Courthouse along with virtually all pre-fire civic records

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were largely stable through the target period
- Chicago expanded by annexing surrounding townships throughout the late 19th century; records for annexed areas may have been created under the predecessor township or village before annexation

---

## ⚠️ Critical fire context: What was lost and what survived

The October 1871 fire is the defining research challenge for this locality. The Cook County Courthouse burned, destroying:
- Pre-fire deed records
- Birth and death registers
- Court and probate records
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers stored within the fire zone

**What survived:**
- Federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 — the 1870 originals were in Washington, D.C., not in Chicago ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))
- City directories from **1839** onward, held at the Newberry Library ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- Some Cook County naturalization records (Circuit Court and Superior Court, from the 1840s onward)
- Church registers from parishes outside the fire zone or that stored records off-site

**What was reconstructed:**
- The **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register deeds; this re-filed series is the primary land record source for pre-fire ownership
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company** insurance and title records (Chicago History Museum) substitute for pre-fire property ownership

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Level:** County (Cook County Clerk) and city (Chicago Board of Health)
- **⚠️ Illinois statewide registration began in 1916** — far later than most states, and compliance improved through the 1920s ([Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration)). Do **not** assume statewide records exist before 1916.
- **Cook County local registration:** Birth and death records begin from 1871 at the county level, though coverage is incomplete through the 1870s
- **What exists on FamilySearch — indexed + images:**
  - Birth Certificates 1871–1940: **1,450,000 records** (collection 2024189)
  - Death Records 1871–1947: **980,000 records** (collection 1913456)
  - Marriage Records 1871–1920: **620,000 records** (collection 1756321)
- **Pre-fire vital records:** Birth, marriage, and death registers held at the courthouse were destroyed; church baptismal and burial registers are the primary substitute for events before October 1871
- **Gaps:** Records for the fire days (Oct. 8–10, 1871) and the chaotic weeks immediately after may be absent; fire victim deaths are better documented in newspapers and relief records

### Church records
- **Level:** Parish
- **Denominations:** Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, Jewish
- **What exists on FamilySearch — indexed + images:**
  - Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 — **285,000 records** (collection 1803978)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Survival:** Many pre-fire registers were destroyed when parishes within the fire zone burned; parishes outside the zone survived; re-established parishes began new registers after October 1871
- **Key repository:** Archdiocese of Chicago's **Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers; FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire Cook County church records ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories))
- **Language:** German-language records for Lutheran and Catholic congregations; Swedish-language records for Scandinavian parishes

### Census records
- **Federal census (key years):**
  - **1860 and 1870:** Survived — 1870 originals held in Washington, unaffected by the fire — **indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry; these are the primary pre-fire household snapshots
  - **1880:** First post-fire federal census; shows rebuilt households — **indexed + images**
  - **1890:** Destroyed nationally in a 1921 Washington fire — no federal census for 1890 Chicago families
  - **1900:** Next available; essential for tracing fire-era survivors into the next generation — **indexed + images**
- **Illinois state census:** Illinois took state censuses in 1845, 1855, and 1865; not held at the Cook County Courthouse and largely intact; held at the Illinois State Archives ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for Cook County for 1860, 1870, and 1880 (deaths in the year preceding each census); the 1870 mortality schedule may capture individuals who died around the time of the fire

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire status:** Destroyed in the fire
- **Reconstructed pre-fire copies on FamilySearch:**
  - Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871 — imageGroupNumber **009982110** — 38 images — **0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only** (must be viewed image by image with no search)
- **Post-fire property re-recordings on FamilySearch:**
  - Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880 — imageGroupNumber **009982111** — 112 images — **41% indexed** (partially name-searchable)
- **Naturalization:** Some Cook County Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records survive from the 1840s onward — not all pre-fire court records were lost; held at NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) and IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Public Land Survey System (rectangular) — Illinois is a federal-land state
- **Original patents:** At the BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) — free, not affected by the fire
- **Pre-fire county deed records:** Destroyed in the fire
- **Burnt Record Act re-filings (1872+):** Primary deed source for pre-fire transactions; partially indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 009982111, 41% indexed)
- **Insurance/title substitute:** Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum (physical access only)
- **Testate/intestate note:** Post-fire probate records begin anew after 1871 at the Cook County Circuit Court Clerk; search wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) separately

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Illinois was a major source of Union troops
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (indexed on Fold3.com); Civil War draft registrations (1863); Illinois adjutant general records at the Illinois State Archives
- **Survival:** NARA military records were held in Washington and completely unaffected by the Chicago fire; Civil War pension files are especially rich — they name the widow, children, their ages, and family relationships
- **Access:** Fold3.com for indexed Civil War records; FamilySearch for related collections; Illinois State Archives for adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (1860–), Rosehill Cemetery (1859–), Calvary Catholic Cemetery (1859–), Mount Olivet Cemetery (1885–), Jewish Waldheim Cemetery
- **Online:** FindAGrave.com covers major Chicago cemeteries with headstone photographs — free access
- **Physical:** Sexton and burial registers held at individual cemeteries; contact each cemetery directly for pre-digital records
- **Fire victims specifically:** Newspaper reports and the Chicago Relief and Aid Society records are more likely to identify fire fatalities than cemetery registers

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (1847–present) — the Tribune office survived the fire and continued publishing; it is the single best contemporary source for fire victim names, survivor accounts, and property loss notices

- **Online:** Newspapers.com and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project; Newberry Library holds newspaper microfilm

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden through 1890; Ellis Island from 1892), Baltimore, New Orleans, Quebec; some German and Scandinavian immigrants entered via the Great Lakes

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Chicago Fire (1840–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a town 1833, city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** The fire of October 8–10, 1871 left more than 100,000 residents homeless (Wikipedia); Chicago was one of the fastest-growing cities in North America through this period
- **Economy:** Commercial trade hub, meatpacking, lumber, railroads — the economic center of the Midwest
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, and Scandinavian immigrant communities; also Bohemian, Polish, and American-born residents drawn by economic opportunity
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations — many serving distinct immigrant communities
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, left 100,000+ residents homeless, and obliterated the Cook County Courthouse with virtually all pre-fire civic records

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were largely stable through the target period
- Chicago expanded by annexing surrounding townships throughout the late 19th century; records for annexed areas may have been created under the predecessor township or village before annexation

---

## ⚠️ Critical fire context: Record losses and substitutes

The October 1871 fire is the defining research challenge for this locality. The Cook County Courthouse burned, destroying:
- Pre-fire deed records
- Birth and death registers
- Court and probate records
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers held within the fire zone

**What survived the fire:**
- Federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 — the 1870 originals were held in Washington, D.C., and were not destroyed ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))
- City directories from 1839 onward, held at the Newberry Library ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- Some Cook County naturalization records (Circuit Court and Superior Court, from the 1840s onward)
- Church registers from parishes outside the fire zone or that stored records off-site

**What was reconstructed:**
- Property/deed records: the Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register deeds; the re-filed series is the primary land record source for pre-fire ownership
- Insurance/title records (Chicago Title and Trust Company, at the Chicago History Museum) serve as substitute evidence for pre-fire property

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Level:** County (Cook County Clerk); city (Chicago Board of Health)
- **Illinois statewide registration start:** 1916 — compliance improved through the 1920s ([Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration)). Do **not** assume statewide records exist before 1916.
- **Cook County local registration:** Birth and death records begin from 1871 at the county level, though coverage is incomplete through the 1870s
- **What exists on FamilySearch (indexed + images):**
  - Birth Certificates 1871–1940: 1,450,000 records (collection 2024189)
  - Death Records 1871–1947: 980,000 records (collection 1913456)
  - Marriage Records 1871–1920: 620,000 records (collection 1756321)
- **Pre-fire vital records:** Birth, marriage, and death registers held at the courthouse were destroyed; church baptismal and burial registers are the primary substitute for events before October 1871
- **Gaps:** Records for the fire days (Oct. 8–10, 1871) may be absent or chaotic; fire victim deaths are better documented in newspapers and relief records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations
- **What exists on FamilySearch:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 — 285,000 records (collection 1803978) — **indexed + images**
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Survival note:** Many pre-fire church registers were destroyed when parishes within the fire zone burned; registers from parishes outside the zone survived; re-established parishes began new registers after October 1871
- **Key repository:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives and Records Center holds Catholic parish registers; FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire Cook County church records ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories))
- **Language:** German-language records for Lutheran and Catholic congregations; Swedish-language records for Swedish Lutheran parishes

### Census records
- **Federal census (key years for the fire period):**
  - 1860 and 1870: survived — 1870 originals held in Washington, not destroyed — **indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry; these are the primary pre-fire household snapshots
  - 1880: first post-fire federal census; shows rebuilt households — **indexed + images**
  - 1890: destroyed nationally in a 1921 Washington fire — no federal census for 1890 Chicago families
  - 1900: next available; important for tracing fire-era survivors — **indexed + images**
- **Illinois state census:** Illinois took state censuses in 1845, 1855, and 1865; these were not held at the Cook County Courthouse and survive; held at the Illinois State Archives ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for Cook County for 1860, 1870, and 1880 (recording deaths in the year preceding each census); the 1870 mortality schedule may capture individuals who died in or around the fire period

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire status:** Cook County probate and court records before October 8, 1871 were held at the courthouse and were destroyed
- **Reconstructed copies:** FamilySearch holds Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871 — imageGroupNumber 009982110 — 38 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only** (must be viewed image by image)
- **Post-fire property re-recordings:** imageGroupNumber 009982111 — 112 images, 41% indexed — **partially indexed**; these document the Burnt Record Act re-filings 1871–1880
- **Naturalization:** Some Cook County Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records survive from the 1840s onward; post-fire records are at NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) and IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Public Land Survey System (rectangular survey) — Illinois is a federal-land state
- **Original patents:** At the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) — free, not affected by the fire
- **Pre-fire county deed records:** Destroyed in the fire
- **Burnt Record Act re-filings (1872+):** Primary deed source for pre-fire transactions; partially indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 009982111, 41% indexed)
- **Insurance/title substitute:** Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum (physical access only) document pre-fire property ownership

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Chicago-area men served in Illinois regiments
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (indexed on Fold3.com); Civil War draft registrations (1863); Illinois adjutant general records at the Illinois State Archives
- **Survival:** NARA military records were held in Washington and were unaffected by the Chicago fire; Civil War pension files are especially valuable — they name widow, children, ages, and relationships
- **Access:** Fold3.com for indexed military records; FamilySearch for related collections; Illinois State Archives for state-level adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (1860–), Rosehill Cemetery (1859–), Calvary Catholic Cemetery (1859–), Mount Olivet Cemetery (1885–), Jewish Waldheim Cemetery
- **Online:** FindAGrave.com covers major Chicago cemeteries with headstone photographs — free access
- **Physical:** Sexton and burial registers held at individual cemeteries; contact each cemetery directly for pre-digital records
- **Fire victims specifically:** Newspaper reports and relief records are more likely than cemetery records to identify fire fatalities

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (1847–present); the Tribune office survived the fire and continued publishing — it is the single best contemporary source for fire victim names, survivor accounts, insurance notices, and relief distribution
- **Content value for this research:** Fire victim lists, property loss notices, relief society announcements, and obituaries published October–December 1871 are among the highest-value substitute sources for fire-affected families
- **Online:** Newspapers.com and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project; Newberry Library holds newspaper microfilm

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA (indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch); naturalization records in Cook County courts (some pre-1871 naturalization records survived from the 1840s; post-fire records at NARA Great Lakes Region)
- **Ethnic community sources:** German-language and Swedish-language church registers; fraternal society records (some at Chicago History Museum)
- **Note:** Passenger arrival records were held at the ports of entry, not in Chicago, and were unaffected by the fire

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire:** Cook County tax rolls before October 1871 were held at the courthouse and destroyed
- **Post-fire:** New tax assessments began 1872; Cook County Assessor's office
- **Illinois state tax records:** May survive for pre-fire periods at the Illinois State Archives

### 🔥 Fire-specific records (unique to this locality)

Three record types exist here that have no parallel in most jurisdictions:

1. **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records** — The Society coordinated disaster relief for 100,000+ displaced persons; its records (aid applications, family lists, household composition, pre-fire addresses) are held at the **Chicago History Museum** — physical access by research appointment
2. **Fire insurance claims / Chicago Title and Trust records** — Insurance and title records at the **Chicago History Museum** document pre-fire property ownership; these substitute for the destroyed deed books
3. **Burnt Record Act filings (1872+)** — Property owners re-registered deeds and often described prior ownership history; partially indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 009982111)

### City directories

City directories for Chicago survive from **1839** and were not stored in the courthouse; they are among the most important sources for placing individuals in the city between census years, especially across the pre-fire/post-fire gap. The **Newberry Library** holds the most complete run ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))

- **Religious denominations:** Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations — many serving distinct immigrant communities
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, left 100,000+ residents homeless, and obliterated the Cook County Courthouse with virtually all pre-fire civic records

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were largely stable through the target period
- Chicago expanded by annexing surrounding townships throughout the late 19th century; records for annexed areas may have been created under the predecessor township or village before annexation

---

## ⚠️ Critical fire context: Record losses and substitutes

The October 1871 fire is the defining research challenge for this locality. The Cook County Courthouse burned, destroying:
- Pre-fire deed records
- Birth and death registers
- Court and probate records
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers held within the fire zone

**What survived the fire:**
- Federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 — the 1870 originals were held in Washington, D.C., and were not destroyed ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))
- City directories from 1839 onward, held at the Newberry Library ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- Some Cook County naturalization records (Circuit Court and Superior Court, from the 1840s onward)
- Church registers from parishes outside the fire zone or that stored records off-site

**What was reconstructed:**
- Property/deed records: the Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register deeds; the re-filed series is the primary land record source for pre-fire ownership
- Insurance/title records (Chicago Title and Trust Company, at the Chicago History Museum) serve as substitute evidence for pre-fire property

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Level:** County (Cook County Clerk); city (Chicago Board of Health)
- **Illinois statewide registration start:** 1916 — compliance improved through the 1920s ([Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration)). Do **not** assume statewide records exist before 1916.
- **Cook County local registration:** Birth and death records begin from 1871 at the county level, though coverage is incomplete through the 1870s
- **What exists on FamilySearch (indexed + images):**
  - Birth Certificates 1871–1940: 1,450,000 records (collection 2024189)
  - Death Records 1871–1947: 980,000 records (collection 1913456)
  - Marriage Records 1871–1920: 620,000 records (collection 1756321)
- **Pre-fire vital records:** Birth, marriage, and death registers held at the courthouse were destroyed; church baptismal and burial registers are the primary substitute for events before October 1871
- **Gaps:** Records for the fire days (Oct. 8–10, 1871) may be absent or chaotic; fire victim deaths are better documented in newspapers and relief records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic, German Lutheran, Swedish Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations
- **What exists on FamilySearch:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 — 285,000 records (collection 1803978) — **indexed + images**
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Survival note:** Many pre-fire church registers were destroyed when parishes within the fire zone burned; registers from parishes outside the zone survived; re-established parishes began new registers after October 1871
- **Key repository:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives and Records Center holds Catholic parish registers; FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire Cook County church records ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories))
- **Language:** German-language records for Lutheran and Catholic congregations; Swedish-language records for Swedish Lutheran parishes

### Census records
- **Federal census (key years for the fire period):**
  - 1860 and 1870: survived — 1870 originals held in Washington, not destroyed — **indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry; these are the primary pre-fire household snapshots
  - 1880: first post-fire federal census; shows rebuilt households — **indexed + images**
  - 1890: destroyed nationally in a 1921 Washington fire — no federal census for 1890 Chicago families
  - 1900: next available; important for tracing fire-era survivors — **indexed + images**
- **Illinois state census:** Illinois took state censuses in 1845, 1855, and 1865; these were not held at the Cook County Courthouse and survive; held at the Illinois State Archives ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for Cook County for 1860, 1870, and 1880 (recording deaths in the year preceding each census); the 1870 mortality schedule may capture individuals who died in or around the fire period

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire status:** Cook County probate and court records before October 8, 1871 were held at the courthouse and were destroyed
- **Reconstructed copies:** FamilySearch holds Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871 — imageGroupNumber 009982110 — 38 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only** (must be viewed image by image)
- **Post-fire property re-recordings:** imageGroupNumber 009982111 — 112 images, 41% indexed — **partially indexed**; these document the Burnt Record Act re-filings 1871–1880
- **Naturalization:** Some Cook County Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records survive from the 1840s onward; post-fire records are at NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) and IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Public Land Survey System (rectangular survey) — Illinois is a federal-land state
- **Original patents:** At the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) — free, not affected by the fire
- **Pre-fire county deed records:** Destroyed in the fire
- **Burnt Record Act re-filings (1872+):** Primary deed source for pre-fire transactions; partially indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 009982111, 41% indexed)
- **Insurance/title substitute:** Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum (physical access only) document pre-fire property ownership

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Chicago-area men served in Illinois regiments
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (indexed on Fold3.com); Civil War draft registrations (1863); Illinois adjutant general records at the Illinois State Archives
- **Survival:** NARA military records were held in Washington and were unaffected by the Chicago fire; Civil War pension files are especially valuable — they name widow, children, ages, and relationships
- **Access:** Fold3.com for indexed military records; FamilySearch for related collections; Illinois State Archives for state-level adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (1860–), Rosehill Cemetery (1859–), Calvary Catholic Cemetery (1859–), Mount Olivet Cemetery (1885–), Jewish Waldheim Cemetery
- **Online:** FindAGrave.com covers major Chicago cemeteries with headstone photographs — free access
- **Physical:** Sexton and burial registers held at individual cemeteries; contact each cemetery directly for pre-digital records
- **Fire victims specifically:** Newspaper reports and relief records are more likely than cemetery records to identify fire fatalities

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (1847–present); the Tribune office survived the fire and continued publishing — it is the single best contemporary source for fire victim names, survivor accounts, insurance notices, and relief distribution
- **Content value for this research:** Fire victim lists, property loss notices, relief society announcements, and obituaries published October–December 1871 are among the highest-value substitute sources for fire-affected families
- **Online:** Newspapers.com and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project; Newberry Library holds newspaper microfilm

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden through 1890, Ellis Island from 1892), Baltimore, New Orleans, Quebec; some German and Scandinavian immigrants entered via the Great Lakes
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA (indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch); naturalization records in Cook County courts (some pre-1871 naturalization records survived from the 1840s; post-fire records at NARA Great Lakes Region)
- **Ethnic community sources:** German-language and Swedish-language church registers; fraternal society records (some at Chicago History Museum)
- **Note:** Passenger arrival records were held at the ports of entry, not in Chicago, and were unaffected by the fire

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire:** Cook County tax rolls before October 1871 were held at the courthouse and destroyed
- **Post-fire:** New tax assessments began 1872; Cook County Assessor's office
- **Illinois state tax records:** May survive for pre-fire periods at the Illinois State Archives

### 🔥 Fire-specific records (unique to this locality)

Three record types exist here that have no parallel in most jurisdictions:

1. **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records** — The Society coordinated disaster relief for 100,000+ displaced persons; its records (aid applications, family lists, household composition, pre-fire addresses) are held at the **Chicago History Museum** — physical access by research appointment
2. **Fire insurance claims / Chicago Title and Trust records** — Insurance and title records at the **Chicago History Museum** document pre-fire property ownership; these substitute for the destroyed deed books
3. **Burnt Record Act filings (1872+)** — Property owners re-registered deeds and often described prior ownership history; partially indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 009982111)

### City directories

City directories for Chicago survive from **1839** and were not stored in the courthouse; they are among the most important sources for placing individuals in the city between census years, especially across the pre-fire/post-fire gap. The **Newberry Library** holds the most complete run ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))

---

---

## Records NOT online

- **Chicago Relief and Aid Society family relief records** (Chicago History Museum — physical access only; research appointment required)
