- **Illinois state census records** (1845, 1855, 1865) for Cook County — at Illinois State Archives; not fully digitized
- **Pre-1906 surviving Cook County naturalization records** — microfilmed but accessed via NARA Great Lakes Region or IRAD

---

## Known record losses

| What was lost | When / Why | Best substitute sources |
|---|---|---|
| Cook County deed records | Fire, Oct. 8–10, 1871 | Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872+, FamilySearch IGN 009982111); Chicago Title and Trust records at Chicago History Museum |
| Cook County birth and death registers | Fire, Oct. 8–10, 1871 | Post-fire county registration from 1871 (FamilySearch colls. 2024189, 1913456); church registers; newspapers |
| Cook County court and probate records | Fire, Oct. 8–10, 1871 | Re-filed probate petitions; newspaper legal notices; some reconstructed copies (FamilySearch IGN 009982110, browse-only) |
| Cook County tax rolls | Fire, Oct. 8–10, 1871 | City directories; insurance records; Illinois State Archives tax records |
| Pre-fire church registers (many parishes) | Fire, Oct. 8–10, 1871 | Re-established parish registers from late 1871; Archdiocese Archives |
| 1890 federal census (nationwide) | Fire, Washington D.C., 1921 | 1880 and 1900 census; city directories; state census |

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the 1870 and 1880 federal censuses** as your anchors. The 1870 survived because the originals were held in Washington; the 1880 shows the rebuilt household. These two records bracket the fire and are your foundation ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)).

2. **The Chicago Relief and Aid Society records (Chicago History Museum)** are the single best fire-specific source for displaced families — they document household composition, pre-fire address, and relief received. Request a research appointment.

3. **Never exhaust online searches hoping to find a pre-fire Cook County record** — the underlying record was almost certainly destroyed in the fire itself. Pivot immediately to substitute sources rather than extending a fruitless online search.

4. **City directories from 1839 (Newberry Library)** are the most important intercensal source and were not destroyed; use them to trace a family's address year by year across the fire gap.

5. **Illinois statewide vital registration began in 1916** — far later than most states. For births, marriages, and deaths before 1916, Cook County local registration (from 1871) and church registers are your primary civil and quasi-civil sources ([Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration)).

6. **Some pre-fire Cook County naturalization records survived** — the Circuit Court and Superior Court records from the 1840s onward were not all stored at the courthouse; check NARA Great Lakes Region and IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University ([Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records)).

7. **Search the Chicago Tribune (Newspapers.com)** for October–December 1871 fire victim lists, survivor accounts, insurance claim notices, and relief distribution announcements — these are among the richest fire-era substitutes for identifying specific families.

8. **For immigrant families**, passenger lists and naturalization records were held at ports or federal/court repositories outside Chicago and were unaffected by the fire; trace the arrival record independently of the local record loss.

9. **The 1870 mortality schedule** records deaths in the year before the 1870 census and may capture individuals from the immediate pre-fire period; the 1880 mortality schedule covers the reconstruction era.

10. **Illinois is a federal-land (public land survey) state** — original land patents are at the BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) and were not affected by the fire.

# Louisiana Locality Guide: French Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdictional Context

**Critical boundary note — the 1700s were split between two colonial powers.** The French colonial period covers **1699–1762**. By the **Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)**, France secretly ceded territory west of the Mississippi to Spain; the eastern strip went to Britain. Effective Spanish administration began only in **1769** after the French governor was expelled. So the latter third of the 1700s — roughly 1769–1800 — is **Spanish colonial Louisiana**, with its own distinct record repositories in Seville, Spain. Families spanning the transition generated records under both regimes.

Louisiana was organized around **Catholic parishes**, not counties. No English-style county courthouse existed. The **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)** was the primary civil governing body under French rule. There was **no civil vital registration** during any part of the 1700s — Catholic parish registers are the only vital records source for this entire century.

---

## Record Types

### 1. 📜 Catholic Parish Registers — PRIMARY vital records source

**What they contain:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. The **Code Noir** (Black Code) legally required the Catholic Church to baptize all enslaved persons, so these registers also document enslaved individuals — often the only record of their existence.

**Coverage:** St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans holds registers **from 1720**. Rural parishes generally began later; survival rates vary.

**Language:** **French** before 1769; **Spanish** afterward. Researchers must read both.

**On FamilySearch:** Collection **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (ID: 1612905) — approximately 987,654 records with ~493,827 images. The image count being roughly half the record count suggests partial digitization; some volumes may be browse-only.
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905

**Physical access:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans) and individual parish archives.

---

### 2. 🏛️ Superior Council Records — essential civil documents

**What they contain:** Land grants (*concessions*), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories, and civil disputes. Under French rule the Superior Council was the equivalent of county courts for all later periods.

**Coverage:** French colonial period (1699–1762). After 1769 the Spanish Cabildo replaced it, with its own parallel records.

**Repository:** **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans. Records are partially digitized; many volumes are browse-only or require an in-person visit. Contact the Center directly for current online availability.

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)"*
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records

---

### 3. 📋 Notarial Records — contracts, wills, marriage settlements

**What they contain:** Marriage contracts (common under French civil law), wills, property transactions, and other notarized instruments. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives** is the oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America, with records from the **1730s** onward.

**Why important:** Under French (and later Spanish) civil law, major family events were routinely notarized. Marriage contracts frequently name parents and siblings on both sides; wills name heirs in detail.

**Repository:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — public access. Some records are partially digitized; many require in-person research.

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants"*
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants

---

### 4. 🌍 Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) — French government records

**What they contain:** Administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls, military and militia records, official dispatches, and immigration lists for the **French colonial period (1699–1762)**. This is the primary archive for France's overseas colonial administration.

**Location:** Aix-en-Provence, France. A growing portion of the ANOM holdings is accessible online via their portal.
🔗 https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr/

**For the Spanish period (1762–1800):** The equivalent repository is the **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)** in Seville, Spain — specifically the **Papeles Procedentes de Cuba** series, which covers Louisiana under Spanish rule. Accessible via the PARES online portal: https://pares.mcu.es/

---

### 5. 🗺️ Land Records — concessions and grants

**What they contain:** French *concessions* (land grants) document who settled where and often name family members, neighbors, and property boundaries.

**Repositories:**
- **American State Papers: Public Lands** — compiled French concessions and Spanish grants; available via HathiTrust and other online platforms.
- **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge) — colonial and territorial-era land patent records.
- **ANOM** (France) — original concession documents for the French period.

**On FamilySearch:** Collection **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (ID: 2078341) — ~456,789 records, ~228,394 images; covers the colonial period from 1756 and includes estate and land-related proceedings.
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341

---

### 6. 🧾 Colonial Census Rolls

**What they contain:** Occasional administrative enumeration rolls listing heads of household, family members, enslaved persons, and livestock. These were not systematic annual counts but periodic administrative surveys.

---

# Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide
**Target period: ca. 1870–1900**

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

Pennsylvania's coal region divides into two geographic belts, each with its own county structure:

**Anthracite (northeastern PA):** Schuylkill County (formed 1811), Carbon County (formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton), Luzerne County, Lackawanna County (formed 1878 from Luzerne), Northumberland County, Columbia County

**Bituminous (western/southwestern PA):** Cambria County (formed 1804), and the Allegheny, Westmoreland, Fayette, Washington, Greene, Indiana, Clearfield, and Jefferson county belt

> **Critical quirk — Lackawanna County:** Lackawanna was carved from Luzerne County in 1878. Records for Scranton and surrounding mining towns before 1878 are filed under Luzerne County. For any event in that area, search Luzerne first for pre-1878, then Lackawanna for 1878 onward — these form one continuous research trail despite the different county names.

---

## Vital Records

**Pennsylvania did not have statewide civil death registration until 1906.** The FamilySearch collection [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) (4.2 million records, fully indexed with images) begins after the 1870–1900 target window, but it is still worth checking — it frequently names parents, birthplace, and siblings of miners who died after 1906.

For births and deaths during 1870–1900, **church registers are the primary source** (see below). Do not assume civil vital records exist for this period.

**Marriage records on FamilySearch — indexed collections covering part or all of 1870–1900:**

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 | [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 1885–1950 | ~524,000 records, indexed |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | ~312,000 records, indexed |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | ~199,000 records, no images — index only |

---

## Church Records — Highest Priority for This Period

The FamilySearch wiki notes that ethnic parishes serving specific mining communities often hold the most detailed family data for 1870–1900, frequently containing the only contemporaneous birth, marriage, and burial records. The coal region drew heavily from:

- **Irish** — Roman Catholic parishes
- **Welsh** — Congregational and Baptist chapels
- **German** — Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed congregations
- **Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, Ukrainian** — arriving in larger numbers from the 1880s onward, each group typically forming its own national parish

**Where to find them:** Check both the denomination's own archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings. FamilySearch's collections search returned one Schuylkill County church records item flagged as a test fixture and not citable as an operational collection — confirm current digitization status directly on FamilySearch for church record coverage in your specific county.

*(Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide))*

---

## Mining-Industry Records ⛏️

This is the category most distinctive to coal-town research. The FamilySearch wiki specifically identifies ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)):

**State Mine Inspector Reports (annual, 1870 onward)**
- List every fatal mining accident by name, age, nationality, and cause of death
- Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg)
- Invaluable for confirming a miner's identity, approximate age, and country of origin

**Company Employment and Payroll Records**
- Employment cards, payroll ledgers, and accident reports survive fragmentarily at the PA State Archives and at county-level historical societies
- Three digitized volumes found on FamilySearch for this period:

| Volume | Place | Record Type | Years | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 002240015 | Schuylkill County | Mine Worker Employment Cards | 1870–1900 | 410 | **Indexed (95%) + full-text searchable** — searchable by name |
| 002240016 | Luzerne County | Mine Accident Reports | 1870–1895 | 287 | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image |
| 002240017 | Lackawanna County | Colliery Payroll Ledgers | 1878–1900 | 199 | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image |

> ⚠️ The volume search returned 23 total volumes for this period but only 3 were returned in this page of results. Additional volumes covering other counties or record types likely exist — browse the next pages on FamilySearch directly.

**United Mine Workers of America (UMWA, founded 1890)**
Membership rolls and grievance files; check the [Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources) wiki page for current holdings information.

---

## Federal Census (1870–1900)

The federal censuses of 1870, 1880, 1900 (and the 1890 — nearly entirely destroyed) are fully indexed and available at FamilySearch and Ancestry.com. Miners are consistently recorded with the occupation "miner." These schedules are the backbone of family reconstruction for this period, especially given the absence of civil vital records.

- **1880 Soundex** is fully indexed at FamilySearch
- **1900 census** added months/years of immigration and citizenship status — especially useful for the wave of Eastern European miners arriving in the 1880s–1890s

---

## Immigration and Naturalization

Immigration is central to coal-town research. The FamilySearch wiki notes ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)):

- Most miners arrived through **Philadelphia** or **New York** — passenger lists at NARA and searchable via Ancestry.com and FamilySearch
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** were filed in any court of record (federal, state, or local) and are geographically scattered. **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- After September 1906, naturalizations were centralized through the federal Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization — use NARA for those.

---

## Probate Records

[Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — ~893,000 records, indexed with images. Covers the full 1870–1900 window. Wills and estate inventories can reveal family members, property, and—for miners—tools and equipment as personal property.

---

## Military Records

For veterans of the Civil War (many miners were veterans by the 1870s–1880s):
- **Pension files** at NARA are the richest source — they often include affidavits from neighbors and relatives, marriage certificates, and detailed personal histories
- **[Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)** holds digitized service records and pension index cards
- Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant general records

---

## Newspapers

[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical newspapers including titles from the anthracite coal region (Pottsville, Scranton, Wilkes-Barre). Mining accident notices, obituaries, and labor strike coverage frequently name individuals. Check also for **Welsh-language newspapers** (*Y Drych*, "The Mirror") which served Welsh mining communities.

---

## Repositories Summary

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports (1870+), Schuylkill County naturalizations, state-level records | Physical and some online via PA state portal |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local mining collections, newspapers, local histories | Physical visit |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton) | Mining community records, labor records | Physical visit |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Marriage, probate, census, mining employment volumes (see above) | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census, passenger lists, newspapers | Subscription |
| **NARA** (Philadelphia regional branch + Washington) | Naturalization records, passenger lists, pension files | Physical and online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Fold3.com** | Civil War service and pension records | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave.com** | Cemetery transcriptions for coal-town cemeteries | Free online |

---

## Gaps and Coverage Notes

- **Vital registration gap:** No civil birth or death records exist at the state level before 1906 for the target period. Church registers and the federal census are the substitutes.
- **Browse-only mining volumes:** The Luzerne mine accident reports and Lackawanna payroll ledgers must be browsed page by page with no name search — budget time accordingly.
- **23 total digitized volumes** were found for this period; only 3 were returned in this result set. Check FamilySearch directly for the full list, particularly for Carbon, Cambria, and Northumberland counties.
- **Population data** was not returned by the place population tool for this query — consult Wikipedia or the PA State Archives for census population figures by county.
- **FamilySearch Wiki** returned a generic guide rather than Pennsylvania-specific pages. For Pennsylvania-specific research strategy guidance, visit [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania) directly.

---

**Where to start:** If you have a miner ancestor and know the approximate county, begin with the **1880 and 1900 federal census** to establish the household, then check **church records** for vital events, and **Mine Inspector reports** if you need to confirm identity or find a death. For immigrants arriving after 1880, add a **passenger list search** and look for **county naturalization records** at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

# Locality Research Guide: Massachusetts, 1620–1700 (Puritan Settlements)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Two **separate colonies** operated in what is now Massachusetts during this period — they had different governing bodies and distinct record series:

- **Plymouth Colony (1620–1691):** Founded by the Pilgrims (Separatists) at Plymouth. Its records are published and indexed **separately** from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691):** The larger Puritan colony centered at Boston. Governor John Winthrop led the Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640. (Wikipedia)

After 1691, both colonies were consolidated into the **Province of Massachusetts Bay** under a royal charter.

**County formation:** Four original counties were established in 1643 — Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Hampshire. County-level records (deeds, probate) begin at or shortly after county formation. Before 1643, those records were kept at the colony level.

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk — Plymouth vs. Massachusetts Bay:** Before 1691, always establish which colony your ancestor lived in. Plymouth Colony records are indexed and published in a completely separate series from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Searching only one set will miss the other.

---

## ⚠️ Important Note on Vital Registration Dates

Massachusetts **town clerks** were mandated by the General Court to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** — this is a **town-level** requirement, one of the earliest civil registration mandates in North America. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

**Statewide** civil registration did not begin until **1841**. These are two entirely different events. For the 1620–1700 period, you are searching town-level records, not a central state registry.

---

## Record Types, Collections, and Access

### 1. 🏘️ Town Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
**Target period coverage:** Yes — 1620 onward | **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

The cornerstone of early Massachusetts genealogy. Town clerks were required to register births, marriages, and deaths from 1639; some towns recorded earlier. This is the first place to search for any event in this period.

- **FamilySearch:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* — Collection ID [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — 3,456,789 records, 1,728,394 images (as returned by FamilySearch).
- **Published abstracts:** The multi-volume *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series (Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for more than 200 Massachusetts towns. Available at NEHGS and many libraries. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Physical originals:** Town clerk offices and the Massachusetts Archives (Columbia Point, Boston).

> **Quirk:** The 1639 mandate did not guarantee compliance. Coverage varies by town and by decade — some early volumes are sparse or lost. Always check both the published abstract series *and* the original town volumes.

---

### 2. ⛪ Church Records (Congregational/Puritan)
**Target period coverage:** Yes — 1630 onward | **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

Congregational meetings were the established church of the colony. Their registers — member rolls, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments) — often document individuals and family connections not captured in civil records.

- **FamilySearch:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* — Collection ID [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — 987,654 records, 493,827 images (as returned by FamilySearch).
- **Published transcriptions:** Many early registers are published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society volumes. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Physical originals:** Individual churches (where still active), the Massachusetts Archives, NEHGS, and local historical societies.

> **Quirk:** Not all congregations kept equally detailed records, and some early registers are lost entirely. Disciplinary records can document names and family relationships found nowhere else. Church *membership* lists typically cover only baptized adults — servants, non-members, and some women may appear only in town or court records.

---

### 3. 📜 Probate Records
**Target period coverage:** Yes — 1635 onward | **Digitization level:** Indexed + images

Probate files (wills, inventories, administration bonds, guardianship records) are among the richest sources for family relationships in this period and begin at the county level from 1635.

- **FamilySearch:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* — Collection ID [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — 567,890 records, 283,945 images (as returned by FamilySearch).
- **Physical originals:** County probate courts and the Massachusetts Archives.

> **Quirk:** Before county formation in 1643, probate was handled at the colony level. For events before 1643, search the Massachusetts Archives colony-level records rather than a county probate court.

---

### 4. 🏡 Land Records (Deeds, Grants, Patents)
**Target period coverage:** Yes — 1630s onward | **Digitization level:** Physical/microfilm; partial digitization

Land grants, deeds, and patents were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and "survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds." ([FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)) FamilySearch's indexed collections did not return a standalone Massachusetts deeds collection for the 1620–1700 window in this survey — land records for this period must be searched at county registries or through NEHGS.

- **County Registries of Deeds** (one per county — Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Hampshire): Hold original deed volumes from county formation (1643).
- **Colony-level grants (pre-1643):** Massachusetts Archives, Boston.
- **Plymouth Colony land records:** Published — see Plymouth Colony section below.
- **NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org):** Holds indexes and transcripts for many early deed series.

> **Quirk:** Land records are among the most complete surviving records from this era and frequently name neighbors, witnesses, and family members absent from vital and church records. Town proprietors' records — who received land grants when a new town was incorporated — are a key supplement.

---

### 5. ⚖️ Court Records (Colony and County Courts)
**Target period coverage:** Yes — 1620s onward | **Digitization level:** Published transcripts; partial digitization

The General Court, Court of Assistants, and county courts heard civil, criminal, and ecclesiastical matters. Court files name litigants, witnesses, jurors, and sureties — often documenting individuals who appear nowhere in vital or church records.

- **Massachusetts Archives** (Columbia Point, Boston): Original colony court records and governor's correspondence from the 1620s onward. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- Published transcripts of Essex, Suffolk, Middlesex, and Plymouth county court records exist in multi-volume print editions, available at NEHGS.

---

### 6. 🚢 Plymouth Colony Records (1620–1691)
**Target period coverage:** Yes | **Digitization level:** Published, indexed separately

Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) records are published and indexed **independently** from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)) These include vital, land, court, and church records for the Plymouth area.

- **Key published source:** *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England* (12 volumes) — available at NEHGS and major libraries.
- After the 1691 merger, Plymouth-area records appear in the Massachusetts provincial series.

---

### 7. 🚢 Great Migration / Passenger Arrivals (1620–1643)
**Target period coverage:** Yes — 1620–1643 | **Access:** Published; NEHGS

The approximately 20,000 settlers who arrived during the Great Migration are documented in a dedicated published study — the first resource to consult for any ancestor arriving in this window.

- **Great Migration Study (NEHGS):** Documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643, aggregating citations to original sources. Available at NEHGS and genealogical libraries. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

---

## Oklahoma Locality Guide — Land Run Era, 1889–1910

### Jurisdictional Context

The 1889–1910 window spans **two distinct civil regimes**, which directly determines where records were created and are now held:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Capital / Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-Apr 22, 1889 | Unassigned Lands / Indian Territory | No settler civil government |
| Apr 22, 1889 – May 1, 1890 | Post-Land Run, pre-Organic Act | Federal land offices (Guthrie, Kingfisher) |
| May 2, 1890 – Nov 15, 1907 | **Oklahoma Territory** (Organic Act) | Guthrie; territorial district courts |
| Concurrent 1889–1907 | **Indian Territory** (eastern OK) | Five Civilized Tribes nations; separate federal jurisdiction |
| Nov 16, 1907 onward | **State of Oklahoma** | Oklahoma City (after 1910) |

**Critical quirk:** Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma, where the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee/Creek, and Seminole nations held land) coexisted *alongside* Oklahoma Territory as a completely separate federal jurisdiction until statehood. A family in 1900 Oklahoma could be under either territory depending on exactly where they lived — the record regime that applies differs accordingly. Search both streams if the county is near the boundary.

Subsequent land runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened additional areas; the Organic Act counties were reorganized as each new district opened. Early county boundaries shifted significantly between 1890 and 1907 — verify which county your township fell in *on the date of the event*, not at statehood. [(Wikipedia: Land Run of 1889)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Run_of_1889)

---

### ⭐ Record Class 1 — Land & Homestead Records
**The single most important record class for Land Run research.**

**What they are:** Each homestead claim generated a file that typically contains the original application, proof of settlement with witness testimony, and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive and can be equally informative about families. The General Land Office (GLO) administered the filings.

**Where they are:**
- **National Archives, Washington D.C.** — Record Group 49, General Land Office. Original homestead case files.
- **BLM GLO Records website** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — searchable index of federal land patents for Oklahoma; many patents are imaged online.
- **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (Collection [1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)): 234,567 indexed records with 117,283 images. Covers both the territorial and Indian Territory land systems through 1907.

**Access level:** Name-indexed and imaged on FamilySearch. Also searchable by name at glorecords.blm.gov.

**Research note:** Land offices at Guthrie and Kingfisher were the original 1889 filing points. Later runs added offices at Perry, Enid, and Woodward. The filing office for a claim is noted in the patent and can help you identify the specific land run your ancestor participated in. [(FamilySearch Wiki: Oklahoma Land Records)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)

---

### Record Class 2 — Indian Censuses, Rolls & Tribal Records
**Essential even for non-Native families — neighbors, witnesses, and mixed-heritage families appear here.**

**What they are:** Federal and tribal censuses of the Five Civilized Tribes, the Dawes Rolls (the definitive enrollment, 1898–1914, required for tribal citizenship), and earlier annuity/census rolls.

**Where they are:**
- **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (Collection [1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)): 567,890 indexed records with 283,945 images. This is the largest Oklahoma collection on FamilySearch and covers the full territorial and early-state period.
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — original Dawes Rolls enrollment jackets; these files often contain family statements, affidavits, and correspondence far richer than the printed rolls.
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — supplementary tribal records and enrollment records.

**Access level:** Name-indexed and imaged on FamilySearch.

**Research note:** The Dawes Rolls enrolled citizens of the Five Civilized Tribes between 1898 and 1914. Anyone in eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory) with tribal heritage — or claiming it — should be searched here. The rolls distinguished "citizens by blood," "citizens by marriage," "freedmen" (formerly enslaved people of the nations), and "Delaware and Shawnee adopted" citizens.

---

### Record Class 3 — Census Records

**1890 Federal Census:** Almost entirely destroyed by fire. However, the **Oklahoma Territory special census of 1890** is one of the rare surviving fragments from that year. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds this record; it documents very early territorial settlers. [(FamilySearch Wiki: Oklahoma Land Records)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)

**1900 Federal Census:** Oklahoma Territory was enumerated fully. This is the primary census for Land Run–era families. Available on Ancestry.com ([U.S. Federal Census Collection](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) and FamilySearch (free).

**1910 Federal Census:** State of Oklahoma — taken three years after statehood. Families who arrived in the Land Run are now well-established; birthplaces and ages can be cross-checked against land files. Also on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.

**County-level tax rolls (1890s):** Territorial-era tax rolls at the Oklahoma State Archives help document settlers between federal censuses. [(FamilySearch Wiki: Oklahoma Territorial Records)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

---

### Record Class 4 — Vital Records

**Birth and death registration:** Oklahoma did **not** require statewide registration of births and deaths until October 1908 — more than a year after statehood. For 1889–1908, expect no routine civil birth or death records. Substitute sources: church registers, family Bibles, cemetery records, obituaries in newspapers, and doctor/midwife records.

**Marriage records:** County clerks began recording marriages when counties were organized under the Organic Act (1890). FamilySearch has *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* (Collection [2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)): 456,789 indexed records covering 913,578 persons, with 228,394 images. This is name-indexed and imaged — the primary source for territorial-era marriages.

**Access level:** Marriages — name-indexed and imaged on FamilySearch from 1890. Births and deaths before 1908 — no civil record; use substitutes.

---

### Record Class 5 — Church & Mission Records

Denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic) established congregations rapidly in new towns after 1889. Records begin sporadically from 1889 and become more consistent by the mid-1890s.

**FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (Collection [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)): 123,456 indexed records with 61,728 images. Pre-1889 entries in this collection cover mission activity in Indian Territory (a valuable parallel resource).

**Access level:** Name-indexed and imaged on FamilySearch.

**Research note:** For eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory), Presbyterian and Baptist mission records documenting the Five Civilized Tribes communities predate 1889 by decades and may name mixed-heritage families.

---

### Record Class 6 — Territorial Court Records

Oklahoma Territory district courts (1890–1907) created records covering:
- **Probate** — wills, estate inventories, guardianships
- **Naturalization** — pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; territorial district courts are the primary Oklahoma venue
- **Civil and criminal cases** — land disputes, claim jumping, and contract suits were extremely common in the Land Run era

**Where they are:**
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — primary repository for Oklahoma territorial court records
- **Oklahoma State Archives** — supplementary holdings [(FamilySearch Wiki: Oklahoma Territorial Records)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

**Access level:** Physical records at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives; limited digitization. Plan an in-person visit or hire a local researcher for intensive court research.

**Research note:** Claim-jumping disputes and contests over homestead filings generated substantial court files that name multiple family members, neighbors, and witnesses — rich sources beyond just vital facts.

---

### Record Class 7 — Military Records

**Spanish-American War (1898):** Many Oklahoma Territory men served. Service records and pension files at NARA Washington, D.C. Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) has indexed Spanish-American War records.

**Territorial/National Guard:** Oklahoma Territory had a militia; records may be at the Oklahoma State Archives.

**Civil War veterans in Oklahoma:** Many Land Run participants were Union or Confederate veterans who came to Oklahoma in middle age. Pension files at NARA are rich biographical sources for these men and their widows.

---

### Record Class 8 — Newspapers

Land Run–era newspapers began publishing almost immediately in new towns (Guthrie had a paper within hours of the April 22, 1889 opening). Papers covered claim disputes, community news, arrivals, legal notices, and deaths.

- **Newspapers.com** — [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) — subscription service with Oklahoma territorial newspapers
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — extensive newspaper holdings, including microfilm of many territorial-era papers
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — some Oklahoma territorial newspapers digitized

---

### Record Class 9 — Tracing Origins (Departure-State Research)

Land Run settlers came overwhelmingly from Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Arkansas, and other nearby states. Many families have no Oklahoma record before 1889 — their full life histories are in their origin state.

**Strategy:** Use the 1900 census birthplace column and the homestead proof statements (which often name the state of prior residence) to identify where the family came from, then search that state's records for the preceding generation.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (free) | Land records, Indian rolls, marriages, church records | Online — familysearch.org |
| **BLM GLO Records** (free) | Land patents | Online — glorecords.blm.gov |
| **National Archives, Washington D.C.** | Homestead case files (RG 49), military pension files | In-person or fee-based copy requests |
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Territorial court records, Indian Territory records | In-person or written requests |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | 1890 territorial census, newspapers, state records | In-person; some online — okhistory.org |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** | State records post-1907, some territorial records | In-person — Oklahoma City |
| **Ancestry.com** (subscription) | 1900 and 1910 federal censuses, newspaper collections | Online |
| **Fold3** (subscription) | Military service and pension records | Online |
| **FindAGrave** (free) | Cemetery and memorial records | Online — findagrave.com |

---

### Key Quirks & Cautions

1. **Two parallel jurisdictions, 1889–1907.** Oklahoma Territory (west/central) and Indian Territory (east) were completely separate until statehood. Which one applies depends on the exact location — verify before searching the wrong court or record system.
2. **1890 federal census is gone — but the territorial special census survives.** The Oklahoma Historical Society holds the 1890 territorial census, one of the nation's rarest surviving 1890 records.
3. **No statewide birth or death registration until October 1908.** Expect no civil vital records for the entire territorial period and the first year of statehood. Use church records, newspapers, cemetery records, and court files instead.
4. **County boundaries shifted frequently, 1890–1907.** An event in 1893 may have been recorded in a different county than the same township in 1901. Check boundary histories before assuming which county courthouse holds the record.
5. **Homestead proof statements are biographical gold.** Each final homestead proof required the settler to give testimony — age, origin, family composition, neighbors as witnesses — under oath. Do not stop at the patent; request the full case file from NARA.
6. **Sooner vs. Boomer claims were contested.** Many homestead filings faced challenge. Contest records at NARA contain adversarial testimony about both claimants — both records are worth finding.
7. **Origins research is mandatory.** Most Land Run families arrived as adults with full lives in Kansas, Missouri, Arkansas, or Texas. The richest genealogical records for these families are in their origin states, not in Oklahoma.
8. **Pre-1906 naturalizations scattered across territorial courts.** Oklahoma Territory settlers who naturalized before 1906 could have done so in any territorial district court — not just the one nearest their home. Check all districts if a naturalization is not found locally.

# Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, circa 1800 (Pre-Statehood)

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

Around 1800 the "Alabama region" was not a single jurisdiction — it was three overlapping ones, and which one a family falls under determines entirely where their records were created and are now held.

**Mississippi Territory (1798–1817)**
The US organized most of present-day Alabama under the Mississippi Territory, established in 1798. This territory covered both present-day Alabama and Mississippi. Records — land entries, court proceedings, tax lists, militia rolls — were generated under territorial authority and are held primarily at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery and at the National Archives.

**Spanish West Florida / Mobile District (to 1813)**
The southern strip of present-day Alabama — roughly everything south of the 31st parallel, centered on Mobile — remained under Spanish rule until April 1813, when US forces seized Mobile. Before 1813, the Mobile district was administered by Spain, and before that by France (1702–1763) and Britain (1763–1780). Records for this zone before 1813 are Spanish (and earlier French or British) colonial documents, in foreign archives. This is a completely separate archival lineage from the US territorial records.

**Alabama Territory (1817–1819)**
When Mississippi achieved statehood in 1817, the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory became the Alabama Territory. Alabama reached statehood on December 14, 1819.

**Indigenous Territory**
The Creek Nation controlled much of central and southern Alabama; the Cherokee occupied the northeast. US settler record-keeping in the interior effectively did not begin until after the Creek War of 1813–14 opened those lands to Anglo-American settlement. If your family was in the interior before 1814, there are essentially no US records for them.

---

## Critical Research Quirks

- **Split jurisdiction, split archives.** A Mobile-area family around 1800 falls under Spanish West Florida records. A northern/central Alabama family falls under Mississippi Territory records. These are entirely different archival systems — searching only one will miss the other.
- **No civil vital registration.** There was no territorial or early-statehood requirement to register births, marriages, or deaths. Church records are the only source for vital events, and outside the Mobile Catholic community, coverage before 1810 is extremely thin.
- **Mississippi Territory records cover Alabama.** Pre-1817 records are filed under the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama. FamilySearch collections indexed under Mississippi often cover present-day Alabama for this era. Search both.
- **Federal (public-land) state.** Alabama received its land through the US federal government, not state grants. Original land entries go through the General Land Office. The BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) is therefore central for land research — a free, browsable source.
- **Territorial censuses, not federal census, are the main population tool.** Four territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama; they are held at ADAH. The 1810 federal census also covered the Mississippi Territory and includes portions of present-day Alabama. *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*
- **Creek War boundary.** The Treaty of Fort Jackson (1814) transferred a huge swath of central Alabama to the US. Families living on that land before 1814 have no US records from the earlier period; their documentation, if any, is Indigenous or missionary in nature.

---

## Record Types: What Exists, Where It's Held, and Digitization Status

### 1. Census and Census Substitutes

**What exists:**
- Territorial censuses: 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 — enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. Held at ADAH, Montgomery. *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*
- 1810 federal census: covered the Mississippi Territory, including the Alabama region.

**FamilySearch collections:**
- *Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890* — collection [2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756); 287,634 indexed records, no images. Starts at 1810 (the final territorial year).
- *Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890* — collection [1927171](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171); 198,340 indexed records, no images. Starts in 1792 and covers the Mississippi Territory period, which includes the Alabama region.

**Digitization level:** Index only (name-searchable, no browse-by-image). The underlying territorial census documents are at ADAH.

---

### 2. Land Records

This is the richest and most consistently digitized record class for this period.

**Federal land patents (BLM GLO):** Alabama is a public-land state, so original patents were issued by the US General Land Office. The BLM GLO Records website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) provides a **free, searchable database with downloadable images** of the original patent documents. This is the single best online browse-and-search resource for pre-statehood Alabama land.

**Mississippi/Alabama Territorial and State Land Records (FamilySearch):** The collection *Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907* — collection [1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) — begins in 1798 (the first year of the Mississippi Territory) and runs to 1907. It contains 312,450 indexed records and 156,225 images. Because the Mississippi Territory covered the Alabama region, this collection is directly relevant for pre-statehood Alabama land research. **This is an indexed collection with images** — the best-digitized FamilySearch source for the period.

**Spanish land grants (Mobile area):** Spanish authorities issued land grants in the Mobile district that were later confirmed by US authorities. These originals are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. Physical/microfilm only outside those repositories. *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))*

**British land grants (1763–1780):** In British archives (UK National Archives, Colonial Office records); some copies at NARA.

**Digitization level:** Federal patents — **indexed + images, free online** (BLM GLO). FamilySearch territorial land collection — **indexed + images**. Spanish and British grants — **physical/microfilm only** (foreign archives or Library of Congress).

---

### 3. Tax Records

**What exists:** Territorial tax lists documented property owners and serve as a census substitute for years without a census. Tax lists for the Mississippi Territory/Alabama region exist for this period and are held at ADAH. *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*

**FamilySearch coverage:** No dedicated tax list collection for pre-statehood Alabama appeared in `collections_search`. Tax records may be included within the Alabama census substitutes index (collection 2016756) as compiled substitutes.

**Digitization level:** Primarily physical or microfilm at ADAH. FamilySearch digitization coverage for this record class is unclear from tool results — a gap to investigate directly at ADAH.

---

### 4. Militia Rolls and Military Records

**What exists:**
- Territorial militia rolls: documented able-bodied men in the Mississippi Territory. Held at ADAH. *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*
- War of 1812 / Creek War service records (1813–14): Especially rich for Alabama given the major campaigns there. Service records and pension files are at NARA.

**Online access:**
- [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized War of 1812 service records and pension files (subscription required).
- [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) holds originals; pension files are particularly valuable as they often contain family details.

**Digitization level:** War of 1812 records — **indexed + images on Fold3** (subscription). Territorial militia rolls — **primarily physical/microfilm at ADAH**.

---

### 5. Court Records

**What exists:** The Mississippi Territory had district and county courts handling civil suits, criminal cases, and administrative matters. County courts were established as counties were carved out of the territory (Madison County, for example, was created in 1808 in northern Alabama).

**FamilySearch:** *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* — collection [1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) — begins in 1799, covering the territorial period, with 245,670 indexed records and 122,835 images. This Mississippi-scope collection covers the Alabama region for the territorial era.

**Digitization level:** **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch (filed under Mississippi scope).

---

### 6. Probate Records

**What exists:** County-level probate records (wills, estate inventories, guardianships, letters of administration) began as counties were organized in the Alabama region. The earliest Alabama-area counties date from approximately 1800–1810.

**FamilySearch:** *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* — collection [1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) — begins at 1809, capturing the final decade of the territorial period, with 438,210 indexed records and 219,105 images.

**Digitization level:** **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch.

---

### 7. Marriage Records

**What exists:** County marriage registers began as counties were organized. The earliest civil marriages in the Alabama region were recorded by county clerks starting around 1800–1810. Before county organization, Mobile-area Catholic marriages appear in church registers.

**FamilySearch:** *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* — collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) — begins at 1809 with 612,345 indexed records and 306,172 images.

**Digitization level:** **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch.

---

### 8. Church Records

**What exists:**
- **Mobile Catholic registers:** The Catholic Church was the dominant institution in Mobile from the French colonial era. Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) for Mobile exist from the early 18th century. These are the main vital-records source for the Mobile area throughout the colonial and territorial periods.
- **Protestant records:** Baptist and Methodist churches began appearing in northern Alabama with Anglo-American settlement after 1800, but pre-1810 records are sparse.

**FamilySearch:** *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* — collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) — begins at 1803 with 156,789 indexed records and 78,394 images.

**Pre-1803 Mobile Catholic registers:** Not in the FamilySearch collection. Held at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Mobile), the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives, and in French and Spanish archives. Microfilm is available at the Mobile Municipal Archives. *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))*

**Digitization level:** FamilySearch collection (1803+) — **indexed + images**. Pre-1803 Mobile Catholic registers — **physical and microfilm only** (local and foreign archives).

---

### 9. Colonial Records — Mobile Area (pre-1813)

For any family in or near Mobile before 1813, three layers of colonial records may apply. These are the records most researchers overlook, and they are largely **not digitized**.

**French (1702–1763):** Census returns, land concessions, notarial records. *Held at: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.* *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))*

**British (1763–1780):** Land grants, court records, administrative correspondence. *Held at: UK National Archives (Colonial Office records); some copies at NARA.*

**Spanish (1780–1813):** Census returns, church registers, land grants, notarial records. *Held at: Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Copies at the Library of Congress.* *(Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))*

**Digitization level:** All three layers are **physical or microfilm only** outside the Library of Congress and the Mobile Municipal Archives. No FamilySearch browse volumes or indexed collections appeared in tool results for these records.

---

### 10. Newspapers

**What exists:** Territorial newspapers began appearing in the Alabama region around 1812–1815. The *Mobile Centinel* and papers published near St. Stephens (the territorial capital in Washington County) are among the earliest. Before ~1812, newspapers in present-day Alabama were essentially nonexistent.

**Online access:** [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) (Library of Congress) has some early Alabama territorial newspapers, though pre-1819 coverage is limited. [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) is another option but pre-statehood coverage is sparse.

**Digitization level:** Limited and patchy for this period.

---

## Digitized Browse-Only Volumes: The Direct Answer

You specifically asked about **digitized, browsable volumes** — image sets you can page through even without a name index.

**FamilySearch `volume_search` returned zero image volumes** tagged to pre-statehood Alabama across all searches (with and without date filters, with and without record-type filters). This is a genuine digitization gap: FamilySearch's volume browser does not surface dedicated image sets for this period and place.

**What IS online and browsable/searchable:**

|---|---|---|---|
| [BLM GLO](https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free | Yes — name searchable + image |
| FamilySearch collection [1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) | MS Territory land records, 1798– | Free | Yes — indexed + images |
| FamilySearch collection [1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) | MS Territory court records, 1799– | Free | Yes — indexed + images |
| FamilySearch collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) | AL county marriages, 1809– | Free | Yes — indexed + images |
| FamilySearch collection [1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) | AL probate records, 1809– | Free | Yes — indexed + images |
| FamilySearch collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) | AL church records, 1803– | Free | Yes — indexed + images |
| [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) | War of 1812 service/pension | Subscription | Yes — indexed + images |
| [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) | Early territorial newspapers | Free | Partial |

**Physical/microfilm only (not online):**
- ADAH: territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810), tax lists, militia rolls
- Mobile Municipal Archives: French colonial microfilm
- Archivo General de Indias: Spanish colonial originals
- ANOM (France): French colonial originals

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings for This Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **ADAH, Montgomery** | Territorial censuses, tax lists, militia rolls, court records | In-person; some digitized |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 AL collections (1803–) + 4 MS Territory collections (1798–); no pre-1819 browse volumes | Free online |
| **BLM GLO** | Federal land patents with images | Free online |

| **Fold3** | War of 1812 military records | Subscription |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** | Spanish colonial records for Mobile district | In-person; copies at LC |
| **ANOM, Aix-en-Provence** | French colonial records for Mobile | In-person; microfilm at Mobile Archives |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish/French colonial records | In-person; some digitized |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | French colonial microfilm | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Mobile** | Catholic sacramental registers (colonial–) | In-person |

---

## Summary of Genuine Gaps

- **No FamilySearch browse-only image volumes** exist for pre-statehood Alabama in the volume browser — confirmed by tool results.
- **Vital records (births, deaths):** effectively nonexistent outside Mobile Catholic registers; no civil registration requirement existed.
- **Interior Alabama families (pre-1814):** no US records for families in Creek or Cherokee territory before the Creek War.
- **Spanish and French colonial records for Mobile:** in foreign archives or on microfilm; not freely available online.
- **Tax lists and early territorial militia rolls:** primarily at ADAH, not yet widely digitized.
- **The 1798–1803 window** has the thinnest FamilySearch coverage — the earliest collections begin at 1803 (church records) and 1809–1810 (marriages, probate, census substitutes).

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Counties (1860s–1890s)
*Schuylkill · Luzerne · Carbon · Northumberland · Columbia · Lackawanna*

---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Counties covered:** Schuylkill (formed 1811 per FamilySearch place data), Luzerne, Carbon, Northumberland, Columbia, and Lackawanna — the six counties of the anthracite coal belt in northeastern and east-central Pennsylvania.
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Jim Thorpe (Carbon), Sunbury (Northumberland), Bloomsburg (Columbia), Scranton (Lackawanna).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (statehood 1787).
- **Population during period — Schuylkill County (census data confirmed by place_population tool):**
  - 1860: 89,510 | 1870: 116,428 | 1880: 129,974 | 1900: 172,927
- **Economy:** Anthracite (hard coal) mining dominated all six counties. Irish immigrant workers, many arriving via Philadelphia in the wake of the Great Famine, formed a large share of the workforce from the 1840s onward. Colliery occupations included loaders, breaker boys, mule drivers, and mine laborers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish (dominant 1840s–1860s), Welsh, English, and — growing from the 1870s onward — Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and Ukrainian immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish and later Eastern European communities), Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Presbyterian, Lutheran (German and Welsh congregations), Episcopal.
- **Key events:** Great Famine Irish immigration surge (1845–1855); Molly Maguires activities and trials (1860s–1877); formation of Lackawanna County from Luzerne (1878); Mine Workers organizing efforts (1880s–1890s); periodic mine disasters generating inquest and coroner records.

---

## Boundary changes

- **Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne County in 1878.** All records for the Scranton/Carbondale area (northern anthracite field) before 1878 were created and filed under Luzerne County. Always search Luzerne County first for Lackawanna-area ancestors before that year.
- **Schuylkill County formed 1811** (FamilySearch place dateRange: +1811). Pre-1811 records for this territory fall under its parent jurisdiction(s).
- **Columbia County formed from Northumberland County** — pre-formation records for the Columbia County area are in Northumberland County's books.
- **Carbon County** formed 1843; pre-1843 records fall under Northampton and Monroe counties.
- Five of the six counties (all except Schuylkill) did not resolve to county level in the FamilySearch place tools — Schuylkill is the only county with confirmed county-level volume data below; treat those volumes as representative of the type of holdings to expect across the region, and search each county's holdings separately.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Pennsylvania had NO statewide vital registration during the 1860s–1890s.** The FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* ([collection 2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317)) confirms statewide death registration did not begin until 1906 — after the entire target period. No statewide birth registration existed either.
- **County-level marriages begin 1885.** FamilySearch holds *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* ([collection 1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317)): 524,189 records / 1,048,378 persons / 312,045 images — **indexed + images**, searchable by name. This is the first systematic marriage record source for the late target period.
- **Civil marriage compilations** extend further back: *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* ([collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)): 312,045 records / 156,023 images — **indexed + images**. *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* ([collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)): 198,765 records — **indexed, no images**.
- **For births and deaths in the 1860–1895 period, church records are the primary source** (see below). No civil birth or death registration exists at any level for this window.

### Church records

The most critical substitute for civil vital records for Irish Catholic miners:

- **Diocese of Scranton** (established 1868): holds baptismal registers for Catholic parishes in the northern anthracite counties (Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon) post-1868. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- **Diocese of Harrisburg**: holds Catholic registers *pre-1868* across the entire region, and continues to hold records for Schuylkill, Northumberland, and Columbia counties throughout the whole period. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- Many coal-region Catholic parishes were established between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- **FamilySearch digitized Schuylkill County church volumes:** Image group 007936751 — 187 images, dates 1842–1895, languages **English and German**. **Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed page by page. Note: these volumes include German Lutheran and Reformed congregation records alongside Irish Catholic registers — do not skip German-language entries.
- **Access:** Diocese of Scranton Archives (Scranton, PA) for post-1868 northern counties; Diocese of Harrisburg Archives for pre-1868 records and for Schuylkill, Northumberland, and Columbia counties throughout the period.

### Census records

- **Federal census years covering the target period:** 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 are fully available and indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The **1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed** in the 1921 Commerce Department fire; only a small 1890 Union Veterans and Widows Schedule fragment survives for Pennsylvania. Compensate with triennial tax assessments (see specialized records below).
- Census records name birthplace (often just "Ireland") and can identify entire household compositions. Use mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880) to trace deaths in the year preceding enumeration — a substitute for death records.
- Note: Census collection IDs for these six counties were not returned by the volume search in the 1860–1895 window; use FamilySearch's main record-search interface and Ancestry's federal census collections directly.

### Probate and court records

- **FamilySearch state-level collection:** *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* ([collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)): 893,214 records / 446,607 images — **indexed + images** at the statewide level.
- **Schuylkill County probate volumes on FamilySearch:** Image group 007936749 — 412 images, dates 1851–1930. **Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- Probate is held at the county Orphans' Court level in Pennsylvania. Court of Common Pleas records include naturalization petitions, guardianships, and civil cases — all valuable for Irish immigrant families.

### Land records

- **Pennsylvania is a state-land state** — land grants and patents are held by the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg, not the federal BLM/GLO.
- **Schuylkill County deed volumes on FamilySearch:** Image group 007936752 — 543 images, dates 1815–1900. **Partially indexed: 22% name-indexed**; the remaining 78% must be browsed image by image. Not full-text searchable. This is the only volume among Schuylkill's five FamilySearch volumes with any name indexing.
- Physical deed books are held at each county's Recorder of Deeds office.

### Naturalization records ⭐

Among the most valuable sources for establishing Irish origins, as pre-1906 papers may name birthplace, last foreign residence, port of arrival, and arrival date.

- **Schuylkill County naturalization volumes on FamilySearch:** Image group 007936750 — 298 images, dates 1849–1915. **Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed page by page.
- Pre-1906 naturalization could be filed in any court of record; county Courts of Common Pleas were the most common venue. Check all six counties.
- Post-1906 naturalizations: NARA Philadelphia Regional Archives.

### ⭐ Coal-region specialized records (unique to the anthracite field)

These record classes exist nowhere else and are the most distinctive sources for Irish coal-mining ancestors:

**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898**
The single most important coal-region finding aid — names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Each entry records occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and — critically — **parish of origin where stated**, providing a direct genealogical link back to Ireland. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

**Company payroll ledgers and employment records**
Mining company records list worker names, nationalities, and sometimes prior residence. The **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville, PA) holds payroll ledgers for several collieries. ([Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Coal Mining Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records))

**Pennsylvania state triennial tax assessments (from 1853)**
State assessors enumerated coal-region residents every three years. Each ledger entry includes: householder name, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — the nativity field can confirm Irish birth. The 1889 assessment is the primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 census. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

**Molly Maguires records**
Active among Irish miners in Schuylkill County during the 1860s–1870s, the Molly Maguires generated **court records, trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton detective reports** naming hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families. This adversarial but genealogically rich source documents the Irish mining community in granular detail. Historical Society of Schuylkill County is the primary access point. ([Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Molly Maguires](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires))

**Mine inspection and accident reports**
Organized by colliery (not by person) — useful for confirming where an ancestor worked after identifying him through payroll or census records. Distinguished from payroll indexes, which are the direct genealogical finding aid. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records — Choosing an index](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

### Marriage records (county-level)

- **Schuylkill County marriage volumes on FamilySearch:** Image group 007936753 — 94 images, dates 1870–1910. **Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- State-level indexed county marriages begin 1885 (see Vital Records above).
- Catholic parish marriage registers cover the pre-1885 period (see Church Records).

### Military records

- The Civil War (1861–1865) falls within the target period. Irish miners from all six counties served in Pennsylvania regiments.
- Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants: NARA (Washington, DC and Philadelphia regional archives). **Civil War pension files are especially valuable** — widows' applications frequently record marriage date and place, children's names, and the soldier's birthplace.
- Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level military records and muster rolls.

### Immigration records

- **Primary port of entry for Irish immigrants to the Pennsylvania coal region: Philadelphia.** Famine-era arrivals and subsequent chain migrants reached the anthracite region overwhelmingly via Philadelphia. Passenger lists for Philadelphia arrivals are available through FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- Naturalization records typically yield more specific Irish origin information than passenger lists (see above).
- Declarations of intention (first papers) and petitions for naturalization may reference the specific Irish county, townland, or port of departure.

### Newspapers

- Local coal-region papers covered mining accidents, court proceedings (including the Molly Maguires trials), labor disputes, and Irish community events throughout the period. Obituaries and marriage notices appeared regularly.
- **Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) — published from 1825, a primary regional paper for the southern anthracite field.
- Pennsylvania newspaper archives: State Library of Pennsylvania (Harrisburg); partial digitization through Newspapers.com and the Library of Congress's *Chronicling America*.

### Tax records

- Pennsylvania state triennial assessments from 1853 (see Coal-Region Specialized Records above) are the primary tax substitute source, especially for bridging the destroyed 1890 census.
- County tax records held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### Physical repositories

| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville PA | Colliery payroll ledgers, Molly Maguires materials, local newspapers | In-person; write ahead |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg PA | Triennial tax assessments, state military records, land patents | In-person; some holdings online |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives, Scranton PA | Catholic parish registers post-1868 (Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon) | Write or in-person |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives, Harrisburg PA | Catholic registers pre-1868 (all counties) and post-1868 for Schuylkill/Northumberland/Columbia | Write or in-person |
| NARA Philadelphia Regional Archives | Federal naturalizations post-1906; federal court records | In-person / online request |
| County Courthouses (all 6 counties) | Deed books, probate files, naturalization petitions, court records | In-person / mail |
| State Library of Pennsylvania, Harrisburg PA | Newspaper archives including *Miners' Journal* | In-person; partial digitization |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Company payroll/employment records** beyond the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index — surviving colliery records held physically at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.
- **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (1853 onward)** — held at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not digitized or name-indexed online for the 1860s–1890s period.
- **Mine inspection and accident reports** — Pennsylvania State Archives; physical access only.
- **Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports** — Historical Society of Schuylkill County and court archives; not fully digitized.
- **Catholic parish registers** not yet microfilmed — many pre-1870 registers for smaller coal-region parishes are held only at the diocesan archives.
- **County coroner's inquest records** for mine accidents — individual county courthouses.

---

## Known record losses

- **1890 federal census** — almost entirely destroyed. Compensate with the 1889 triennial tax assessment and the 1880/1900 census as bookends.
- **Five of six counties did not resolve to county-level in the FamilySearch volume tool.** This is a tool-resolution gap, not necessarily a records gap — browse each county's FamilySearch holdings separately.
- No courthouse fire or flood losses for these specific six counties were returned by the survey tools. Verify with individual county historical societies before concluding any record class is absent.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898)** for any ancestor in the northern anthracite field. ~41,000 entries with occupation and sometimes parish of origin make it the most direct bridge back to Ireland. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
2. **Naturalization records are your bridge to Ireland.** Browse Schuylkill Co. vol. 007936750 (1849–1915, 298 images) image by image. Pre-1906 declarations often name the specific Irish county or port of departure.
3. **For Lackawanna-area ancestors before 1878, search Luzerne County first.** Deed books, court files, and naturalization petitions all filed under Luzerne before the 1878 county split.
4. **Diocesan archives are essential for 1860–1895 births and deaths.** With no statewide registration in this period, Catholic baptismal and burial registers are the only systematic vital record source. Diocese of Scranton for post-1868 northern counties; Diocese of Harrisburg for pre-1868 everywhere and for Schuylkill/Northumberland/Columbia throughout.
5. **The Schuylkill church volumes on FamilySearch include German-language records.** Vol. 007936751 (1842–1895) mixes German Lutheran/Reformed and Irish Catholic congregation records — do not skip entries you cannot immediately read.
6. **Use the 1889 triennial tax assessment as a 1890 census substitute.** It enumerates householders with occupation and sometimes nativity, bridging the 1880–1900 gap. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
7. **Molly Maguires records name hundreds of Irish miners in Schuylkill County.** Even if your ancestor was never charged, court records, depositions, and Pinkerton reports may document him or his associates in the 1860s–1877 period. ([Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Molly Maguires](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires))
8. **Distinguish payroll indexes from mine inspection reports.** Payroll-derived indexes name individual workers — use these first. Inspection/accident reports are organized by colliery, not by person. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
9. **Philadelphia passenger lists** (1845–1870) are the highest-value immigration source for Irish Famine-era arrivals to the coal region. Search FamilySearch and Ancestry passenger list collections filtered to Philadelphia.
10. **Civil War pension files** can supply marriage dates, children's names, and the soldier's Irish birthplace — far more biographical detail than the service record alone.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Counties (1860s–1890s)
*Schuylkill · Luzerne · Carbon · Northumberland · Columbia · Lackawanna*

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Ethnic composition:** Irish (1840s–1860s dominant), Welsh, English, then Eastern European from 1870s

## Boundary changes
- Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne County 1878 — search Luzerne for pre-1878 Scranton/Carbondale area records
