## Available record types

### Vital records
No statewide PA vital registration 1860-1895. County marriages available from 1885 (collection 1921317, indexed + images). Church records are the only birth/death source for the full period.

### Church records
- Diocese of Scranton (post-1868): northern counties (Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon)
- Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868 all counties; post-1868 Schuylkill/Northumberland/Columbia)
- FamilySearch Schuylkill church volumes: 007936751, 187 images, 1842-1895, English + German, browse-only

### Census records
- Federal census 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 available and indexed
- 1890 almost entirely destroyed — use triennial tax assessments as substitute

### Probate and court records
- PA Probate Records 1683-1994 (collection 1999196): indexed + images
- Schuylkill probate volumes: 007936749, 412 images, 1851-1930, browse-only

### Land records
- Pennsylvania is a state-land state (patents at PA State Archives)
- Schuylkill deed volumes: 007936752, 543 images, 1815-1900, 22% indexed

### Naturalization records
- Schuylkill naturalization volumes: 007936750, 298 images, 1849-1915, browse-only
- Pre-1906 papers may name Irish birthplace, last foreign residence, port of arrival

### Coal-region specialized records
**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** ~41,000 workers, occupation, wage, parish of origin
**Company payroll ledgers:** Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds colliery payrolls
**Triennial tax assessments (from 1853):** occupation + nativity, held at PA State Archives

**Mine inspection/accident reports:** organized by colliery, not by person

### Military records
- Civil War service records, pension files at NARA
- Widows' pension applications document marriage details and Irish birthplace

### Immigration records
- Philadelphia was primary port of entry for Irish coal-region immigrants
- Passenger lists on FamilySearch and Ancestry (Philadelphia collections)

### Newspapers
- Miners' Journal (Pottsville, from 1825): primary southern anthracite paper
- State Library of Pennsylvania; partial digitization on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America

## Repository guide

### Online

- Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg PA: triennial assessments, military records, land patents
- Diocese of Scranton Archives: Catholic registers post-1868 northern counties
- Diocese of Harrisburg Archives: Catholic registers pre-1868 all counties
- NARA Philadelphia: post-1906 naturalizations
- County Courthouses: deed books, probate, naturalization petitions
- State Library of Pennsylvania: newspaper archives

## Records NOT online
- Company payroll/employment records beyond the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (1853 onward)
- Mine inspection and accident reports
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports (not fully digitized)
- Many pre-1870 Catholic parish registers (diocesan archives only)
- County coroner's inquest records for mine accidents

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census almost entirely destroyed — use 1889 triennial tax assessment
- No courthouse fires confirmed by survey tools for these six counties

## Research tips
1. Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index for northern field ancestors
2. Browse Schuylkill naturalization volumes (007936750) for Irish origin information
3. Search Luzerne County for Lackawanna-area ancestors before 1878
4. Contact diocesan archives for 1860-1895 births and deaths
5. Use 1889 triennial tax assessment as 1890 census substitute
6. Check Molly Maguires records for Schuylkill Co. Irish miners 1860s-1877
7. Search Philadelphia passenger lists for Famine-era arrivals (1845-1870)

quirks: Lackawanna County was not formed until 1878 — all records for the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 were filed under Luzerne County; search Luzerne first for pre-1878 ancestors in the northern anthracite field.

Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration for births or deaths during the 1860-1895 period; church records (Catholic diocesan archives) are the primary substitute for births and deaths across the entire window.
County marriages become available from 1885 (collection 1921317); before 1885 only church marriage registers survive.
Catholic parish records pre-1868 are held by the Diocese of Harrisburg for all six counties; post-1868 northern county records (Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon) transfer to the Diocese of Scranton.
Schuylkill County church volumes on FamilySearch (image group 007936751, 1842-1895) include German-language Lutheran and Reformed records alongside English-language Catholic registers.
All five Schuylkill County FamilySearch volumes (naturalization, church, probate, deed, marriage) are browse-only images except deed records, which are 22% name-indexed.

The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855-1898) names ~41,000 colliery workers with occupation, wage rate, and sometimes parish of origin — the most direct Irish-origin finding aid for coal-region miners.

Pennsylvania state triennial tax assessments (from 1853) list householder, occupation, and sometimes nativity — the primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census; held at Pennsylvania State Archives, not digitized online.
Molly Maguires court records, depositions, and Pinkerton detective reports (1860s-1877) name hundreds of Irish-born miners in Schuylkill County — held at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.
Distinguish payroll-derived indexes (name individual workers — use first) from mine inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person).
Columbia County formed from Northumberland County — pre-formation records for the Columbia County area are in Northumberland County books.
Carbon County formed 1843 from Northampton and Monroe counties — pre-1843 records fall under those parent counties.
Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Irish immigrants to the anthracite coal region; search Philadelphia passenger list collections for Famine-era arrivals (1845-1870).

Five of the six counties (all except Schuylkill) did not resolve to county level in the FamilySearch place tools — volume search results above are Schuylkill-specific; run separate searches for each of the remaining five counties.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Counties (1860s–1890s)
*Schuylkill · Luzerne · Carbon · Northumberland · Columbia · Lackawanna*

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Counties covered:** Schuylkill (formed 1811), Luzerne, Carbon, Northumberland, Columbia, and Lackawanna
- **Population during period — Schuylkill County:** 1860: 89,510 | 1870: 116,428 | 1880: 129,974 | 1900: 172,927
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; Irish immigrant workers dominant from 1840s
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish (1840s–1860s dominant), Welsh, English, then Eastern European from 1870s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Episcopal

## Boundary changes
- Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne County 1878 — search Luzerne for pre-1878 Scranton/Carbondale area records
- Schuylkill formed 1811; Columbia from Northumberland; Carbon from Northampton and Monroe (1843)

## Available record types

### Vital records
No statewide PA vital registration 1860-1895. County marriages available from 1885 (collection 1921317, indexed + images). Church records are the only birth/death source for the full period.

### Church records
- Diocese of Scranton (post-1868): northern counties (Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon)
- Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868 all counties; post-1868 Schuylkill/Northumberland/Columbia)
- FamilySearch Schuylkill church volumes: 007936751, 187 images, 1842-1895, English + German, browse-only

### Census records
- Federal census 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 available and indexed
- 1890 almost entirely destroyed — use triennial tax assessments as substitute

### Probate and court records
- PA Probate Records 1683-1994 (collection 1999196): indexed + images
- Schuylkill probate volumes: 007936749, 412 images, 1851-1930, browse-only

### Land records
- Pennsylvania is a state-land state (patents at PA State Archives)
- Schuylkill deed volumes: 007936752, 543 images, 1815-1900, 22% indexed

### Naturalization records
- Schuylkill naturalization volumes: 007936750, 298 images, 1849-1915, browse-only
- Pre-1906 papers may name Irish birthplace, last foreign residence, port of arrival

### Coal-region specialized records
**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** ~41,000 workers, occupation, wage, parish of origin
**Company payroll ledgers:** Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds colliery payrolls
**Triennial tax assessments (from 1853):** occupation + nativity, held at PA State Archives
**Molly Maguires records:** court records, depositions, Pinkerton reports naming hundreds of Irish miners
**Mine inspection/accident reports:** organized by colliery, not by person

### Military records
- Civil War service records, pension files at NARA
- Widows' pension applications document marriage details and Irish birthplace

### Immigration records
- Philadelphia was primary port of entry for Irish coal-region immigrants
- Passenger lists on FamilySearch and Ancestry (Philadelphia collections)

### Newspapers
- Miners' Journal (Pottsville, from 1825): primary southern anthracite paper
- State Library of Pennsylvania; partial digitization on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America

## Repository guide

### Online
- FamilySearch: PA County Marriages 1885-1950 (1921317), PA Probate 1683-1994 (1999196), PA Civil Marriages (1571957), PA Compiled Marriages (1502909); Schuylkill volumes 007936749-007936753
- Ancestry: Federal census 1860-1900 (all counties)

### Physical
- Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville PA: colliery payrolls, Molly Maguires materials
- Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg PA: triennial assessments, military records, land patents
- Diocese of Scranton Archives: Catholic registers post-1868 northern counties
- Diocese of Harrisburg Archives: Catholic registers pre-1868 all counties
- NARA Philadelphia: post-1906 naturalizations
- County Courthouses: deed books, probate, naturalization petitions
- State Library of Pennsylvania: newspaper archives

## Records NOT online
- Company payroll/employment records beyond the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (1853 onward)
- Mine inspection and accident reports
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports (not fully digitized)
- Many pre-1870 Catholic parish registers (diocesan archives only)
- County coroner's inquest records for mine accidents

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census almost entirely destroyed — use 1889 triennial tax assessment
- No courthouse fires confirmed by survey tools for these six counties

## Research tips
1. Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index for northern field ancestors
2. Browse Schuylkill naturalization volumes (007936750) for Irish origin information
3. Search Luzerne County for Lackawanna-area ancestors before 1878
4. Contact diocesan archives for 1860-1895 births and deaths
5. Use 1889 triennial tax assessment as 1890 census substitute
6. Check Molly Maguires records for Schuylkill Co. Irish miners 1860s-1877
7. Search Philadelphia passenger lists for Famine-era arrivals (1845-1870)
8. Civil War pension files often supply Irish birthplace and family details

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1749–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during target period:** Not a state. Vermont existed as contested territory (1749–1777) then as the **Republic of Vermont** (1777–1791) before admission as the 14th U.S. state on **March 4, 1791**.
- **Administrative center:** No single colonial capital. The Vermont Republic held its General Assembly in various towns; **Westminster** and later **Windsor** served as early meeting places. Montpelier became the state capital only in 1805.
- **Parent jurisdictions (contested):** The territory was simultaneously claimed by **New Hampshire** (which issued land grants from 1749) and **New York** (which claimed authority from 1764 and issued its own competing patents). Neither colony/state successfully administered the area in practice after 1770.
- **Population during period:** No formal census was taken during the Republic years. Vermont's 1791 population in the first federal census was approximately **85,000**. Settlement accelerated sharply after 1760 when the French and Indian War ended.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, timber, potash and pearl ash production, grist- and sawmilling. Lake Champlain served as the main corridor for trade northward into Canada and southward into New York.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-speaking settlers from southern New England — principally Connecticut and Massachusetts — who came north following the NH Grants. Smaller numbers from New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and New York. French Canadians were present in the Champlain Valley and northwestern towns. A small number of Abenaki remained in the region.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant among New England migrants), Baptist, Presbyterian, and a scattering of Methodist, Quaker, and Episcopal congregations. Few formal church buildings existed in the earliest settlement years; many congregations initially met in homes or taverns.
- **Key historical events:** New Hampshire Grants controversy (1749–1777); Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York (1770s); Vermont Declaration of Independence (January 15, 1777); Vermont Constitution (July 1777, the first to prohibit adult slavery); Revolutionary War (Vermont units fought at Ticonderoga, Hubbardton, Bennington, and Saratoga); Republic period and failed statehood negotiations (1777–1791).

---

## Boundary changes and jurisdictional complexity

This is the single most important research challenge for this period. **Three overlapping jurisdictional claims produced three separate record streams** — and your ancestor may appear in any of them:

1. **New Hampshire Grants era (1749–1764):** Governor Benning Wentworth issued 138 township grants west of the Connecticut River. Settlers holding NH grants appear in **New Hampshire colonial records**, held at the New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management (Concord, NH). The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**, prepared under New York colonial authority, enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of NH grants that New York refused to recognize — this is the earliest systematic resident list for the territory. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*

2. **New York authority era (1764–1777):** The British Privy Council ruled in 1764 that the Connecticut River was the boundary between NH and NY, placing Vermont under New York. New York issued its own competing patents and kept records of Vermont territory in **New York colonial records** (New York State Archives, Albany).

3. **Vermont Republic era (1777–1791):** Vermont established its own civil institutions — courts, town governments, probate districts — and created records independently of both NH and NY. These records are the primary source for most genealogical purposes in this period. The Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) is the main repository.

**Quirk:** A settler arriving in the 1750s or 1760s may hold an NH grant *and* appear in NY colonial records under a competing patent for the same land — and then appear in Vermont Republic records after 1777. All three trails may need to be searched.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date (town level):** Vermont's 1777 Constitution established town governments, and some towns began recording births, marriages, and deaths from the late 1770s. Coverage is **uneven** — some towns have records starting in the 1770s; others have gaps well into the 1800s. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **Start date (statewide):** Statewide civil registration did not begin until **1857**. Do not expect a uniform statewide series for the pre-1791 period. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **Where held:** Individual **town clerk offices** are the primary repositories. Access requires contacting each town directly. The Vermont State Archives holds some early vitals collections. FamilySearch has microfilmed a number of town vital records volumes.
- **Digitization level:** Varies sharply by town. Some volumes are available on FamilySearch as **browse-only images** (not name-indexed); others remain **physical only** at the town clerk office.
- **Gaps:** Many towns founded in the 1770s–1780s have no surviving vital records for that first decade. Fires and poor storage have damaged some volumes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below), family bibles, gravestone inscriptions, probate records listing family members and ages, and 19th-century town histories that reprint early vital statistics.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (most common in this period), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, and Episcopal. Anglican/Episcopal congregations were stronger in the Champlain Valley; Quaker meetings existed in a few southwestern towns.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (called "christenings" in some registers), marriages, deaths/burials, and membership lists (useful for placing people in time and location).
- **Where held:** Early Vermont church registers are scattered. The **Vermont Historical Society** (Barre) holds transcriptions and some originals. Individual denominational archives — particularly **Congregational/United Church of Christ archives** — hold regional registers. Some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical only** or **browse-only microfilm**. Not systematically indexed online.
- **Important note:** For the earliest settlements (1760s–mid-1770s), many communities had no organized congregation. Look to the **home congregation in the sending community** (Connecticut, Massachusetts) for baptism and marriage records of settlers who left before establishing a Vermont church.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The **1790 federal census** is the first and covers Vermont just before statehood (Vermont was included even though it became a state only in March 1791 — the census was taken throughout 1790–1791). It lists heads of household with household member counts by age/sex category. **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **No colonial census:** Neither New Hampshire nor New York conducted a formal census of the Vermont territory during the colonial period.
- **No Vermont Republic census:** The Vermont Republic did not conduct a population census.
- **Substitute enumerations:** The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (~1,800 grantees) functions as the closest pre-census population list for the territory. Tax lists and early town meeting records can substitute for the pre-1790 period (see Tax Records below).
- **Mortality schedules:** Begin only with the 1850 census — outside this target period.

### Probate and court records
- **Probate:** Vermont established **probate districts** in **1778**, one of the first civil institutions organized by the Republic. Early probate records (wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships) date from the late 1770s. These records are filed at the **county probate court** in each Vermont county; some of the earliest counties were Bennington, Chittenden, Orange, Rutland, Washington, and Windham — all formed 1778–1781.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (physical) and the Vermont State Archives. Some volumes have been microfilmed by FamilySearch and are available as **browse-only images**.
- **Court records:** The Vermont Supreme Court was established in 1779. County courts heard civil and criminal matters. Early court records are at the **Vermont State Archives** and county courthouses.
- **Value:** Probate records for this period are particularly valuable because they often name children, spouses, and neighbors — filling in vital-record gaps. Inventories describe occupations and economic circumstances.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (not the federal rectangular survey, which did not apply to Vermont as a state-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Vermont is a **state-land state** — grants and patents were issued by colonial governments (NH and NY) and then by the Vermont Republic itself, not by the federal General Land Office.
- **Types and date ranges:**
  - *New Hampshire grants* (1749–1764): Wentworth township grants, held at the **New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management**.
  - *New York patents* (1764–1777): Competing patents issued by NY colonial authorities, held at the **New York State Archives** (Albany).
  - *Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule*: ~1,800 grantees enumerated under NY authority; noted on the FamilySearch Wiki as the earliest systematic resident list. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
  - *Vermont Republic town proprietors' records* (1777–1791): Each town had a proprietors' body that allocated land within the grant. Proprietors' records (meetings, lotting records) are among the most genealogically rich sources for early Vermont. Some survive in town clerk offices or at the Vermont Historical Society.
  - *Town land records / deeds* (from ~1778 onward): Deed books recorded at the **town clerk** level (Vermont records deeds at the town level, not the county level — a critical difference from most other states).
- **Digitization level:** Town deed books on FamilySearch are **browse-only images** for early volumes; some are not yet digitized (**physical only**). NH and NY colonial grants are largely **physical only** or microfilm.
- **Critical quirk:** Vermont records deeds at the **town** level, not the county level. You must identify the specific town your ancestor lived in to locate their deed. Searching at the county level will find nothing.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:**
  - *French and Indian War* (1754–1763): Pre-settlement for most of Vermont; some NH and NY rangers operated in the region. Look in NH and NY colonial records.
  - *Revolutionary War* (1775–1783): Vermont contributed heavily — the **Green Mountain Boys**, Vermont militia units, and Vermont-raised Continental Army regiments (1st–4th Vermont Regiments). The Battle of Bennington (August 1777) and the capture of Fort Ticonderoga involved Vermont forces prominently.
- **Record types:**
  - *Revolutionary War service records* and *pension/bounty land warrant files*: Held at **NARA** (Washington, DC / National Personnel Records Center); many are digitized on **Fold3** (subscription). Service records are indexed; pension files contain the richest biographical detail (ages, family names, residences, sworn testimony).
  - *Vermont State Papers*: Published multi-volume series covering 1777–1791, including muster rolls, pay vouchers, and military correspondence. Held at the Vermont State Archives and many research libraries.
  - *Vermont militia records*: Some at the Vermont State Archives and the Vermont Historical Society.
- **Digitization level:** NARA Revolutionary War service records — **indexed + images** on Fold3 (subscription) and partially on FamilySearch (free). Pension files — **indexed + images** on Fold3. Vermont State Papers — **physical + some digitized volumes** at the Vermont State Archives website.

### Cemetery records
- **Early cemeteries:** Town burial grounds (often called "old burying grounds") were established as towns were settled. The oldest date from the late 1760s–1770s. Some are private family plots on farm land, poorly documented.
- **Online coverage:** **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) and **BillionGraves** have volunteer-transcribed coverage for many Vermont cemeteries, including early ones, though pre-1800 stones are frequently weathered and transcriptions may be incomplete or absent. FS curated FindAGrave as a resource for Vermont.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they exist, are at town offices. The Vermont Old Cemetery Association has documented many early burial grounds.
- **Note:** Gravestone inscriptions for this period are a primary source for birth, death, and family relationships when church and civil records are absent.

### Newspaper records
- **Earliest Vermont papers:** The *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington, est. 1781) and the *Vermont Journal* (Windsor, est. 1783) are among the earliest papers. Most Vermont towns had no local paper before statehood.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (probate, land transactions), death notices (rare in this period), marriage announcements (occasional), political and military news (valuable for placing an ancestor in context).
- **Where held:** The **Vermont Historical Society** holds microfilm collections. Some early Vermont newspapers are digitized through **Newspapers.com** (subscription) and the **Chronicling America** project (free, Library of Congress), though pre-1791 coverage on Chronicling America is limited.
- **Digitization level:** Patchy. Most pre-1791 Vermont papers are **browse-only microfilm** or **physical only**.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Most Vermont settlers in this period were internal migrants from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island), not transatlantic immigrants.
- **Relevant ports:** Boston, New Haven, Providence, and Newport handled transatlantic arrivals for New England. Settlers arriving via the Champlain Valley corridor from Canada came through no formal port of entry.
- **Record types:** Pre-1790 passenger lists are sparse and inconsistent. Look for the ancestor's origin in sending-community records (Connecticut or Massachusetts town vital records, church registers, land records) rather than immigration manifests.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable for most Vermont settlers, who were British subjects before 1776 and American citizens after. French Canadian neighbors who crossed into Vermont would be found in Vermont naturalization records (post-1791) if they formalized citizenship.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Vermont conducted property valuations (grand lists) and poll tax lists from the late 1770s onward. These function as a pre-census population list — a man who does not appear in the 1790 census but is known to have lived in a town can often be found in the town's grand list from 1778–1789.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices (original grand lists) and the Vermont State Archives (some consolidated series). Some have been published or transcribed by genealogical societies.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical only** or **browse-only microfilm**.
- **Substitute value:** Grand lists cover every taxable male, including those who do not appear in any vital record. They are one of the most reliable pre-census sources for the Vermont Republic period.

### Other record types
- **Vermont State Papers (1777–1791):** A published multi-volume series edited by E.P. Walton (19th century) and ongoing supplements. Includes General Assembly proceedings, Governor and Council records, land grants, military records, petitions, and correspondence. Widely available in research libraries and partially digitized. An essential source for any ancestor involved in Vermont's early civil affairs.
- **Town proprietors' records:** Meetings and votes of the original town proprietors (the group holding the township grant) recorded allocations, roads, and mills. Some survive in town clerk offices, others at the Vermont Historical Society. **19th-century town histories** (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **Vermont Constitution and early laws:** The Vermont Constitution of 1777 and early statutes are published and digitized; they establish which civil records were required and when — essential for understanding record-creation context.
- **DAR and genealogical society transcriptions:** The Vermont Daughters of the American Revolution chapters transcribed many early vital, cemetery, and church records in the early 20th century. These transcriptions (held at the Vermont Historical Society and DAR library) may be the only surviving copy of records since lost.

## Known record losses

- **No systematic courthouse destruction** comparable to Southern "burned counties" is documented for Vermont's early period.
- **Uneven early survival:** Many towns simply did not record vital events in their first years of existence. The absence of a record in this period is not evidence the event did not occur — it reflects the incompleteness of early recording, not destruction.
- **NH and NY competing-claim records:** Records in New Hampshire and New York that pertain to Vermont were sometimes separated, microfilmed incompletely, or held in administrative series not organized by subject/person — they require knowledge of the issuing authority to locate.

## Research tips

1. **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is your first-stop ancestor list.** If your ancestor (or their father) was among the approximately 1,800 grantees of NH grants that New York refused to recognize, they appear in this record — the earliest systematic enumeration of Vermont residents. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*

2. **Always start with the 1790 federal census.** Vermont is fully covered and the records are indexed. Use it to establish a household and then work backward using land, probate, and town records.

3. **Identify the specific town, not just the county.** Vermont recorded deeds, vital records, and grand lists at the **town level**, not the county level. A county-level search will not find these records. Confirm which town your ancestor lived in before searching.

4. **Search three jurisdictions for land records.** For any pre-1777 land transaction, search New Hampshire (Wentworth grants), New York (competing patents), and Vermont Republic (post-1777 re-grants and confirmations). A single piece of land may appear in all three. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*

5. **Town histories can be a breakthrough source.** 19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise very difficult to access. Many are available through Google Books, HathiTrust, or the Vermont Historical Society. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*

6. **Search sending-community records in parallel.** Most Vermont settlers came from Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island. These states had **town-level vital registration dating from the 17th century** — birth, marriage, and death records for your ancestor's early life will be in their origin town, not in Vermont. Work the Connecticut or Massachusetts record set alongside the Vermont one.

7. **Revolutionary War pension files are among the richest biographical sources for this period.** Pensioners gave sworn testimony about their birth, parentage, service, and family. Many Vermont men applied for pensions in the 1820s–1840s. Search by name on Fold3 (subscription) or through NARA's online catalog.

8. **The Vermont grand lists substitute for a pre-census population count.** Search grand lists for the town in question for every year between 1778 and 1789 to track when your ancestor appears and disappears — indicating arrival, departure, or death.

9. **Northern Vermont / Champlain Valley researchers:** Check Quebec and Lower Canada records for French Canadian neighbors and mixed families. The National Archives of Canada and Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec (BAnQ) hold parish registers that may name Vermont-adjacent families.

10. **Adjoining jurisdictions matter.** Vermont borders New Hampshire to the east (across the Connecticut River), New York to the west, Massachusetts to the south, and Lower Canada to the north. Families near these borders generated records on both sides. For the New Hampshire side, the Connecticut River valley towns of both states were closely connected; check NH town records (Cheshire and Grafton Counties, NH) for families in eastern Vermont. For the New York side, check Rensselaer, Washington, and Clinton Counties, NY for western Vermont families.

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |

| **Status during target period** | Contested territory (1749–1777), then independent **Republic of Vermont** (1777–1791), admitted as 14th U.S. state March 4, 1791 |
| **Administrative center** | No single capital; Vermont Republic General Assembly met in various towns (Windsor, Westminster) |
| **Parent jurisdictions (contested)** | New Hampshire (grants, 1749–1764) and New York (claimed authority, 1764–1777) — neither effectively governed the territory after 1770 |
| **Population** | ~85,000 in the 1791 census; no formal count during the Republic years |
| **Economy** | Subsistence farming, timber, potash/pearl ash production, grist- and sawmilling; Lake Champlain the main trade corridor |
| **Settlers' origins** | Predominantly English-speaking settlers from Connecticut and Massachusetts; smaller numbers from NH, Rhode Island, and NY; French Canadians in the Champlain Valley and northwest |
| **Religion** | Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Episcopal — few formal church buildings in earliest settlement years |
| **Key events** | NH Grants controversy (1749–1777); Green Mountain Boys resistance to NY (1770s); Vermont Declaration of Independence (Jan. 15, 1777); Vermont Constitution (July 1777, first to prohibit adult slavery); Revolutionary War (Bennington, Ticonderoga, Hubbardton, Saratoga) |

## Boundary changes and jurisdictional complexity

This is the central research challenge for this period. **Three overlapping claims produced three separate record streams** — your ancestor may appear in any or all of them:

| Era | Jurisdiction | Records held at |
|---|---|---|
| 1749–1764 | New Hampshire (Wentworth grants) | NH Division of Archives and Records Management, Concord NH |
| 1764–1777 | New York colonial authority (competing patents) | New York State Archives, Albany NY |
| 1777–1791 | Republic of Vermont (own courts, town governments, probate) | Vermont State Archives, Montpelier VT; town clerk offices |

The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**, prepared under New York colonial authority, enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of NH grants that NY refused to recognize — the earliest systematic resident list for the territory, and the closest thing to a colonial-era census for Vermont. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*

> **Key quirk:** A settler arriving in the 1750s–1760s may hold an NH grant, appear in NY colonial records under a competing patent for the same land, and then appear in Vermont Republic records after 1777. All three trails may need to be searched.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Town-level records:** Some Vermont towns began recording births, marriages, and deaths from the **late 1770s**, after the Republic established town governments in 1777. Survival is **very uneven** — some towns have records back to the 1770s; others have gaps well into the 1800s. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **Statewide registration:** Did not begin until **1857**. There is no uniform statewide series for the pre-1791 period. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **Where held:** Individual **town clerk offices** (primary — must contact each town directly). Vermont State Archives holds some early collections. FamilySearch has microfilmed a number of town vital record volumes.
- **Digitization level:** Varies by town. Some volumes are **browse-only images** on FamilySearch; others remain **physical only** at the town clerk office.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family bibles, gravestone inscriptions, probate records (which often list children and ages), and 19th-century town histories that reprint early vital statistics.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (most common in this period), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, deaths/burials, membership lists.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society (Barre) holds transcriptions and some originals. Congregational/UCC denominational archives hold regional registers. Some volumes microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical only** or **browse-only microfilm** — not systematically name-indexed online.
- **Important note for earliest settlements (1760s–mid-1770s):** Many communities had no organized congregation yet. Look to the **home congregation in the sending community** (Connecticut, Massachusetts) for baptism and marriage records predating the Vermont church.

### Census records
- **1790 federal census:** The first federal census covers Vermont and is the prime starting point. Lists heads of household with household counts by age/sex. **Indexed + images** — free on FamilySearch, subscription on Ancestry.
- **No colonial or Republic-era census:** Neither NH, NY, nor the Vermont Republic conducted a population census of this territory.
- **Substitute enumerations:** Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (~1,800 grantees); Vermont grand lists (tax valuations) from the late 1770s onward — together these are the closest pre-census population lists available.

### Probate and court records
- **Probate districts established 1778** — one of the Vermont Republic's first civil institutions. Early records (wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships) date from the late 1770s.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (physical) and Vermont State Archives. Some volumes microfilmed by FamilySearch — **browse-only images**.
- **Court records:** Vermont Supreme Court established 1779; county courts also operated. Records at Vermont State Archives and county courthouses — **not digitized**.
- **Value for this period:** Probate records name children, spouses, and neighbors — critical gap-fillers when vital records are absent. Inventories document occupations and economic circumstances.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds. Vermont is a **state-land state** — grants and patents were issued by NH, NY, and the Vermont Republic, not the federal General Land Office.
- **Types and date ranges:**
  - *New Hampshire grants (1749–1764):* Wentworth township grants — NH Division of Archives and Records Management, Concord NH
  - *New York patents (1764–1777):* Competing patents — New York State Archives, Albany NY
  - *Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:* ~1,800 grantees enumerated under NY authority *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
  - *Vermont Republic town proprietors' records (1777–1791):* Meetings and lotting records of the original town proprietors — town clerk offices and Vermont Historical Society
  - *Town deed books (from ~1778 onward):* Recorded at the **town level**, not the county level
- **Digitization level:** Early town deed books on FamilySearch are **browse-only images** for early volumes; some not yet digitized (**physical only**). NH and NY colonial grants largely **physical only** or microfilm.
- **⚠️ Critical quirk:** Vermont records deeds at the **town level**, not the county level. A county-level search will find nothing. You must first identify the specific town.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (look in NH/NY colonial records); Revolutionary War (1775–1783) — Green Mountain Boys, Vermont militia, Vermont Continental Army regiments (1st–4th Vermont Regiments). Battles of Bennington (Aug. 1777), Ticonderoga, Hubbardton, Saratoga.
- **Record types and access:**
  - *Revolutionary War service records and pension/bounty land warrant files:* NARA, Washington DC — **indexed + images** on Fold3 (subscription); some on FamilySearch (free)
  - *Vermont State Papers (1777–1791):* Published multi-volume series including muster rolls, pay vouchers, military correspondence — Vermont State Archives and research libraries
  - *Vermont militia records:* Vermont State Archives and Vermont Historical Society — **physical only**
- **Pension files** are among the richest biographical sources for this period: pensioners gave sworn testimony about birth, parentage, service, and family. Many Vermont men applied in the 1820s–1840s.

### Cemetery records
- **Early cemeteries:** Town burial grounds dating from the late 1760s–1770s. Some are private family farm plots, poorly documented.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) and BillionGraves — volunteer-transcribed; pre-1800 stones are frequently weathered and transcriptions may be incomplete. FamilySearch's curated external links include FindAGrave for Vermont.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at town offices; Vermont Old Cemetery Association has documented many early burial grounds.

### Newspaper records
- **Earliest Vermont papers:** *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington, est. 1781); *Vermont Journal* (Windsor, est. 1783). Most Vermont towns had no local paper before statehood.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society microfilm collections. Some early issues on Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress) — pre-1791 digital coverage is limited.
- **Digitization level:** Most pre-1791 Vermont papers are **browse-only microfilm** or **physical only**.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Most Vermont settlers in this period were internal migrants from southern New England — not transatlantic immigrants. There are no formal immigration manifests to search.
- **Strategy:** Look for the ancestor's origin in sending-community records (Connecticut or Massachusetts town vital records, church registers, land records) rather than arrival manifests.
- **French Canadian border:** Settlers crossing from Canada into northern Vermont appear in Quebec parish registers (Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec — BAnQ) rather than U.S. immigration records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Vermont grand lists (property valuations) and poll tax lists from the late 1770s onward — the primary substitute for a pre-1790 census.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices (original grand lists); Vermont State Archives (some consolidated series). Some transcribed by genealogical societies.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical only** or **browse-only microfilm**.
- **Value:** Grand lists cover every taxable male. Searching every year from 1778 to 1789 tracks when your ancestor appears or disappears — indicating arrival, departure, or death.

### Other record types
- **Vermont State Papers (1777–1791):** Essential for any ancestor involved in Vermont's early civil affairs — General Assembly proceedings, Governor and Council records, land grants, military records, petitions and correspondence. Published volumes widely available in research libraries; Vermont State Archives website has some digitized material.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1749–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during target period:** Not a state. Vermont existed as contested territory (1749–1777) then as the **Republic of Vermont** (1777–1791) before admission as the 14th U.S. state on **March 4, 1791**.
- **Administrative center:** No single colonial capital. The Vermont Republic held its General Assembly in various towns; Windsor and Westminster served as early meeting places.
- **Parent jurisdictions (contested):** The territory was simultaneously claimed by **New Hampshire** (which issued land grants from 1749) and **New York** (which claimed authority from 1764 and issued its own competing patents). Neither colony/state successfully administered the area in practice after 1770.
- **Population during period:** No formal census during the Republic years. Vermont's 1791 population in the first federal census was approximately **85,000**. Settlement accelerated sharply after 1760.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, timber, potash and pearl ash production, grist- and sawmilling. Lake Champlain served as the main corridor for trade northward into Canada and southward into New York.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-speaking settlers from Connecticut and Massachusetts, with smaller numbers from New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and New York. French Canadians present in the Champlain Valley and northwestern towns.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, and Episcopal. Few formal church buildings in earliest settlement years.
- **Key historical events:** New Hampshire Grants controversy (1749–1777); Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York (1770s); Vermont Declaration of Independence (January 15, 1777); Vermont Constitution (July 1777); Revolutionary War (Bennington, Ticonderoga, Hubbardton, Saratoga); Republic period (1777–1791).

---

## Boundary changes and jurisdictional complexity

This is the single most important research challenge for this period. **Three overlapping jurisdictional claims produced three separate record streams:**

1. **New Hampshire Grants era (1749–1764):** Governor Benning Wentworth issued 138 township grants west of the Connecticut River. The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (prepared under New York colonial authority) enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of NH grants that New York refused to recognize — the earliest systematic resident list for the territory. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
2. **New York authority era (1764–1777):** The British Privy Council ruled Vermont was under New York. New York issued competing patents; records held at the New York State Archives (Albany).
3. **Vermont Republic era (1777–1791):** Vermont established its own courts, town governments, and probate districts. These records (at the Vermont State Archives and town clerk offices) are the primary genealogical source for this period.

**A settler arriving in the 1750s–1760s may hold an NH grant, appear in NY colonial records under a competing patent, and then appear in Vermont Republic records after 1777. All three trails may need to be searched.**

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date (town level):** Some towns began recording births, marriages, and deaths from the late 1770s. Coverage is very uneven. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **Start date (statewide):** Statewide civil registration did not begin until **1857**. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **Where held:** Individual **town clerk offices** (primary). Vermont State Archives holds some early collections. FamilySearch has microfilmed some town vital records volumes.
- **Digitization level:** Varies by town — some volumes are **browse-only images** on FamilySearch; others remain **physical only** at the town clerk office.
- **Gaps:** Many towns founded in the 1770s–1780s have no surviving vital records for that first decade.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family bibles, gravestone inscriptions, probate records, 19th-century town histories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (most common), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, deaths/burials, membership lists.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society (Barre), denominational archives, some FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical only** or **browse-only microfilm**.
- **Important note:** For earliest settlements (1760s–mid-1770s), look to the home congregation in the sending community (Connecticut, Massachusetts) for baptism and marriage records before the Vermont church was established.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The **1790 federal census** covers Vermont and is the first systematic population enumeration. Lists heads of household with household member counts. **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).
- **No colonial/Republic census:** Neither NH, NY, nor the Vermont Republic conducted a population census of this territory.
- **Substitute enumerations:** Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (~1,800 grantees); Vermont grand lists (tax valuations) from the late 1770s onward.

### Probate and court records
- **Probate:** Vermont established probate districts in **1778**. Early wills, administrations, inventories, and guardianships date from the late 1770s.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (physical) and Vermont State Archives. Some volumes microfilmed by FamilySearch (**browse-only images**).
- **Court records:** Vermont Supreme Court established 1779; county courts also heard civil and criminal matters. Records at Vermont State Archives and county courthouses.
- **Value:** Probate records name children, spouses, and neighbors — critical gap-fillers when vital records are absent.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (state-land state — not the federal rectangular survey).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Vermont is a **state-land state** — grants and patents were issued by NH, NY, and the Vermont Republic, not the federal GLO.
- **Types and date ranges:**
  - *New Hampshire grants* (1749–1764): Wentworth township grants — NH Division of Archives and Records Management (Concord, NH).
  - *New York patents* (1764–1777): Competing patents — New York State Archives (Albany, NY).
  - *Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:* ~1,800 grantees enumerated. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
  - *Vermont Republic town proprietors' records* (1777–1791): Town proprietors' meeting records allocating land — town clerk offices and Vermont Historical Society.
  - *Town deed books* (from ~1778): Recorded at the **town level** (not county level).
- **Digitization level:** Early town deed books on FamilySearch are **browse-only images**; some not yet digitized (**physical only**). NH and NY colonial grants largely **physical only** or microfilm.
- **Critical quirk:** Vermont records deeds at the **town level**, not the county level. You must identify the specific town before searching.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (look in NH/NY colonial records); Revolutionary War (1775–1783) — Green Mountain Boys, Vermont militia, Vermont Continental Army regiments (1st–4th Vermont Regiments). Battles of Bennington, Ticonderoga, Hubbardton, Saratoga.
- **Record types:**
  - *Revolutionary War service records and pension/bounty land warrant files:* NARA (Washington, DC). **Indexed + images** on Fold3 (subscription); some on FamilySearch (free).
  - *Vermont State Papers:* Published multi-volume series covering 1777–1791, including muster rolls, pay vouchers, and military correspondence. Vermont State Archives and research libraries.
  - *Vermont militia records:* Vermont State Archives and Vermont Historical Society.
- **Pension files:** Contain sworn testimony about birth, parentage, service, and family — among the richest biographical sources for this period.

### Cemetery records
- **Early cemeteries:** Town burial grounds from the late 1760s–1770s; some are private family farm plots.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) and BillionGraves — volunteer-transcribed; pre-1800 stones may be weathered/absent.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at town offices; Vermont Old Cemetery Association has documented many early burial grounds.

### Newspaper records
- **Earliest Vermont papers:** *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington, est. 1781), *Vermont Journal* (Windsor, est. 1783).
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society microfilm; some on Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress) — pre-1791 coverage is limited.
- **Digitization level:** Most pre-1791 Vermont papers are **browse-only microfilm** or **physical only**.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most Vermont settlers were internal migrants from southern New England — not transatlantic immigrants. Look for origins in sending-community records (Connecticut/Massachusetts town vitals, church registers, land records).
- **French Canadian border:** Settlers crossing from Canada into northern Vermont are found in Quebec parish registers (BAnQ) rather than U.S. immigration manifests.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Vermont grand lists (property valuations) and poll tax lists from the late 1770s onward — the closest substitute for a pre-1790 census.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices (original grand lists); Vermont State Archives (some consolidated series).
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical only** or **browse-only microfilm**.
- **Substitute value:** Grand lists cover every taxable male and can track arrival/departure/death between 1778 and 1789.

### Other record types
- **Vermont State Papers (1777–1791):** Multi-volume published series — General Assembly proceedings, Governor and Council records, land grants, military records, petitions. Widely available in research libraries.
- **Town proprietors' records:** Allocations, roads, mills — town clerk offices or Vermont Historical Society. **19th-century town histories** (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
- **DAR transcriptions:** Vermont DAR chapters transcribed early vital, cemetery, and church records in the early 20th century — may be the only surviving copy of some records. Held at Vermont Historical Society and DAR library.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for Vermont pre-1791 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule; 1790 federal census (indexed + images); some town vital records and probate volumes (browse-only images); microfilmed church records. Check FamilySearch Catalog by town. | Free |
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War service records and pension files (indexed + images) | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); some Vermont vital and land collections | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions statewide, including early burial grounds | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Some early Vermont newspapers (limited pre-1791 coverage) | Subscription |
| **NARA Online / archives.gov** | Finding aids; Revolutionary War records via Fold3/Ancestry | Free finding aids |
| **Vermont State Archives digital** | Some Vermont State Papers volumes and early records | Free |

> **Coverage note:** FamilySearch's curated external-link index returned only 6 national-level resources for Vermont in the 1750–1791 window (Ancestry census, FS Wiki vital records, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — none Vermont-specific. FamilySearch `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not available in this environment; check the FamilySearch Catalog directly for Vermont town and county holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration** (Montpelier, VT) | Vermont Republic records (1777–1791), early court records, military and land records | In-person; some by written request |
| **Vermont Historical Society** (Barre, VT) | Town histories, DAR transcriptions, church records, newspapers, manuscripts | In-person; some collections online |
| **Individual town clerk offices** (each VT town) | Town vital records, deed books, grand lists, town meeting minutes | In-person or mail request |
| **County probate courts** (county seats) | Probate files from 1778 onward | In-person or mail |
| **NH Division of Archives and Records Management** (Concord, NH) | New Hampshire grants (1749–1764), NH colonial vital and land records | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **New York State Archives** (Albany, NY) | New York colonial patents for Vermont territory (1764–1777) | In-person; digital finding aids |
| **National Archives (NARA)** (Washington, DC) | Revolutionary War service and pension records, 1790 census | In-person; many records on Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Denominational archives** (varies) | Congregational, Baptist, Methodist church registers | Contact specific regional archive |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Town vital records (pre-1800):** Mostly physical at town clerk offices or browse-only microfilm on FamilySearch. No name-indexed database covers this period comprehensively.
- **Town proprietors' records:** Nearly all physical at town clerk offices or Vermont Historical Society.
- **Vermont grand lists (tax valuations, 1778–1790):** Largely physical at town offices; some society transcriptions but not broadly digitized.
- **Early church registers:** Scattered among denominational archives, local historical societies, and private hands.
- **NH colonial land grant files:** Physical at NH State Archives; microfilm at some research libraries.
- **NY colonial patents for Vermont territory:** Physical at NY State Archives.
- **Early Vermont court records (1779–1791):** Vermont State Archives; not digitized.

---

## Known record losses

- No systematic courthouse destruction comparable to Southern 'burned counties' is documented for Vermont's early period.
- Many towns simply did not record vital events in their first years of existence. Absence of a record reflects incomplete early recording, not destruction.
- NH and NY competing-claim records for Vermont territory may be filed in administrative series not organized by person — knowing the issuing authority is required to locate them.

---

## Research tips

1. **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is your first-stop ancestor list.** If your ancestor (or their father) was among the ~1,800 NH grantees, they appear here — the earliest systematic enumeration of Vermont residents. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
2. **Always start with the 1790 federal census.** Vermont is fully covered and indexed. Use it to establish the household, then work backward.
3. **Identify the specific town, not just the county.** Vermont recorded deeds, vital records, and grand lists at the town level. A county-level search will not find them.
4. **Search three jurisdictions for any pre-1777 land transaction:** New Hampshire (Wentworth grants), New York (competing patents), and Vermont Republic (post-1777 grants and confirmations). *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
5. **Town histories can be a breakthrough source.** 19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise very difficult to access. Available through Google Books, HathiTrust, or the Vermont Historical Society. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
6. **Search sending-community records in parallel.** Most settlers came from Connecticut, Massachusetts, NH, and Rhode Island — which had town-level vital registration from the 17th century. Birth, marriage, and early-life records will be in the origin town, not in Vermont.
7. **Revolutionary War pension files are among the richest biographical sources.** Pensioners gave sworn testimony about birth, parentage, service, and family. Search by name on Fold3 (subscription) or through NARA's online catalog.
8. **Vermont grand lists substitute for a pre-census population count.** Search grand lists for every year 1778–1789 to track when your ancestor appears and disappears.
9. **Northern Vermont / Champlain Valley researchers:** Check Quebec parish registers (BAnQ) for French Canadian neighbors and mixed families near the border.
10. **Search adjoining jurisdictions.** For eastern Vermont, check Cheshire and Grafton County NH town records. For western Vermont, check Rensselaer, Washington, and Clinton County NY records.

- **DAR transcriptions:** Vermont DAR chapters transcribed early vital, cemetery, and church records in the early 20th century — may be the only surviving copy of some records. Held at Vermont Historical Society and DAR library.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for Vermont pre-1791 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule; 1790 federal census (indexed + images); some town vital records and probate volumes (browse-only images); microfilmed church records. Check FamilySearch Catalog by town. | Free |
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War service records and pension files (indexed + images) | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); some Vermont vital and land collections | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions statewide, including early burial grounds | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Some early Vermont newspapers (limited pre-1791 coverage) | Subscription |
| **NARA Online / archives.gov** | Finding aids; Revolutionary War records via Fold3/Ancestry | Free finding aids |
| **Vermont State Archives digital** | Some Vermont State Papers volumes and early records | Free |

> **Coverage note:** FamilySearch's curated external-link index returned only 6 national-level resources for Vermont in the 1750–1791 window (Ancestry census, FS Wiki vital records, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — none Vermont-specific. FamilySearch `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not available in this environment; check the FamilySearch Catalog directly for Vermont town and county holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration** (Montpelier, VT) | Vermont Republic records (1777–1791), early court records, military and land records | In-person; some by written request |
| **Vermont Historical Society** (Barre, VT) | Town histories, DAR transcriptions, church records, newspapers, manuscripts | In-person; some collections online |
| **Individual town clerk offices** (each VT town) | Town vital records, deed books, grand lists, town meeting minutes | In-person or mail request |
| **County probate courts** (county seats) | Probate files from 1778 onward | In-person or mail |
| **NH Division of Archives and Records Management** (Concord, NH) | New Hampshire grants (1749–1764), NH colonial vital and land records | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **New York State Archives** (Albany, NY) | New York colonial patents for Vermont territory (1764–1777) | In-person; digital finding aids |
| **National Archives (NARA)** (Washington, DC) | Revolutionary War service and pension records, 1790 census | In-person; many records on Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Denominational archives** (varies) | Congregational, Baptist, Methodist church registers | Contact specific regional archive |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Town vital records (pre-1800):** Mostly physical at town clerk offices or browse-only microfilm on FamilySearch. No name-indexed database covers this period comprehensively.
- **Town proprietors' records:** Nearly all physical at town clerk offices or Vermont Historical Society.
- **Vermont grand lists (tax valuations, 1778–1790):** Largely physical at town offices; some society transcriptions but not broadly digitized.
- **Early church registers:** Scattered among denominational archives, local historical societies, and private hands.
- **NH colonial land grant files:** Physical at NH State Archives; microfilm at some research libraries.
- **NY colonial patents for Vermont territory:** Physical at NY State Archives.
- **Early Vermont court records (1779–1791):** Vermont State Archives; not digitized.

---

## Known record losses

- No systematic courthouse destruction comparable to Southern 'burned counties' is documented for Vermont's early period.
- Many towns simply did not record vital events in their first years of existence. Absence of a record reflects incomplete early recording, not destruction.
- NH and NY competing-claim records for Vermont territory may be filed in administrative series not organized by person — knowing the issuing authority is required to locate them.

---

## Research tips

1. **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is your first-stop ancestor list.** If your ancestor (or their father) was among the ~1,800 NH grantees, they appear here — the earliest systematic enumeration of Vermont residents. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
2. **Always start with the 1790 federal census.** Vermont is fully covered and indexed. Use it to establish the household, then work backward.
3. **Identify the specific town, not just the county.** Vermont recorded deeds, vital records, and grand lists at the town level. A county-level search will not find them.
4. **Search three jurisdictions for any pre-1777 land transaction:** New Hampshire (Wentworth grants), New York (competing patents), and Vermont Republic (post-1777 grants and confirmations). *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
5. **Town histories can be a breakthrough source.** 19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise very difficult to access. Available through Google Books, HathiTrust, or the Vermont Historical Society. *(Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))*
6. **Search sending-community records in parallel.** Most settlers came from Connecticut, Massachusetts, NH, and Rhode Island — which had town-level vital registration from the 17th century. Birth, marriage, and early-life records will be in the origin town, not in Vermont.
7. **Revolutionary War pension files are among the richest biographical sources.** Pensioners gave sworn testimony about birth, parentage, service, and family. Search by name on Fold3 (subscription) or through NARA's online catalog.
8. **Vermont grand lists substitute for a pre-census population count.** Search grand lists for every year 1778–1789 to track when your ancestor appears and disappears.
9. **Northern Vermont / Champlain Valley researchers:** Check Quebec parish registers (BAnQ) for French Canadian neighbors and mixed families near the border.
10. **Search adjoining jurisdictions.** For eastern Vermont, check Cheshire and Grafton County NH town records. For western Vermont, check Rensselaer, Washington, and Clinton County NY records.
